hub.h1: The AI that works in your sector is not the AI being sold into it
hub.lede: Every consultancy publishes a list of AI use cases by industry. They are interchangeable because they are written from the capability end: here is what the technology can do, with no preconditions, no failure modes, no costs and no honesty about where it does not help. These ten briefings are written from the other end — from the actual week's work in each sector, the regulatory line that runs through it, and the applications that reliably disappoint. They exist for the same reason the rest of this practice does: work cannot be handed safely to a machine in a business whose work nobody has mapped, and the reading that tells you where revenue leaks is the same reading that tells you where AI belongs.

patterns.title: The first move is a count, and nobody has the number
patterns.body: Each briefing ends with a first step that costs days of one person's attention and nothing in licences, and in every sector it produces a number the organisation does not currently hold: denied dollars by reason code, your own cite-check failure rate, reviewer-to-reviewer agreement on closed alerts, distinct dated examples of a failure mode, the causes of last cycle's write-offs. The point is not diligence. A vendor's accuracy claim is meaningless without your own. If your two most experienced reviewers agree with each other seventy per cent of the time, a supplier quoting ninety-four per cent is measuring something other than correctness, and no procurement process will catch it. Whoever supplies the baseline controls the evaluation. If you do not have one, you will be using theirs — at selection, at go-live, and again when performance drifts and there is nothing to compare against.

patterns.title: Your history is a record of your interventions, not of the world
patterns.body: Prediction products fail in all ten sectors, and the usual explanation — not enough data — is wrong twice. First, volume is rarely the constraint; what is scarce is labelled examples of the specific event, dated to when it actually happened rather than when someone closed the ticket. Four instances of a failure mode, eleven completed projects, a handful of denials of that exact type. Second, and worse: the record you would train on describes what happened after your people intervened. The machine that never failed is the one the millwright caught on a walk-round. The activity that never slipped is the one the superintendent resequenced in week three. The claim that never escalated had an adjuster who picked up the phone. A model fitted to that record learns your organisation's habits, and is then scored against a future in which those habits are still running. This is why prediction demonstrates beautifully and lands badly.

patterns.title: What survives is what can be checked in seconds against a source already in front of you
patterns.body: The applications that hold up across every one of these sectors share one shape: high volume, the source document in hand, output that is an intermediate rather than a deliverable, and a person who was going to touch the item anyway. A coded claim against the chart. A re-rated freight invoice against the contract in force on the ship date. A submittal against the current set. A pre-bill narrative against the time entry behind it. The check takes seconds and the person doing it would recognise a wrong answer immediately. The inverse is the most reliable failure test available to a buyer: if verifying the output takes as long as producing it would have, the tool has not removed work, it has moved it — usually onto someone more expensive and scarcer. Applications that fail this test tend to be the ones with the best demonstrations, because a demonstration is a performance in which nobody checks.

patterns.title: The cost is the second reader, and it never becomes a transition cost
patterns.body: Licences are the smallest line in every one of these sectors. Three things cost more, and only one of them ever appears in a business case. Getting data out repeatably — an extract a different person could reproduce next year, not a one-off pull for the pilot. The verification step, which is permanent: every deployment that survives a regulator, a peer reviewer, an inspector or an opposing counsel has a named human between the output and the outside world, and that person's time is a running cost, not a ramp. And the record — the ability to reconstruct, two years later, what the system saw, what it said, who reviewed it and against which version. There is a fourth cost nobody prices at all: the reviewer has to come from somewhere. The case most often sold — fewer coders, fewer preparers, fewer analysts, smaller graduate intake — removes precisely the work that manufactures the judgement the review step depends on. No firm in any of these sectors has yet explained how it intends to produce a senior reviewer who never did the junior work.

patterns.title: Almost none of this is new law, and that is the harder position
patterns.body: The decisions AI is being pointed at were already regulated when people made them. Unfair claims settlement practice statutes have governed adjusters for fifty years. A declined credit applicant has long been entitled to the principal reasons for the decision. An agency screening on a client's behalf has duties that do not transfer to its software supplier. An audit conclusion has always needed sufficient appropriate evidence in the workpaper. The newer instruments written specifically for AI — the NAIC model bulletin now adopted by insurance departments in roughly two dozen jurisdictions, New York City's rule on automated employment decision tools — largely codify the same shape of ask: an inventory, an owner by name, documentation, the point at which a human reviews, and a date it was last tested. So the useful question is never "is AI regulated in our sector". It is: if a person made this decision, what would we have to be able to show — and can we still show it when a model produced it? Two organisations running identical models routinely end up in completely different positions, purely on documentation.

patterns.title: Adoption stalls on an unanswered money question, and meanwhile it is already happening
patterns.body: In firm after firm the technology question resolves in weeks and the pilot then sits for a year, because the real blocker is a question leadership has not written down: what happens to the hours, to the bill, to the realisation target, to the utilisation model, to the headcount plan, to the person whose bonus is tied to the volume that is about to shrink. It is a compensation and pricing decision wearing a technology costume, and no IT function can answer it. But the tools cost nothing at the point of use and are already on every phone in the building, so use does not wait for the decision. Every organisation that runs the inventory exercise — from the audit log, not by asking people — finds tools in the decision path that nobody authorised, and usually at least one already inside a notice, audit or disclosure obligation. The deadline here is not competitive. It is evidentiary: the first time this matters is when someone outside asks what was used on a specific piece of work, and "we were still evaluating" is not an answer.

universally_oversold: The assistant over all your own documents — "ask your own files". It inherits a permission model nobody has tested, answers confidently from the wrong document, and is the one application where checking the answer costs as much as finding it yourself.

Prediction trained on your own history — failures, slippage, outcomes, readmissions, demand, attrition. The events you care about are rare, badly dated, and already contaminated by the interventions that stopped them happening.

Agents that run a process end to end without a person at each step. In every one of these sectors the value is concentrated in the step where a named human takes responsibility, and that is exactly the step being removed.

The vendor's own bias audit, fairness certificate or "regulator-ready" claim, used as your compliance position. The duty sits with whoever made the decision about the customer, the claimant or the candidate, and no supplier's certificate transfers it.

Headcount reduction as the business case. The work converts into verification rather than disappearing, and the roles first proposed for cutting are the ones that produce the reviewers the verification depends on.
hub.how_to_use: Read your own sector backwards. Take the section on where AI does not help, and the preconditions that have to be true, before the list of applications — the applications only mean anything once you know what disqualifies them. Then read one sector that is not yours, because the failure modes travel between industries far better than the use cases do. Each briefing ends with a first step that takes days rather than months and costs nothing in software; it is designed to be done before the first vendor meeting, not after the contract.
hub.the_offer: Where we are asked to help, we start with the same count the briefings describe, done on your own work rather than on a reference customer's, because it is the only thing that makes the rest of the conversation honest. From there the work is usually three decisions: what is actually in scope and in what order, a written use policy that says who may use which tools on which material with what verification and what record kept, and how providers are chosen — including what the contract has to contain on audit rights, notice of model changes, training-data terms and exit, and whether a thing should be bought at all or built in-house where the data cannot leave. We take no vendor commissions, no referral fees, and we do not resell software we are paid to place, which is why the recommendation is quite often that the first project is a data or coding discipline project and nothing gets bought this year. Our prices are published, and the scope of each piece of work is fixed before it starts.

sectors.label: Healthcare
sectors.lede: Healthcare's AI opportunity is mostly not clinical. It sits in the revenue cycle and the documentation burden around it: the coder working a DNFB queue, the staffer assembling a prior authorisation packet from a chart, the A/R analyst appealing the same CARC code for the fourth month running, the clinician writing notes at nine in the evening. The line that matters is not technical but regulatory, and it is thin: a tool that drafts a note or assembles an authorisation packet is administrative, and a tool that recommends a diagnosis or decides medical necessity is something else entirely, governed by the FDA, by Section 1557, and increasingly by state statute.

where_it_helps.name: Ambient clinical documentation
where_it_helps.the_work: The clinician carries the visit in their head through clinic and writes the notes afterwards, often at home. Pyjama time. It shows up in EHR usage metrics as time in notes and after-hours minutes, and in exit interviews as the reason someone left.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Records the encounter with patient consent, transcribes it, and drafts a structured note in the specialty's format, pushed into the encounter as a draft for the clinician to edit and sign. Increasingly it also proposes orders and a coding level for the clinician to accept or reject.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Consent captured at the point of recording, which in all-party-consent states is a script and a workflow, not a checkbox. A business associate agreement that covers the audio and the transcript, with retention and training-use terms written down. Integration that writes into the encounter rather than a separate window. Specialty-specific note templates. A decision, in writing, about how long the audio is kept, because it is discoverable. And a plan for 42 CFR Part 2 material, which an undifferentiated audio feed will capture without asking.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: it removes the typing, not the thinking, and not reliably the after-hours work. The largest multi-site evaluation published to date, in JAMA in April 2026, followed roughly 1,800 clinicians across five academic medical centres and found about 16 fewer minutes of documentation time and about 13 fewer minutes in the EHR per eight hours of patient care, no significant change in EHR time outside working hours, and on the order of one additional patient every two weeks among adopters, with larger effects in primary care. Health-system and vendor case studies report considerably more, several minutes per patient; those are unblinded, self-selected and usually measured on enthusiastic early adopters. All of it is an estimate and it depends on baseline documentation burden, specialty and how disciplined the clinician was before. The consistent finding across this literature is that perceived burden and wellbeing improve more reliably than measured minutes do.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Fabricated negatives. The note says the patient denies chest pain when nobody raised chest pain. Plan items that were discussed as possibilities appear as decisions. In a room with a family member, an interpreter or a trainee, attribution slips. Note bloat drifts the E/M level upward, which is an audit exposure. Separately and more banally: licences bought and then left dormant, because use in the multi-site data was inconsistent, so per-clinician cost rises while the benefit concentrates in a minority. The clinician signs the note, so every content error becomes their error, in their record, under their licence.

where_it_helps.name: Computer-assisted coding, with narrow autonomous release
where_it_helps.the_work: Certified coders working a discharged-not-final-billed queue, assigning ICD-10-CM, ICD-10-PCS, CPT and HCPCS codes with modifiers, chasing charge capture gaps, and re-reading notes that do not support the level billed.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Reads the note, orders, results and charge data, proposes the code set with a confidence score, and routes low-confidence work to a human. In a small number of structurally simple, high-volume specialties, high-confidence encounters are released to billing without a human touch.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: A feed of the whole clinical record, not just the signed note. A confidence threshold you set from your own audit results rather than accepting the vendor's. A retained coder-reviewer function with an explicit sampling rate. Revalidation on a calendar: the ICD-10-CM and ICD-10-PCS update each 1 October, CPT each 1 January, HCPCS quarterly. And a documented audit trail showing which encounters were auto-released and why, because that is the first thing an auditor asks for.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: it removes the human touch on encounters that are structurally simple, so coder hours concentrate on the complex and the appealable. Auto-release rates are genuinely high in screening radiology, pathology and some ED facility coding; system-wide they are a fraction of that. Vendor claims of multiples of coder throughput refer to those narrow queues, not to your whole department, and are usually measured against the vendor's own adjudication. Treat any blended number as an estimate that depends entirely on case mix, and insist on seeing it decomposed by service line before it enters a business case.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Silent upcoding, which is the expensive direction, because an identified overpayment carries a 60-day return obligation and extrapolates. Confidence scores calibrated before a code-set update and quietly wrong after it. Accuracy figures computed by the vendor against its own adjudication rather than an independent coding audit. And a department that reduced reviewer headcount on the strength of a pilot run on its cleanest service line.

where_it_helps.name: Denial management: triage, root cause and grounded appeals
where_it_helps.the_work: An A/R team working a denial worklist sorted by age rather than by dollars, writing appeals from Word templates, while the same reason code recurs every month from the same payer for the same service line because nobody owns the upstream registration step that causes it.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Clusters denials by CARC/RARC reason code, payer, service line and originating department to expose where they are made. Drafts appeals grounded in the payer's own current medical policy and the specific chart evidence. Flags the denials that are administratively correct, where appealing is pure cost.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: 835 remittance data joined to 837 claims and to the chart, which is usually the real project and usually the thing that takes two quarters. Payer medical policies held with version and effective date, not scraped once. Write access into the billing worklist. Most importantly: someone with the authority to change the front-end process the analysis indicts, or the finding just accumulates.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: it shifts effort from writing appeals to preventing the denial, and stops the appeals that were always going to fail. Published estimates of the administrative cost of reworking a denied claim vary widely by methodology and setting, from roughly $25 a claim in practice-level estimates, through the mid-$40s to high-$50s in hospital surveys, to over $100 for a formal appeal; do not quote a single figure as fact, derive your own from your own cost-to-collect. The point of the range is that the money sits in the claims that never need reworking. Estimate; scales with claim volume and with how bad the current initial denial rate is.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: An appeal that cites a policy version the payer superseded in January. Models trained on historical overturn outcomes learn the payer's past behaviour rather than what the contract entitles you to. And the classic: appeal volume doubles, the overturn rate does not move, and the team is now busier.

where_it_helps.name: Prior authorisation packet assembly (provider side)
where_it_helps.the_work: By the AMA's 2024 physician survey, published in 2025, practices complete about 39 prior authorisation requests per physician per week and physicians and their staff spend about 13 hours a week on them. Staff hunting a chart for the conservative-therapy dates or the failed drug trial that a payer's criteria demand, then submitting through a portal or a fax line and watching a clock.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Reads the payer's criteria for the requested code, finds the matching evidence in the record, assembles the submission in the order the reviewer wants it, and tracks the response against the payer's decision deadline.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Current criteria per payer per code, maintained. Chart access with minimum-necessary scoping. A submission path, which today is portals and fax and from 1 January 2027 will include a FHIR Prior Authorization API for the payers covered by CMS-0057-F. A named owner for the handoff when it is denied and a peer-to-peer is needed, because that is the step a tool cannot take.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: it removes the search-and-assemble step, which is staff hours rather than physician hours, and shortens the resubmission loop caused by incomplete packets. The concentration matters more than the average: in most practices a handful of codes account for most authorisations, and that is where the whole benefit sits. It does not shorten the payer's clock, which from 1 January 2026 is regulated for the covered plan types rather than negotiable. Estimate; depends on payer mix.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Assembling a beautifully evidenced packet for a request the policy plainly excludes, which wastes the reviewer's goodwill as well as your time. Criteria that change without notice, so a template that worked in March quietly stops matching in April and nobody notices until the denial rate moves. And volume: a tool that makes submission cheap encourages submitting things that should have been discussed.

where_it_helps.name: Payer contract analysis and underpayment detection
where_it_helps.the_work: Dozens of managed-care agreements, mostly evergreen, amended repeatedly, referencing external fee schedules by version. Expected reimbursement lives in a spreadsheet one person maintains. Nobody in the organisation has read all the contracts, and the person who negotiated the oldest ones has left.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Extracts terms into a structured comparison: rate basis, lesser-of language, carve-outs, escalators, timely filing, appeal deadlines, termination notice. Flags which amendment changed which term. Supports line-level expected-versus-allowed variance so underpayments surface as a list rather than a suspicion.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Every executed contract and every amendment, which is usually the blocker and often takes longer than the analysis. The referenced fee schedules at the correct version and effective date. Line-level 835 data. And a person who can actually escalate an underpayment to a payer representative and keep escalating.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: it finds terms nobody remembered and lines paid below contract. Recovered underpayment is typically a small fraction of net revenue, but on a large base it is real money, and the larger value is walking into renegotiation knowing what is actually in force. Estimate; depends on contract count and how long it has been since anyone looked. Note that the extraction is the cheap half; the variance engine that applies a fee schedule arithmetically is the half that has to be right.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: A confident extraction from a superseded amendment. Arithmetic that reads as correct because the model summarised a fee schedule instead of applying it. Underpayment claims built on a modelled expectation the payer then disputes term by term, which costs more staff time than the recovery.

where_it_helps.name: In-basket triage and drafted patient replies
where_it_helps.the_work: Message volume that rose after results began releasing automatically and never came back down. Nurse triage pools sorting clinical urgency from refill requests from billing questions, and clinicians answering messages between patients and after clinic.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Classifies incoming messages by urgency and by who should answer, routes accordingly, and drafts a reply with chart context for a human to edit and send.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: The drafting model inside the EHR with chart context, not a general assistant in a browser tab. A hard rule that a licensed or certified health care provider reads and sends every reply, which is also what keeps a California organisation outside AB 3030's disclaimer requirement; review by a non-clinical staffer does not satisfy that exemption. Routing rules owned by the practice rather than configured once by the vendor. Measurement of message volume as well as minutes, because the two move in opposite directions.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: it removes the blank-page cost of each reply more than it removes minutes. Published evaluations find small and inconsistent time effects alongside clearer effects on perceived burden, and some find no significant reduction in time at all. Treat any vendor claim of large in-basket time savings as unproven until reproduced on your own message mix. Estimate.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Longer, warmer replies that invite more replies, so total volume rises. A draft carrying a clinical recommendation that a tired reviewer skims and sends. And the message that should have been a visit being answered efficiently instead of being escalated.

where_it_helps.name: Clinical documentation integrity queries
where_it_helps.the_work: CDI specialists reviewing charts concurrently for specificity gaps that affect the DRG or a risk-adjustment capture, then writing a physician query and waiting for a response that may never come.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Surfaces the charts with a probable documentation gap, so review time goes where there is something to find, and drafts a compliant, non-leading query for CDI to approve.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Enforced query practice standards, because a leading query is a compliance finding, not a style preference. CDI review of every generated query before it reaches a physician. A written line between documenting what the clinician observed and prompting for what pays better. And clinicians who were consulted before the queries started arriving.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: it raises the hit rate of concurrent review, so fewer charts are opened to find the same number of real gaps. Estimate; depends on current CDI coverage, which in most organisations is well under half of eligible charts, and the gain is in review yield rather than in headcount.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Diagnosis capture that reads as upcoding in a risk-adjustment data validation audit. Queries that satisfy the letter of non-leading guidance and are directive in practice. A case-mix index that rises in a quarter and cannot be defended clinically afterwards, which is precisely the pattern that draws an audit.

where_it_does_not.claim: AI that makes the medical-necessity determination, on either side of the authorisation
where_it_does_not.why_not: The determination itself is regulated to a person. California's SB 1120 requires that a denial, delay or modification based on medical necessity be made by a licensed physician or a licensed health professional competent to evaluate the specific clinical issues, and that an algorithmic tool not supplant provider decision-making. CMS has told Medicare Advantage organisations that a coverage decision must rest on the individual patient's circumstances, and that an algorithm reasoning from a larger dataset about similar patients does not satisfy that. Both bind the payer, not you; for a provider organisation their value is as leverage in an appeal, and the mirror-image warning is that a vendor promising authorisation approvals is promising something it does not control. A tool may assemble, route, pre-read and summarise. It may not decide.

where_it_does_not.claim: Automated appeal of every denial
where_it_does_not.why_not: Most denials are not clinical. They are eligibility, registration, authorisation-not-obtained, coordination of benefits, timely filing. No appeal letter fixes an authorisation that was never obtained. High-volume automated appeal raises administrative cost on both sides, and payers respond by batching their review of your batches. The metric that matters is overturn rate and days to resolution, and those move on evidence quality and on fixing the front-end process, not on letter volume. The organisations that do best here appeal fewer denials, better.

where_it_does_not.claim: Off-the-shelf clinical risk prediction: sepsis, deterioration, readmission, no-show
where_it_does_not.why_not: Two separate reasons, and both are fatal on their own. First, local performance rarely matches the published figure. The external validation of a widely deployed proprietary sepsis prediction model at an academic health system, published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021, found an area under the curve well below the vendor's documented range, missed roughly two thirds of sepsis cases, and alerted on a large fraction of hospitalised patients. Second, and more fundamental: the prediction is not the bottleneck. A readmission score changes nothing unless there is transitional-care capacity and a named person who owns the response. Buying the score is the easy tenth of the problem and the only tenth being sold.

where_it_does_not.claim: Patient-facing symptom triage, the AI front door
where_it_does_not.why_not: The FDA's clinical decision support exemption is written for software that supports a health care professional; a tool intended for patients or caregivers falls outside it entirely, and once it gives a patient a specific recommendation about their own condition whose basis the patient cannot independently review, it is plausibly a device. Providers deploying it also run into state scope-of-practice limits on who may triage, and into a liability asymmetry where every good outcome is invisible and every bad one is a deposition. The clinical argument is weaker still: the hard cases on a triage line, the atypical presentation and the patient who under-reports, are exactly the ones these systems handle worst.

where_it_does_not.claim: Point a language model at the data warehouse and ask it revenue questions
where_it_does_not.why_not: The revenue cycle data model defeats it. One encounter has many claims; one claim has many lines; one line has many remittance events; and adjustments are not one thing but contractual write-offs, denials, takebacks, patient responsibility and secondary balances, each with different meaning. Text-to-SQL over this produces answers that are confidently wrong in the specific way nobody catches, because the number is close to the one the executive expected. The people who can check the answer are the people who could have written the query.

where_it_does_not.claim: Headcount reduction in coding and A/R as the business case
where_it_does_not.why_not: The review does not disappear; it changes shape and usually requires more senior people, not fewer. You now need certified reviewers, an audit function and a governance owner you did not previously employ. Organisations that cut first and measure afterwards find themselves re-hiring at contractor rates when accuracy drifts after a code-set update, having lost the institutional knowledge that made the department work. The defensible case is throughput, backlog and DNFB days, stated as capacity you get back, not as posts you delete.

where_it_does_not.claim: Ambient documentation bought as a burnout cure, or as capacity that pays for itself
where_it_does_not.why_not: This is the most successful category in the sector and it is still oversold one step past the evidence. The multi-site work published in 2026 found the measured savings land inside the clinic day, not after it: time in the EHR outside working hours did not move significantly. Wellbeing scores improve, and that is worth buying, but a business case built on recovered after-hours time, or on a throughput gain of roughly one extra patient a fortnight scaled optimistically across a whole medical group, will not survive its own first-year review. Buy it for retention and for the quality of the note, and say so in the paper.

preconditions: A named system of record and an agreed write path. If the output cannot be written back into the EHR or the practice management system with an audit trail showing what the machine proposed and what the human changed, you have built a second inbox and made someone's day longer.

A data-flow map at the level of the individual model call, not the database. HIPAA's minimum necessary standard applies to what goes into the prompt. You must be able to say which PHI fields leave the building, to which subprocessor, under which business associate agreement, with what retention, and whether any of it may be used to train a model. Get the training-use answer in the contract, not in an email.

Someone already owns the process. If nobody can name the person who signs the note, releases the code, writes the appeal or answers the message, then there is no process for the tool to attach to, and the project will fail in a way that gets blamed on the technology.

A measured baseline, taken before anything is switched on. Initial denial rate by payer and reason code. Coder throughput and DNFB days. A/R days and overturn rate. Prior authorisation cycle time and approval rate. Note turnaround and after-hours EHR minutes. Without these, every claim about improvement afterwards is a vendor's claim.

A written administrative-versus-clinical determination for each tool, with the FDA clinical decision support analysis done and retained. The four statutory criteria are not a formality; the fourth, whether a professional can independently review the basis for a recommendation, is the one most products fail. If you cannot articulate why your tool sits outside device regulation, assume it does not.

Permanently budgeted human review, with a stated sampling rate and a written rule for what happens when accuracy drifts below threshold. Review is not a transition cost that tapers. Where it tapers, it is because someone stopped looking.

An AI inventory with a named owner per entry, and monitoring that runs after go-live. Section 1557 obliges covered entities to make reasonable efforts to identify and mitigate discrimination risk in patient care decision support tools, which is impossible if you do not know what is deployed. If you want an external reference point, the Joint Commission and CHAI guidance on the responsible use of AI in healthcare, published in September 2025, and the voluntary certification the Joint Commission announced in May 2026, describe what adequate governance is taken to look like.

A decided position on disclosure and consent, per state, before deployment rather than after. Recording consent for ambient tools. Generative AI disclaimers on patient communications in California unless a licensed or certified provider reviews them. Disclosure of AI use in a patient's care in Texas, where the medical-records and review duties under SB 1188 have applied since September 2025 and the general disclosure duty under HB 149 since January 2026. These are workflow and forms changes, and they take longer to roll out than the software does.

A segmentation answer for 42 CFR Part 2 material and for anything else carrying consent restrictions above the HIPAA baseline, decided before an undifferentiated chart or audio feed is pointed at a vendor. The Part 2 compliance date has passed; discovering the problem afterwards means unpicking a pipeline, not adding a filter.
A rollback that does not strand a queue. If the tool is turned off on a Tuesday, the work it was doing must land somewhere a human can pick it up, in priority order, without a manual export.

regulation.name: HIPAA minimum necessary standard
regulation.what_it_requires: Uses and disclosures of protected health information must be limited to the minimum necessary to accomplish the purpose, with policies identifying who needs access to what. Applied to AI, this constrains the prompt and the context window, not merely the underlying database: sending an entire longitudinal record to a model in order to draft an appeal for one claim is a question you should be able to answer. Disclosures to or requests by a provider for treatment are excepted; revenue cycle and operations uses are not.

regulation.name: Business associate agreements and subcontractor flow-down
regulation.citation: 45 CFR 164.502(e) and 45 CFR 164.504(e); security provisions at 45 CFR 164.308(b)
regulation.what_it_requires: A vendor handling PHI on your behalf is a business associate and must be under a written agreement specifying permitted uses, safeguards, subcontractor flow-down, breach reporting and return or destruction of PHI at termination. Two things routinely go wrong with AI vendors: the model provider behind the vendor is a subcontractor and must be covered, and the agreement is silent on whether your data may be used to improve the vendor's models. Silence is not a prohibition.

regulation.name: ONC/ASTP HTI-1 decision support intervention transparency
regulation.citation: 45 CFR 170.315(b)(11); Predictive Decision Support Intervention defined at 45 CFR 170.102; developers certified to the old CDS criterion at 170.315(a)(9) had to meet the new criterion by 31 December 2024
regulation.what_it_requires: Developers of certified health IT must, for predictive decision support interventions supplied with their module, make available a defined set of source attributes covering how the intervention was developed, the data used to train it, validation and performance, and known limitations, and must employ and publicly summarise intervention risk management practices across validity, reliability, robustness, fairness, intelligibility, safety, security and privacy. The obligation sits on the developer, but it is the reason a provider organisation can now demand this documentation and should refuse to deploy without it.

regulation.name: FDA oversight of software as a medical device and the clinical decision support exemption
regulation.citation: Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act section 520(o)(1)(E), 21 U.S.C. 360j(o)(1)(E); FDA final guidance, Clinical Decision Support Software, 28 September 2022
regulation.what_it_requires: Software is outside the device definition only if it meets all four statutory criteria: it does not acquire, process or analyse a medical image, an in vitro diagnostic signal, or a pattern or signal from a signal acquisition system; it displays, analyses or prints medical information; it supports or provides recommendations to a health care professional about prevention, diagnosis or treatment; and it enables that professional to independently review the basis for the recommendation so that they are not intended to rely primarily on it. The fourth criterion is where most products fail, and FDA's 2022 guidance reads it narrowly. Software intended for patients or caregivers rather than health care professionals falls outside the exemption entirely.

regulation.name: Section 1557 nondiscrimination in patient care decision support tools
regulation.citation: 45 CFR 92.210; compliance date 1 May 2025
regulation.what_it_requires: Covered entities must make reasonable efforts to identify uses of patient care decision support tools, automated or not, that employ input variables or factors measuring race, colour, national origin, sex, age or disability, and must make reasonable efforts to mitigate the resulting discrimination risk. This is an affirmative, ongoing obligation on the deploying organisation rather than the developer. Other portions of the 2024 Section 1557 rule are subject to court stays and injunctions on grounds unrelated to this provision, which as at September 2026 remains in the Code of Federal Regulations; confirm current status with counsel before relying on any summary, including this one.

regulation.name: CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule
regulation.citation: CMS-0057-F, 89 FR 8758, published 17 January 2024; operational requirements from 1 January 2026, APIs from 1 January 2027
regulation.what_it_requires: Impacted payers, including Medicare Advantage organisations, Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service and managed care, and qualified health plan issuers on the federally facilitated exchanges, must give a specific reason for a prior authorisation denial and publicly report authorisation metrics. The decision timeframes, 72 hours for expedited and seven calendar days for standard requests, apply to the government programme payers but not to QHP issuers on the exchanges, who remain under the existing claims-procedure timeframes. From 1 January 2027 impacted payers must operate FHIR-based Patient Access, Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer and Prior Authorization APIs. For provider organisations this changes the plumbing of authorisation, not the clinical judgement, and it is the reason to build authorisation workflow against a standard interface rather than around a portal.

regulation.name: Medicare Advantage coverage determination rules on algorithms
regulation.citation: 42 CFR 422.101(c), with internal coverage criteria requirements at 42 CFR 422.101(b)(6); CMS memorandum, FAQs related to coverage criteria and utilization management requirements in CMS final rule CMS-4201-F, 6 February 2024
regulation.what_it_requires: A Medicare Advantage organisation must base a medical necessity determination on the individual patient's circumstances, including medical history, physician recommendations and clinical notes, and CMS has stated that an algorithm or software reasoning from a larger dataset about similar patients cannot substitute for that determination or be used to deviate from coverage criteria. CMS also reminded plans of their Section 1557 nondiscrimination obligations in this context. If you are a provider building an authorisation and appeal strategy, this is the rule your appeals cite.

regulation.name: California SB 1120, the Physicians Make Decisions Act
regulation.citation: SB 1120 (2024), amending California Health and Safety Code section 1367.01 and Insurance Code section 10123.135; effective 1 January 2025
regulation.what_it_requires: A health care service plan or disability insurer using artificial intelligence or an algorithmic tool for utilisation review or utilisation management must base determinations on the enrollee's own medical history and clinical circumstances, apply the tool fairly and equitably, not supplant provider decision-making, and be subject to audit. A denial, delay or modification of services based on medical necessity may be made only by a licensed physician or a licensed health care professional competent to evaluate the specific clinical issues.

regulation.name: California AB 3030, generative AI in patient communications
regulation.citation: AB 3030 (2024), adding Chapter 2.13 (commencing with section 1339.75) to Division 2 of the California Health and Safety Code; effective 1 January 2025
regulation.what_it_requires: Health facilities, clinics, physician offices and group practice offices using generative AI to produce written or verbal communications about patient clinical information must include a disclaimer that the communication was generated by generative AI and clear instructions for contacting a human health care provider. Placement is specified by medium: prominently at the beginning of written communications such as letters and emails, displayed throughout continuous online interactions such as chat-based telehealth, delivered verbally at the start and the end of audio interactions, and displayed throughout video interactions. A communication read and reviewed by a licensed or certified human health care provider is exempt, which is the practical design constraint: build clinician review into the send path and the requirement does not attach.

regulation.name: Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act
regulation.citation: Texas HB 149 (2025), adding Chapter 552 to the Texas Business and Commerce Code, health care disclosure at section 552.051; effective 1 January 2026
regulation.what_it_requires: A provider of a health care service or treatment in which artificial intelligence is used must disclose that use to the patient or their representative, clearly, conspicuously and in plain language, not later than the date of the service or treatment, with an exception for emergency care where disclosure follows as soon as reasonably possible. Enforcement sits with the Texas Attorney General, with civil penalties, and for physicians the Texas Medical Board's licence sanctions sit behind it. The section number is reported consistently in practitioner guidance; confirm against the enrolled text before drafting your disclosure.

regulation.name: Texas SB 1188, AI in medical records and diagnostic use
regulation.citation: Texas SB 1188 (2025); effective 1 September 2025
regulation.what_it_requires: A practitioner may use artificial intelligence in diagnosis and treatment only within their scope of licence, must review AI-generated records consistently with Texas Medical Board standards, and must disclose the use of AI to the patient. Practically it means an ambient scribe or an AI-drafted record cannot be filed unreviewed, and that the review is the practitioner's duty rather than the vendor's feature. Texas therefore has two overlapping AI duties for clinicians with different effective dates; review both with counsel rather than treating TRAIGA as the whole picture.

regulation.name: Confidentiality of substance use disorder patient records
regulation.citation: 42 CFR Part 2; final rule published February 2024, compliance date 16 February 2026
regulation.what_it_requires: Records from federally assisted substance use disorder programmes carry consent and redisclosure restrictions stricter than HIPAA, and the permitted-use rules differ, though the 2024 final rule aligned enforcement, breach notification and penalties with HIPAA. Any tool that ingests an undifferentiated chart feed, an ambient scribe or a coding engine included, may pull Part 2 material into a pipeline that was scoped only against HIPAA. Segmentation is the hard part and it is rarely solved by the vendor.

regulation.name: Information blocking
regulation.citation: 45 CFR Part 171
regulation.what_it_requires: Practices that are likely to interfere with access, exchange or use of electronic health information are prohibited unless an exception applies. This constrains the instinct to delay automated results release while an AI-generated explanation is reviewed, and it constrains how an organisation may restrict third-party application access to data. For providers the consequence is a set of CMS-administered disincentives rather than civil monetary penalties, which are reserved for developers and networks. Any workflow that introduces a hold on information must be mapped to a specific exception, documented at the time.

regulation.name: Overpayment return obligation and the False Claims Act
regulation.citation: Affordable Care Act section 6402(a), 42 U.S.C. 1320a-7k(d); Medicare reporting and returning of overpayments at 42 CFR 401.305; False Claims Act at 31 U.S.C. 3729 et seq.
regulation.what_it_requires: An identified overpayment under Medicare or Medicaid must be reported and returned within 60 days of identification, and retaining it beyond that creates an obligation actionable under the False Claims Act. This is the rule that turns an AI coding error into a repayment event rather than a correction: identification includes what you would have known through reasonable diligence, errors extrapolate across a claim population, and a pattern draws an audit. It is the single most important reason the reviewer function and the audit trail are not optional.

regulation.name: State scope-of-practice and corporate practice of medicine limits
regulation.citation: described, not cited
regulation.what_it_requires: Every state defines by statute and board regulation which activities constitute the practice of medicine or nursing, who may triage, and in many states whether a corporate entity may employ physicians or direct clinical judgement. These rules were not written with software in mind and are applied by boards case by case. A tool that produces clinical advice without a licensed human in the loop can implicate them, particularly in patient-facing deployments and across state lines in telehealth. Requires state-by-state analysis, not a national policy.

regulation.name: State recording consent laws
regulation.citation: described, not cited
regulation.what_it_requires: Ambient documentation records a conversation. Roughly a dozen states require the consent of all parties to a recording rather than one, and the details vary on what constitutes consent, whether it must be renewed, and how it applies to a multi-state telehealth encounter where the parties are in different states. This drives a script, a documented consent workflow and a decision about what happens when a patient declines, which needs to be answerable at the bedside without delaying care.

regulation.name: Colorado's automated decision-making law
regulation.citation: SB 26-189 (2026), repealing and replacing the Colorado AI Act, SB 24-205 (2024); effective 1 January 2027
regulation.what_it_requires: Colorado replaced its 2024 AI Act, which had been delayed and never took effect, with a narrower transparency and disclosure framework for automated decision-making technology used in consequential decisions, a category that includes health care services. The details and the effective date have already moved twice in two years, so treat this as a reason to keep a state-law watch item rather than as a stable requirement, and confirm the current text before designing a disclosure around it.

regulation.name: Proposed HIPAA Security Rule update
regulation.citation: Notice of proposed rulemaking published 6 January 2025; comment period closed 7 March 2025; not finalised as at September 2026
regulation.what_it_requires: The proposal would remove the addressable/required distinction and mandate specific controls including asset inventories, network mapping, encryption at rest and in transit, multi-factor authentication and regular vulnerability testing, with obligations flowing to business associates. It is not law: the target date for final action has slipped repeatedly, now sitting in 2027 on the regulatory agenda, and more than a hundred provider organisations have formally asked HHS to withdraw it. Do not build to it as a requirement; do note that its asset-inventory and mapping expectations describe what you will need anyway to govern a fleet of AI tools.

sectors.economics: The licence is the smallest line and the only one in the proposal. Ambient documentation is typically priced per clinician per month, in the low hundreds of dollars; coding tools are usually per encounter or a share of collections; revenue cycle platforms are often contingency-priced, which sounds free and is not. As a planning estimate rather than a benchmark, assume the licence is a quarter to a third of the true first-year cost, and make the vendor's own implementation quote defend the rest. What nobody budgets: integration into the system of record, which is the dominant hidden cost and is frequently charged twice, once by the AI vendor and once by the EHR vendor for interface and app-orchestration work, plus months of an analyst's time, a test environment, and a build queue you do not control. Then the parallel run, where humans do the work and check the machine simultaneously, which is the only honest way to set a confidence threshold and typically costs a full quarter of duplicated effort. Then human review, permanently: a sampling rate, senior reviewers, and an audit function. This does not taper, and if it appears to, someone has stopped looking. Then governance and documentation: an AI inventory, a named owner, risk assessments, the Section 1557 identify-and-mitigate work, monitoring that actually runs, and revalidation after every model version change and every code-set update. For a mid-sized system that is plausibly a quarter to a full FTE before anything is deployed at scale, and it is a role that did not exist on the org chart. Then the disclosure and consent workflow, which is forms, scripts, training and a registration change, and takes longer to roll out than the software. Then the licences nobody uses: adoption of ambient tools is uneven in the published multi-site data, so budget on measured active use, not on seats issued, and write a reclamation rule into the rollout. And then the failure cost, which in this sector has a particular shape: it is a repayment. Coding error does not stay an error; an identified overpayment carries a 60-day return obligation, it extrapolates across a claim population, and a pattern draws an audit that costs more in response time than in dollars returned. The False Claims Act sits behind that. On the clinical side, the failure cost is a note in a permanent record saying something a patient did not say, found years later by opposing counsel. A useful discipline: before signing, write down what the recovery costs if the tool is materially wrong for ninety days before anyone notices. If that number is unknowable, the monitoring is not designed yet, and the project is not ready.
sectors.first_step: Export twelve months of 835 remittance data and build a denial Pareto: dollars denied and claim counts, cut by CARC/RARC reason code, by payer, by service line, and by the department where the claim originated. Then take the single largest bucket, sit for one full shift with the person who works it, and write down every system they touch, every re-keying, every place they wait on someone else, and every decision they make from memory rather than from a rule. That one page tells you whether your problem is coding, authorisation, registration or contracting, and it is the difference between buying a tool for the thing that hurts and buying a tool for the thing that was being sold.

sectors.label: Law firms
sectors.lede: Your firm has been adopting AI since 2012, whether or not it called it that: every TAR protocol you have negotiated in a meet-and-confer was a decision to let a classifier decide what a human never sees. What has changed is that generative tools now produce work product that reads like a third-year associate's and fails in ways a third-year associate's does not — fluently, confidently, and in the citations. The technology question is no longer the hard part in most firms; the unsettled question is what happens to the hours, and until a partnership answers that in writing, adoption stalls at the pilot and the tools get used quietly by the people whose realisation nobody checks.

where_it_helps.name: First-pass responsiveness review and issue coding (TAR/CAL, and the newer LLM classifiers layered on it)
where_it_helps.the_work: Contract attorneys and junior associates coding a review population document by document against a review protocol, at a per-document rate, with the protocol changing in week two and a production deadline that does not move.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Continuous active learning ranks the collection as reviewers code batches, so review stops when a validated recall estimate is met and most of the population is never eyes-on. That part is fifteen years old and has case law behind it. The newer layer — an LLM classifying against a protocol written in prose rather than against a coded seed set, returning a short rationale per document — does the same job without a training round, and has none of the validation literature or judicial history that supervised TAR has. Treat the two as different maturities inside one workflow: the ranking is settled, the prose-prompt classifier is a 2024-onward technique you validate yourself.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: A processed, deduplicated, email-threaded collection in a review platform; a written review protocol that is frozen or versioned; a reviewer panel disciplined enough to code consistently, because the model learns their inconsistency too; a validation protocol (control set, elusion sample, a stated recall target and how it will be measured) raised at the Rule 26(f) conference rather than invented at the end; and a Rule 502(d) order entered before anything runs.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: The mechanism is that fewer documents reach a human who is paid per document — a per-document rate multiplied by documents never opened, which is easy to model honestly before you buy anything. On a large, low-richness collection, eyes-on volume is commonly cut by a majority relative to linear review; ranges in the region of 60-80% are what practitioners and the TAR literature report. That is an estimate, it scales with collection size and inversely with richness, and it is offset by set-up, training and validation overhead that frequently exceeds the saving below roughly fifty thousand documents, where linear review is the cheaper answer. The overhead you cannot avoid is the validation sample, and it is the part opposing counsel will ask about.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Recall is measured against a sample, not against the case. A run validated at 85% recall on the population can still miss the single email the matter turns on, because the documents that matter are rare and stylistically odd — a nickname, a photograph of a whiteboard, an attachment with no text layer, a thread where the operative sentence sits inside a forwarded quote. The second failure is protocol drift: the responsiveness call changes mid-review, nobody re-trains, and the ranking silently becomes a ranking for the old question. The third is specific to the LLM variant — it produces a fluent rationale for a wrong call, and reviewers who are checking rationales rather than documents stop catching it within about a week.

where_it_helps.name: Deposition and transcript work
where_it_helps.the_work: The associate who takes a 250-page transcript and produces a page:line summary, a list of admissions, an impeachment chart against prior testimony and the errata review — overnight, before the next deposition starts at nine.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Summarises against the transcript itself with a page:line citation behind every assertion, builds topic indexes, and surfaces candidate contradictions across transcripts in the same matter. The output is a draft to be verified, not a deliverable.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Clean text transcripts rather than scans, exhibits mapped to the testimony that discusses them, a house summary format so output is comparable across a matter, and a standing rule that any citation which will appear in a filing or a designation is opened and read before it goes anywhere.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: The mechanism is that drafting is replaced by verification, which is a faster activity when every assertion carries a page:line pointer. A summary that consumed most of a day becomes a verification pass often measured in well under an hour per transcript. That is an estimate, it assumes the verifier actually opens the cites, and it only matters at volume — in a document-heavy or multi-plaintiff matter it is significant, in a two-deposition case it is noise.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Confident paraphrase that drops the qualifier. "I don't recall, but I believe" becomes an admission, and the page:line cite next to it is correct, which is what makes it dangerous — the verification step looks satisfied. Attribution drift in multi-speaker colloquy, misattributed objections, and rough ASCII with wrong speaker labels all produce wrong summaries carrying correct-looking citations. Rated workable rather than proven for one reason: the citation-grounded generative summary is a recent technique with no equivalent of the TAR case law behind it, and the firms using it well are the ones that measured their own error rate against a matter they had already summarised by hand.

where_it_helps.name: Contract abstraction into a schedule
where_it_helps.the_work: The diligence team abstracting nine hundred leases or MSAs into the client's template: assignment and change of control, term and renewal, indemnity caps, governing law, exclusivity, termination for convenience, notice addresses — each with a clause cite, each cell defensible in a disclosure schedule.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Extracts to a fixed schema with a clause-level pin cite, flags deviation from a playbook position, and produces exception lists sorted by how far off market the language sits.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: A written schema agreed before anyone starts, not negotiated cell by cell; a playbook that states what the firm treats as market; documents that are genuinely text, because OCR quality is the single largest determinant of accuracy; correct association of executed versions with their amendments and side letters; and a QC sample drawn at random rather than from the documents the reviewer found interesting.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: The mechanism is that a reviewer verifies a cited extraction instead of hunting for it. Per-document abstraction time commonly drops by a large fraction on a clean, homogeneous population of the client's own paper. That is an estimate driven by document count, scan quality and homogeneity; accuracy falls off sharply on third-party paper and bespoke drafting, and beneath a few hundred documents the schema design and QC set-up rarely pays back.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Amendments. The model reads the four corners of the document it was handed, and the answer lives in a 2019 amendment nobody scanned, so the schedule is confidently wrong rather than blank. Second, silent absence: nothing in an extraction distinguishes "this agreement contains no limitation of liability" from "this field was not checked", and an empty cell in a schedule handed to a buyer is read as the former. Third, definitional indirection — the cap expressed as a multiple of a defined term that is itself defined by reference to a schedule — which is where extraction accuracy quietly collapses and where the number in the cell still looks perfectly reasonable.

where_it_helps.name: First-pass privilege screening and log drafting
where_it_helps.the_work: Building the privilege log: pulling everything that hits the attorney-name list and the law-firm domain list, deciding legal advice from business advice on each one, drafting a description that supports the claim without waiving it, then defending four hundred challenged entries six weeks later.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Two different things sold as one. The mature part is analytics — name and domain hits, threading, family propagation, near-duplicate grouping — which has been in review platforms for years. The new part is a model classifying the substance: in-house counsel acting commercially, forwarded advice, common-interest chains, proposing a per-document description grounded in the document text and flagging families where the parent is privileged and the attachment is not. The second part is where the value is claimed and where the evidence is thinnest.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: A maintained, versioned attorney list covering in-house, departed and outside counsel; intact family and thread relationships; a lawyer with authority to set the legal-versus-business line and to have that line written down; a Rule 502(d) order in place before the first pass runs; a position on log method and timing taken at the Rule 26(f) conference, which the December 2025 amendments now require; and sampled QC on both the withheld set and the produced set, because only the second one finds the errors that hurt.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: The mechanism is bulk drafting of descriptions and a narrowed set of genuinely hard calls. Log drafting time often falls by more than half. The challenge-response work does not fall at all and may rise, because a longer log with more uniform descriptions is easier for an opponent to attack in bulk. Estimate, dependent on log size and on how hard your opponent pushes.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The error is one-way. A false negative is a privileged document in the production; clawback under a 502(d) order restores the legal position but not the fact that opposing counsel has read it. Models over-call privilege wherever legal-sounding language appears in a commercial email and under-call it where the advice has been paraphrased by a business person two hops downstream — which is precisely where the sensitive material lives. A fluent auto-drafted description can also say more about the advice than the claim survives. Rated early, not workable: the classification step is new, the consequence of a miss is asymmetric and irreversible, and no firm should run it without a measured error rate on its own documents and a human second pass over the produced set.

where_it_helps.name: Time-entry reconstruction and narrative cleanup
where_it_helps.the_work: The partner reconstructing four days of unrecorded time on a Sunday night from Outlook, the DMS audit trail and a phone log; and the billing coordinator rewriting "review documents" into something that will not be rejected by the client's e-billing rules for the third cycle running.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Proposes draft entries from passive activity capture — documents opened and edited, calendar, calls, email — attributed to a client-matter, and rewrites narratives to the client's billing guidelines and task codes without altering what was actually done. Passive capture itself is an old, mature category; the drafting and guideline-compliance layer on top of it is the new part.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Passive capture running on every device the work actually happens on, mobile included; reliable client-matter attribution at the file and mail level, which is the genuinely hard part and is a records-management problem rather than an AI one; outside counsel guidelines and e-billing rules in a form a machine can apply; and an absolute rule that the timekeeper approves every entry, because the entry is a representation to a client about what was done.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Two mechanisms, and the smaller one is the drafting. The larger is recovery of time that was performed and never recorded, plus fewer e-billing rejections and appeals. Vendors commonly quote a recovery of a few per cent of recorded hours; treat that as a vendor figure until you have measured your own leakage, because it depends entirely on how undisciplined current timekeeping is, and a firm with genuine contemporaneous capture should expect close to nothing. The e-billing saving is easier to verify honestly: count your rejected and appealed lines for two quarters before you buy.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The narrative that is fluent, compliant and not true. A rewrite that promotes "reviewed" to "analysed and revised" is a misstatement about the fee under Rule 1.5, and a reconstruction that plausibly fills a gap the lawyer cannot actually remember is a fabrication with a timesheet around it. The second failure is duplicate attribution — the same activity proposed against two matters because the file sat in an ambiguous folder — which is double-billing if nobody catches it. The third is that passive capture is itself a surveillance record of every document a lawyer opened: discoverable, subject to your retention policy, and a conversation to have with the general counsel before the pilot rather than after.

where_it_helps.name: AI-assisted legal research
where_it_helps.the_work: Finding the controlling authority, confirming it is still good law, and knowing what the other side is going to cite before they cite it.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Retrieval-augmented answers over a licensed corpus with linked citations, memo drafts, and brief-analysis tools that read an opponent's filing and propose responses. It is genuinely useful for orientation in an unfamiliar area and for discovering that an argument you are circling already has a name.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: A paid research entitlement, a lawyer who already has a rough expectation of what the answer should be and will notice when the output does not match it, and an unbreakable rule that every citation, quotation and pin cite is opened and read in the reporter before it leaves the building.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: The mechanism is a faster first hour, not a finished answer. It shortens orientation and does very little to the last three hours. On a question you can already frame precisely, a well-constructed terms-and-connectors search remains faster and is fully auditable afterwards, which the generative answer is not. Estimate, and it inverts with the seniority of the user — the more you know the area, the less it gives you.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The only preregistered, peer-reviewed evaluation of the purpose-built tools (Magesh and colleagues, Stanford RegLab and HAI; preprint 2024, published in the Journal of Empirical Legal Studies in 2025) reported hallucinated or mis-supported answers in roughly a sixth of benchmark queries for one major vendor's tool and roughly a third for another, against marketing that had claimed hallucination-free linked citations. Those figures measure 2024 products that have since changed and the vendors disputed the methodology; the structural point survives regardless — a linked citation establishes that the case exists, not that it says what the answer asserts it says. The deeper failure is silence. Nothing in the output tells you about the controlling authority it failed to retrieve, the circuit split it flattened into a single rule, or the fact that the case was superseded by statute — and an associate who does not know the area cannot detect an absence.

where_it_does_not.claim: AI conflicts clearance — a model that reads intake forms and clears new matters against the firm's history.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Conflicts is not a language problem, it is an entity-resolution and records problem, and the failure mode is intolerable. A conflict missed under Rules 1.7 or 1.9 and imputed firm-wide under Rule 1.10 produces disqualification, fee disgorgement and a malpractice claim, so the check must be over-inclusive by design — you want the false positives, because a human then clears them. A probabilistic matcher that suppresses a hit for being a weak match is actively worse than the noisy deterministic search it replaces, and no general counsel will accept "the model was 94% confident there was no conflict" as a clearance. The real work sits somewhere unglamorous: corporate family trees kept current, closed-matter records that survived two practice-management migrations, lateral hires' prior client books, adverse-party names captured properly at intake. Fix that data and a deterministic fuzzy match performs well; leave it broken and no model saves you.

where_it_does_not.claim: AI that drafts the filing — "your first draft of the brief in minutes".
where_it_does_not.why_not: The signature on a filing is a Rule 11(b) certification, and Rule 26(g) supplies the parallel certification for discovery, which Rule 11 expressly does not reach. In Mata the court accepted that there is nothing inherently improper about using a reliable AI tool and held that the existing rules place a gatekeeping duty on the signing attorney regardless; the Fifth Circuit, declining in June 2024 to adopt its own AI certification rule, made the same point — that saying "I used AI" will not excuse an otherwise sanctionable filing. That turns every generated sentence into something a lawyer must verify to the standard they would have applied to their own work. For routine, formulaic filings the arithmetic can work. For anything carrying a contested legal argument, the verification tax — opening every case, checking every quotation is verbatim, checking every pin cite, then checking that the authority supports the proposition rather than merely mentioning it — meets or exceeds the drafting time, because verifying an argument you did not construct is slower than constructing one. The public record of sanctions, referrals and suspensions is not a record of bad tools. It is a record of firms that bought the drafting saving and never budgeted the verification.

where_it_does_not.claim: Litigation outcome prediction and AI settlement valuation as a basis for setting reserves or a demand.
where_it_does_not.why_not: The training data is dockets, and dockets are a selected sample. The cases that settle — the overwhelming majority, and the ones you care about — either never produce an outcome to learn from or produce one under seal. Judge-level and jurisdiction-level analytics run on sample sizes that would not survive a Daubert challenge if you tried to put them in front of the court that generated them, and some jurisdictions restrict or frown on judge-level analytics outright. The features that actually determine your outcome — whether the witness is credible, whether the general counsel wants this closed before the audit, what the carrier will fund — appear nowhere in PACER. It is a legitimate input to a conversation among people who know the matter. It is not a valuation, and using it as one transfers a false precision straight into your reserves.

where_it_does_not.claim: A firm-wide knowledge assistant over the document management system — "ask your own precedent".
where_it_does_not.why_not: Two blockers, and the first is not the vendor's to solve. Your DMS permissions and ethical walls exist to prevent imputation under Rule 1.10, and a retrieval layer indexing across matters will leak across them unless it enforces matter-level security on every query, for every user, at retrieval time rather than by filtering results after the fact. Most deployments discover this when a lawyer behind a wall receives an answer sourced from the other side of it, and the discovery is itself a reportable event. The second blocker is the corpus. A DMS is not a precedent bank; it is twenty years of drafts, superseded versions, documents saved to the wrong matter, and one-off accommodations a partner made for a client in 2014. Retrieval cannot distinguish good precedent from the draft that was rejected, and a confident answer built on a rejected draft is worse than no answer. Firms that make this work do the knowledge-management work first — curated, labelled, owned precedent — at which point most of the value arrives before the model does.

where_it_does_not.claim: Client-facing intake bots that answer legal questions or assess whether someone has a case.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Two distinct exposures. Either the bot is giving legal advice, which raises unauthorised-practice questions under Rule 5.5 and puts the firm behind whatever it said, or it is performing a merits screen, in which case a prospective client has disclosed matter facts to you, you owe them duties under Rule 1.18 and may have taken on conflict taint — all before a lawyer has looked at anything. Whatever that conversation produced is also discoverable and sitting in a vendor's environment, and it is exactly the sort of record that surfaces in a bar complaint. Intake automation that schedules, routes, collects documents and runs the conflicts search is genuinely useful and carries none of this. The moment it answers "do I have a case", it has stopped being intake.

where_it_does_not.claim: "Agentic" AI that runs a matter workflow end to end — research to draft to filing, or collection to review to production — with no lawyer in the loop at each step.
where_it_does_not.why_not: The supervision rules make a named human the unit of accountability: Rules 5.1 and 5.3 require reasonable assurance over the conduct, not over the vendor's roadmap, and Formal Opinion 512 reads them as requiring firm policy and independent verification of output rather than delegated judgement. An agent chain also compounds error rather than averaging it — a five per cent error rate at each of five unverified steps is not a five per cent problem — and the one artefact you need when something goes wrong, a record of who decided what, is precisely what the chain destroys. Add the questions nobody has answered: what you bill for agent time under Rule 1.5, what your professional liability carrier makes of it at renewal, and what you tell the client under Rule 1.4 when a step nobody watched produced the error. Automate the steps. Keep the checkpoints human, named and logged.

preconditions: A written position on client consent, and a register that records it per client. ABA Formal Opinion 512 treats informed client consent as required before inputting information relating to a representation into a self-learning tool, and says general boilerplate consent is insufficient; Florida's Opinion 24-1 recommends consent before using a third-party tool where that would disclose confidential information, and notes that an in-house tool disclosing nothing to a third party removes the obligation — so the architecture decision and the consent decision are the same decision. Separately, outside counsel guidelines increasingly speak to AI: permitting it, requiring disclosure, or requiring that time savings appear in the bill. If your billing partners cannot answer "which of my clients has agreed to what" from a system rather than from memory, you are not ready to deploy anything.

A tenancy where client data does not train the model, with the terms of use, retention settings, subprocessor list and incident-notification terms actually read by someone accountable — not accepted at the click-through. Under Rule 1.6(c) this is a reasonable-efforts obligation the firm owns and cannot delegate to a vendor's marketing page. Matter-level security and ethical walls must be enforced inside the AI layer itself, at retrieval time, because a retrieval system that inherits its permissions loosely will cross a wall silently and you will hear about it from the lawyer on the wrong side of it.

A named supervising lawyer for each workflow, a written firm policy under Rules 5.1 and 5.3, and training people actually sit through. The sanctions record in this sector is overwhelmingly not a record of bad models; it is a record of unsupervised use by someone who did not understand what the tool does, and in at least one reported fee award the chain ran from an associate's AI-drafted outline at one firm into a brief signed at another. The policy has to reach contract attorneys, vendors and eDiscovery providers, because 5.3 covers nonlawyer assistance outside the firm as well as inside it.

A verification standard written down per output type, specifying what must be checked, by whom, to what standard, and how the check is recorded. "Lawyers should review AI output" is not a standard. "Every citation, quotation and pin cite in any document bearing a signature is opened in the reporter by a person who did not draft it, and initialled" is one, and it is the one that would have prevented most of the reported sanctions.

Source data clean enough to be worth reading: transcripts as text rather than scans, contracts correctly associated with their amendments, DMS records filed under the right matter, a conflicts database with a maintained corporate hierarchy, an attorney list that includes departed and in-house lawyers. Every application above degrades to the quality of its input, and in most firms this is where the project time actually goes.

A decision, made by the people who set compensation, about what happens to the hours on the affected matter types — taken before the tool is rolled out. This is the real precondition and the one most firms skip. If an associate's realisation falls because they worked faster, the tool will be abandoned or hidden, and you will get neither the efficiency nor the visibility. The answer can be fixed fees on those tasks, a changed budget, a changed utilisation target, or an explicit decision that the saving goes to the client. But it has to be an answer, and it has to come from the compensation committee rather than the innovation committee.

A court-by-court check folded into the filing checklist. There is no uniform federal rule: standing orders on AI disclosure vary by judge rather than by district, some districts have local rules, the Fifth Circuit considered a circuit-wide certification and declined it, and individual orders change without notice. This belongs in the same place as page limits and courtesy-copy rules, owned by the docketing function, not in a memo circulated once.

A decision about privilege-log method and timing taken at the start of the case rather than the end. The amendments effective 1 December 2025 require the parties' discovery plan to address the method and timing of complying with Rule 26(b)(5)(A), and allow the scheduling order to do the same, so any intention to use machine assistance on the privileged population is now something you raise early — alongside the Rule 502(d) order, which should be entered before anything automated touches the collection.
