regulation.name: Duty of technological competence — ABA Model Rule 1.1, Comment [8]
regulation.citation: ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct r. 1.1 cmt. [8]
regulation.what_it_requires: The comment provides that to maintain the requisite knowledge and skill, a lawyer should keep abreast of changes in the law and its practice, including the benefits and risks associated with relevant technology. Note that the word is "should" and that the duty sits in a comment to the competence rule rather than in the black letter; it is nonetheless the hook every AI ethics opinion hangs on. Around forty states plus the District of Columbia have adopted the comment or an equivalent, on the count most commonly cited, and Puerto Rico has gone further with a standalone rule. In practice it cuts both ways: it is the basis for saying a lawyer must understand a tool's limits before using it, and it forecloses ignorance of the technology as an excuse afterwards.

regulation.name: Confidentiality — ABA Model Rule 1.6
regulation.citation: ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct r. 1.6(a), (c)
regulation.what_it_requires: A lawyer must not reveal information relating to the representation unless the client gives informed consent, the disclosure is impliedly authorised in order to carry out the representation, or it is permitted by Rule 1.6(b); and under 1.6(c) must make reasonable efforts to prevent inadvertent or unauthorised disclosure of, or unauthorised access to, that information. Two consequences for AI. Whether putting matter information into a third-party tool is a disclosure at all turns on that tool's actual terms, retention behaviour and access model rather than on the vendor's assurances — and the implied-authorisation argument is far thinner for a self-learning consumer tool than for a closed tenancy. And 1.6(c) is a reasonable-efforts standard, which means it is satisfied by documented diligence and failed by a click-through.

regulation.name: Supervision — ABA Model Rules 5.1 and 5.3
regulation.citation: ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct r. 5.1, r. 5.3
regulation.what_it_requires: Partners and lawyers with comparable managerial authority must make reasonable efforts to ensure the firm has measures giving reasonable assurance that all lawyers conform to the rules, and must make equivalent efforts as to nonlawyer assistance — which under Rule 5.3 includes contractors, vendors and eDiscovery providers outside the firm, not only employees. Both rules also impose direct responsibility on a supervising lawyer who orders or ratifies the conduct, or who learns of it in time to mitigate and does not. Formal Opinion 512 reads these rules as requiring firms to establish clear policies on the permissible use of generative AI and to train people on them.

regulation.name: Fees and expenses — ABA Model Rule 1.5
regulation.citation: ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct r. 1.5(a); ABA Standing Comm. on Ethics & Prof'l Responsibility, Formal Op. 93-379 (1993)
regulation.what_it_requires: A lawyer must not make an agreement for, charge, or collect an unreasonable fee or an unreasonable amount for expenses. Applied to AI: hourly time billed must be time actually spent, so a task completed in fifteen minutes cannot be billed at the two hours it used to take; billing the same work to two matters is the same violation it always was; and whether a tool's cost may be passed through as an expense or must be absorbed as overhead runs through the long-standing billing analysis in Formal Opinion 93-379, which Opinion 512 applies to generative AI. The 93-379 reference is given as the source of the overhead-versus-expense distinction; confirm its exact formulation before quoting it to a client.

regulation.name: ABA Formal Opinion 512, "Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools"
regulation.citation: ABA Standing Comm. on Ethics & Prof'l Responsibility, Formal Op. 512 (July 29, 2024)
regulation.what_it_requires: The first ABA ethics guidance on generative AI. It creates no new rules but maps existing ones: competence requires a reasonable understanding of a tool's capabilities and limitations; client informed consent is required before inputting information relating to a representation into a self-learning tool, and general boilerplate consent is insufficient; lawyers should read and understand the terms of use and privacy terms; firm management must establish clear policies and train staff; output must be independently verified and professional judgement may not be delegated; and on fees, lawyers bill for time actually spent and generally may not charge clients for a general subscription that functions as overhead, nor for their own time learning a tool absent agreement. It is guidance, not law, and is binding nowhere on its own — your state's rules and opinions govern.

regulation.name: Candor to the tribunal and the signature certification
regulation.citation: ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct r. 3.3, r. 1.4; Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b), 11(d), 26(g)
regulation.what_it_requires: Signing a filing certifies that the legal contentions are warranted by existing law or by a non-frivolous argument for extending or changing it, and that the signer made an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances. Rule 11 does not apply to disclosures or to discovery requests, responses and objections — Rule 11(d) carves them out and Rule 26(g) supplies the parallel certification, which matters because machine-assisted review and privilege logging live there rather than under Rule 11. Rule 3.3 forbids knowingly making a false statement of law to a tribunal and requires disclosure of directly adverse controlling authority not disclosed by opposing counsel. Rule 1.4 governs what you must tell the client when something goes wrong. None of these has an AI exception.

regulation.name: The sanctions record for fabricated citations
regulation.citation: Mata v. Avianca, Inc., 678 F. Supp. 3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023); Park v. Kim, 91 F.4th 610 (2d Cir. 2024); Lacey v. State Farm Gen. Ins. Co., No. 2:24-cv-05205 (C.D. Cal. May 6, 2025) (order of the special master)
regulation.what_it_requires: In Mata, two attorneys and their firm were sanctioned $5,000 under Rule 11 for an affirmation citing six fabricated decisions, and were ordered to notify their client and each judge falsely identified as the author of an invented opinion; the court accepted that there is nothing inherently improper about using a reliable AI tool and held that the existing rules place a gatekeeping duty on the signing attorney regardless. In Park, the Second Circuit referred counsel to its Grievance Panel for citing a non-existent decision she admitted she had generated with a chatbot, and directed her to furnish a copy of the decision to her client — the first federal appellate decision of its kind. In Lacey, a special master ordered two firms jointly and severally to pay $31,100 after an AI-drafted outline passed between them into a brief nobody cite-checked, and a corrected refiling introduced further errors. The public tracker most cited in the trade press listed well over a thousand such decisions worldwide by mid-2026, with awards running into five figures and the first suspensions reported. Assume any fabricated citation you file will be found, and will be public.

regulation.name: Technology-assisted review is settled; validation is what is contested
regulation.citation: Da Silva Moore v. Publicis Groupe, 287 F.R.D. 182 (S.D.N.Y. 2012) (Peck, M.J.), adopted by the district judge in April 2012; Rio Tinto PLC v. Vale S.A., 306 F.R.D. 125 (S.D.N.Y. 2015)
regulation.what_it_requires: Da Silva Moore was the first opinion approving computer-assisted review of a large ESI collection. Rio Tinto observed that it had become black-letter law that a producing party wanting to use TAR will be permitted to. What remains contested is validation and transparency — courts look to whether the process was reasonably designed, tested with quality-control measures and proportionate to the burden, and there is no consensus requiring you to disclose seed sets or to give an opponent a veto over your protocol. Two cautions: neither case addresses generative classifiers, so do not read them as blessing an LLM run against a prose protocol; and your validation protocol, not your choice of software, is the defensible artefact.

regulation.name: Privilege log timing and clawback in federal civil practice
regulation.citation: Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(5)(A); Fed. R. Evid. 502(d); amendments to Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(3)(D) and 16(b)(3)(B), effective December 1, 2025
regulation.what_it_requires: Rule 26(b)(5)(A) governs how a privilege claim is asserted and described. Rule 502(d) lets a court order that disclosure connected with the litigation is a waiver neither in that proceeding nor in any other federal or state proceeding — the single most useful protection when any automated process touches a privileged population, and materially stronger than the fact-dependent clawback under Rule 502(b). The amendments effective 1 December 2025 require the parties' discovery plan to state their views and proposals on the method and timing of complying with Rule 26(b)(5)(A), and allow the scheduling order to address it, which moves the decision about how you will log — including whether any of it is machine-assisted — to the start of the case rather than the end. Check the current rule text for the exact subparagraph before citing it in a brief.

regulation.name: Court standing orders on AI disclosure
regulation.citation: Judge Brantley Starr (N.D. Tex.), Mandatory Certification Regarding Generative Artificial Intelligence (May 2023); Fifth Circuit, decision not to adopt its proposed amendment to 5th Cir. R. 32.3 (announced 12 June 2024)
regulation.what_it_requires: There is no uniform federal rule. Judge Starr's standing order, the first of its kind, requires counsel to certify either that no portion of a filing was drafted by generative AI or that any AI-generated language was checked for accuracy by a human, on pain of the filing being struck. Many judges have since issued their own variants and some districts have adopted local rules; others have declined. The Fifth Circuit proposed a circuit-wide certification requirement in late 2023 and, after largely negative comment, announced in June 2024 that it would not adopt it, making the point that saying "I used AI" will not excuse an otherwise sanctionable filing. Standing orders are not published in a reporter and change without notice, so this is a per-judge, per-case docketing task, and the dates and wording above should be re-confirmed against the court's own page before anyone relies on them.

regulation.name: State bar guidance
regulation.citation: Florida Bar Ethics Opinion 24-1 (19 January 2024); State Bar of California, Practical Guidance for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law (COPRAC, approved November 2023, subsequently revised)
regulation.what_it_requires: Florida permits the use of generative AI subject to confidentiality, competent oversight, proper billing and the advertising rules; it recommends obtaining the client's informed consent before using a third-party tool where that would involve disclosing confidential information, observes that an in-house tool disclosing nothing to a third party removes that obligation, and addresses charging the actual cost of a tool to the client. California's guidance applies the existing rules, requires a baseline understanding of the system's capabilities, data sources and limitations before deployment, and is explicit that a lawyer remains responsible for the output and may not abdicate professional judgement. Many other states and bar associations have issued guidance since, including a New York State Bar task force report in 2024; several have been revised. Check your own jurisdiction, and re-check, rather than relying on the ABA opinion alone.

regulation.name: Conflicts of interest, imputation and prospective clients
regulation.citation: ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct r. 1.7, r. 1.9, r. 1.10, r. 1.18
regulation.what_it_requires: Concurrent and former-client conflicts, their imputation across the firm, and the duties owed to a prospective client who has disclosed information are unchanged by technology. Relevant here for three reasons: an automated conflicts screen produces candidates, never a clearance; any AI system that retrieves across matters must respect the screens erected to avoid imputation under Rule 1.10, enforced at retrieval rather than in the display; and an intake tool that takes matter facts from a prospective client can create Rule 1.18 duties and conflict taint before a lawyer has seen anything.

regulation.name: Unauthorised practice of law — ABA Model Rule 5.5
regulation.citation: ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct r. 5.5
regulation.what_it_requires: A lawyer must not practise law where doing so violates the regulation of the profession in that jurisdiction, or assist another in the unauthorised practice of law. The live question for firms is not whether the model is practising law but whether a firm-branded tool answering a member of the public's legal question amounts to the firm assisting unlicensed practice — and whether the firm stands behind the answer either way. Jurisdictions differ sharply on where that line sits and several have active reform work or sandboxes, so treat it as a per-jurisdiction question rather than a settled one.

regulation.name: Outside counsel guidelines and client AI terms
regulation.citation: described, not cited
regulation.what_it_requires: Not regulation, but binding in practice and increasingly the sharper constraint. Client guidelines now commonly address whether AI may be used on their matters at all, whether its use must be disclosed, which tools are approved, whether matter data may leave a defined environment, and whether efficiency gains must be reflected in the invoice. A small number of clients prohibit AI outright; a much larger group is silent, which is not permission. These terms are per-client, they are amended without a negotiation, and they must be tracked at matter level, because the billing partner is the one who signed them and the billing partner is the one who will be asked.

sectors.economics:
Licences are the visible cost and usually the smallest one. Point tools for transcript or contract work run in the hundreds of dollars per user per year; enterprise legal AI platforms and eDiscovery analytics run considerably higher and are often priced per matter, per gigabyte or per document, which means the bill scales with the very thing you were trying to make cheaper. Budget the licence, then budget the following, because these are what blow the number.

Integration into the system of record. This is typically the largest line and the one most often left out. Connecting a tool to the DMS, the practice management system, the eDiscovery platform or the time system means single sign-on, client-matter security enforced at retrieval rather than in the display, ethical walls honoured by the AI layer itself, records-retention and legal-hold behaviour that matches your policy, and audit logging good enough to answer a client who asks what touched their matter. Expect this to be measured in months of someone's time, not in a vendor's onboarding week, and expect it to surface data problems — mis-filed matters, a conflicts database with no entity hierarchy, contracts separated from their amendments — that stayed invisible while only humans were reading.

The human review that does not go away. Verification is a permanent new line item, not a transitional one. The economic shape of every application above is the same: drafting time falls, verification time appears, and the net is positive only where verification is genuinely cheaper than drafting. That holds for a cited transcript summary and a schema-bound contract abstraction, where the machine tells you exactly where to look. It holds much less well for a legal argument, where checking an argument you did not construct is slower than constructing one. Firms that model the drafting saving and omit the verification cost produce a number that does not survive contact with the first matter.

Model governance and documentation. A written policy under Rules 5.1 and 5.3; a register of approved tools with a named owner for each; vendor diligence and terms review by the general counsel's office; per-client consent and outside-counsel-guideline tracking at matter level; training with attendance recorded; and a periodic re-review, because vendors change their terms and swap their underlying models without asking you. In a firm of any size this starts as a part-time role and becomes a full-time one, and it sits with risk and general counsel — people whose time is expensive and already committed.

The fee model. This is the cost nobody puts on a slide. On hourly matters, efficiency on a billable task is revenue reduction on that task. If a firm saves an hour of associate time on document review, that hour was revenue, and the saving accrues to the client whether or not anyone intended it. Model the realisation effect rather than the time saved: which matter types, how many hours, at what rate, and what work replaces them. Clients are asking the same question from the other side — client-side scepticism about whether firms' AI use has yet produced any visible saving is a recurring theme in panel surveys and the trade press, and outside counsel guidelines are beginning to require that savings appear in the invoice. Treat those surveys as directional rather than as a number, and get your own answer ready, because a firm that cannot answer the question will eventually be told the answer.

The failure mode, priced. Fabricated authority in a filing costs: the sanction itself, which has run from $5,000 in the earliest reported matter to a $31,100 joint fee award against two firms in a 2025 order, with individual awards in five figures and the first suspensions now reported; the lawyer's own unbilled hours responding to an order to show cause; mandatory disclosure to the client under Rule 1.4 and, in some orders, to the real judges named as authors of invented opinions; possible fee forfeiture; a malpractice notification that affects the next renewal; and a bar referral. None of that is the largest cost. The largest cost is that the order is public, searchable, indexed under the firm's name and the lawyer's name, aggregated into public trackers that now list thousands of decisions, and reported by the trade press within days. Price it as a business-development event, not as a fine. The confidentiality variant is quieter and can be worse: matter information entering a system it should not have entered means client notification, a records problem, and an argument you very much do not want to have about whether privilege survived.

Professional liability carriers have begun asking about AI use and controls on renewal questionnaires. Whatever you answer there needs to be true, which is a further argument for the tool register existing before the tools do.
sectors.first_step: Run a cite-check audit of your own filings, scoped under privilege. Take every filing your firm submitted in the last ninety days — across practice groups, not a sample chosen by the people who drafted them — and have someone outside the drafting chain open every case citation, every quotation and every pin cite in the reporter. Record three counts: citations that do not exist or do not stand for the proposition they are cited for; quotations that are not verbatim; pin cites that point to the wrong page. Alongside each filing, record who drafted, who checked, and whether any AI tool was involved. Commission it through the general counsel's office as a privileged internal review before anyone starts, because the only thing worse than finding a bad cite is creating an unprotected record that you found it. The audit costs a few days of a paralegal's time and nothing in licences, and it produces the only number that matters before you buy anything: your firm's current verification failure rate. Most firms find it is not zero and that it predates generative AI — which tells you the control you are missing is a cite-checking standard with a name attached to it, not a tool. Any AI deployment then has a baseline to be judged against, and the standing verification rule you write on the back of it is the same control that would have prevented every sanction in the public record.

sectors.label: Accountancy and audit
sectors.lede: Most of what is sold as AI for accounting firms is aimed at preparation, and preparation is not where the constraint sits. The binding limits in a firm are reviewer and signer hours, client responsiveness, and the fact that everything produced has to survive a peer reviewer or an inspector reading the workpaper cold. AI earns its place in this sector in a narrow band: high-volume mechanical work where the source document is in front of you and the output can be checked against it in seconds. Outside that band it produces material that looks finished, reviews slowly, and creates documentation risk you did not have before.

where_it_helps.name: Client document intake, classification and field extraction
where_it_helps.the_work: In late January someone opens a 400-page client bundle, splits it into W-2s, 1099 composites, K-1s, closing statements and mortgage interest statements, names each file to the firm's convention, ties them against the organiser, and emails the client about the four documents that never arrived. On the audit side it is the same job under a different name: receiving PBC items, filing them into the engagement index, and chasing what is outstanding.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Classifies each document by type, extracts the fields, writes them into the tax software or the engagement file index, and produces the outstanding-items list by difference against the prior-year return or the PBC list.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: A connection into the document management system, a working import path into the return or the audit file (a vendor bridge or an API, not a CSV someone re-keys), the prior-year return or PBC list as the expectation, and a side-by-side view of every extracted value against the source image so the preparer verifies rather than trusts. Without the side-by-side view this is not a time saving, it is a transfer of risk to the reviewer.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: it removes the sorting, naming and keying step. It does not remove the checking step. On a 1040 with a dozen source documents that is plausibly 20 to 40 minutes a return; on an audit, perhaps a day of engagement admin. This is an estimate and it scales with volume, not complexity. A firm filing 200 returns will barely notice. A firm filing 3,000 has a real case.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: One wrong field on an otherwise correct form. A 1099-B with wash sale adjustments or basis not reported to the IRS. A K-1 footnote carrying the 199A or state apportionment detail as free text. The preparer glances at the form, sees the familiar numbers are right, and does not re-read the one field that is not. The second common failure is duplicates: a corrected 1099 extracted alongside the original it replaced. Scanned handwriting, photographed documents and brokerage composites that change layout each January are where accuracy falls off first.

where_it_helps.name: Reconciliation and transaction matching
where_it_helps.the_work: The staff accountant clearing the unreconciled column on a bank reconciliation. The intercompany difference that reappears at every consolidation. The AP subledger that sits $4,182 away from the general ledger and has since the system conversion. The three-way match exceptions queue nobody has touched since March.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Matches deterministically first, then proposes pairings for what is left, including partial and one-to-many matches, using how the firm cleared similar items before. The right output is an exceptions queue with a proposed disposition, not a cleared reconciliation. The deterministic layer is decades-old software and is the part that carries the work; the learned suggestion layer is the newer and weaker half, and no part of it should clear an item without a name against the decision.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Both sides of the reconciliation in a stable, repeatable extract. An explicit rule for what counts as a match and what tolerance is acceptable. A recorded disposition for every exception, with a name against it. This is mostly plumbing and very little model, which is why it works.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: the first pass that used to take hours takes minutes. The residual exceptions, which were always the actual work, are untouched. On a high-volume reconciliation it is reasonable to expect the majority of line items to clear without human attention, which might be a third to a half of the elapsed time. An estimate, and it depends almost entirely on transaction volume and on how disciplined the client's payment references are.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The model learns the firm's habit of clearing small differences and begins proposing matches that bury a genuine timing problem. One-to-many matches that straddle a period end net to zero and hide exactly the cut-off error the test existed to find. And a matcher that runs before the client's month-end adjustments will give a different answer on re-run, which is a problem when the workpaper says otherwise.

where_it_helps.name: Full-population journal entry risk scoring
where_it_helps.the_work: The fraud journal entry testing every audit has to do. Pull the general ledger, filter for entries posted by unusual users, at unusual hours, to seldom-used accounts, in round numbers, after the close, manual entries touching revenue. Then select a handful and vouch them to support.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Scores the whole population against risk criteria and clusters it, so the auditor selects from a ranked population rather than from a filter set someone wrote in 2019. It can surface behaviour a filter cannot: a posting user who appeared in Q3, an approval pattern that changed after a controller left.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: A general ledger extract that is complete and ties to the trial balance, user master data with roles, posting timestamps held separately from effective dates, and a documented, repeatable extraction method. The extract is the project. The scoring is the easy part, and firms consistently budget it the other way round.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: coverage rather than hours. In year one it usually saves nothing, because building and testing the extract costs more than the sampling did. In year two and after, when the extract path exists, it may be a few days an engagement across journal entry testing and related-party scanning. An estimate, and it depends on the client's ERP staying still.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Four thousand flagged entries and no disposition plan, so the workpaper evidences effort and not a conclusion. Worse, and more common: the extract quietly omits a module, a sub-ledger or the consolidation layer, so the population is not the population. Establishing the completeness and accuracy of the information analysed is exactly what PCAOB AS 1105 requires on issuer audits and what AU-C 500 requires on non-issuer ones, and an incomplete extract turns a strong-looking procedure into no procedure at all.

where_it_helps.name: Financial statement tie-out and disclosure checklist support
where_it_helps.the_work: The second-year associate tying every number in the draft statements back to the workpapers, casting the statements, checking note 12 agrees to the face of the balance sheet, confirming the cash flow statement reconciles, verifying cross-references point at the right note, agreeing comparatives to last year's signed set. Then running the disclosure checklist. Then doing most of it again on draft three and draft four.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Checks internal consistency across the document: numbers, casts, cross-references, prior-year agreement. Runs a first pass at the disclosure checklist and flags where a required disclosure appears to be absent. The consistency half of this is mechanical and works; the checklist half would rate early on its own and should be treated as a prompt list, not as evidence of compliance.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: The draft statements in a structured form, not a flattened PDF. The prior-year signed set. The firm's current checklist, in a form the tool actually reads. A mapped trial balance. A checklist one release out of date is worse than no checklist, because it produces a clean report.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: tie-out is mechanical, high-volume and repeated across drafts. Plausibly half the tie-out hours on a first draft and rather more on later drafts, where the work is re-checking what moved. An estimate; it depends on statement length and on how many drafts the engagement cycles through.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The checklist reports a disclosure as present because the right words appear, when the substance is not met. Revenue disaggregated at too coarse a level. A going concern note that recites the conditions without reaching the required conclusion. Presence is what the model can judge, and compliance is not presence. Expect reviewers to stop trusting the checklist output quickly once they hit the first false clean report, after which the firm is paying for a tool nobody reads.

where_it_helps.name: Tax research bound to a licensed primary-source corpus
where_it_helps.the_work: A partner asks whether a client's transaction qualifies. Someone spends four to ten hours in the research platform reading code, regulations, rulings and cases, then writes a memo with citations the partner will pick apart.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Retrieves and synthesises across the licensed content, drafts a first-pass memo with every proposition linked back to the authority it came from, and lists contrary authority rather than resolving it.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Retrieval confined to a licensed, current primary-source corpus, with effective dates and a status flag for superseded or obsoleted authority. Every assertion linked to the text it came from, so the preparer reads the source and not the summary. If the tool cannot show you the paragraph, it cannot be used for this.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: it compresses the locate-and-read-around phase, not the judgement. Perhaps 30 to 50 per cent off a routine research memo and close to nothing on a novel question, where the reading was the thinking. An estimate.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Authority that does not exist. Authority that exists but has been superseded, or a regulation superseded by a statutory amendment the corpus has not caught up with. A memorandum decision described as though it were precedent. This happens overwhelmingly on general-purpose assistants with no bound corpus, and Circular 230 and the Statements on Standards for Tax Services are unambiguous that reliance on a tool does not move responsibility for the position off the practitioner who signs.

where_it_helps.name: First-draft workpapers, engagement letters and standard documents
where_it_helps.the_work: Writing the purpose, procedure and conclusion narrative on a workpaper. Rolling forward last year's leadsheets and tickmark legend. Assembling an engagement letter from the firm's clause library. Drafting management letter points from the deficiencies already identified.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Produces drafts from the firm's own templates, clause library and prior-year file, leaving the preparer to edit rather than to type.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: A current template and clause library, controlled prior-year file access, and one hard procedural rule: the narrative is written after the procedure, from what was actually done. Never generated in advance as a prompt to be filled in later. That rule has to be enforced in the workflow, not in a training deck.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: typing, not thinking. Small per workpaper, meaningful across a full file, perhaps half an hour on an engagement letter. An estimate, and the saving is eaten immediately if reviewers start rewriting generated narrative.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The one that ends engagements and occasionally careers. A generated narrative describing a procedure that was not performed, sitting in the document that is the legal record of the engagement. Fluent boilerplate is the natural output of a language model, and boilerplate that overstates the work done is a documentation failure rather than a style problem, of the kind that has produced regulator sanctions and licence action when found. Rolled-forward workpapers carry a second risk: last year's scope silently applied to a year in which the client changed.

where_it_helps.name: Natural-language querying of the client's ledger
where_it_helps.the_work: The ad hoc question in the middle of fieldwork. Which vendors did we pay materially more this year than last. Which customers sit outside normal terms. Today that is an export and a pivot table, and it takes fifteen minutes.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Turns a typed question into a query over the client's trial balance or transaction detail and returns a figure, a table or a chart. The ambiguity that matters is accounting ambiguity: which entities are in the set, posting date or effective date, before or after topside and consolidation adjustments, gross or net of intercompany eliminations, and whether a mapped account grouping or the raw chart of accounts is being summed.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: A curated semantic layer over the client's data, a clean chart of accounts, and visibility of the generated query. All three are absent at most mid-market clients, which is why this demonstrates beautifully and deploys badly.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: it replaces a pivot table. A few minutes per question, given back the first time someone re-runs the question and gets a different number. An estimate, and a small one.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The number cannot go into a workpaper because the derivation is not reproducible by anyone else. The ambiguity lives in the question, not the answer, and the join the tool chose is invisible. On a client with three legal entities, intercompany eliminations and a chart of accounts nobody has cleaned since 2011, the confident answer is usually wrong in a way nobody catches.

where_it_does_not.claim: Test 100 per cent of the population instead of sampling, and the audit gets shorter.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Three separate reasons. Testing every recorded transaction tells you nothing about transactions that were never recorded, so completeness still needs other evidence. The evidence standards require the auditor to establish that the data analysed is itself complete and accurate (PCAOB AS 1105 on issuer audits, AU-C 500 as revised by SAS No. 142 on non-issuer audits), so you acquire an extract-testing obligation roughly where the sampling work used to be. And a scan returning six thousand exceptions is not evidence until every one has been dispositioned and documented, so the hours move from selecting to clearing rather than disappearing. Separately, an analytic run over a population is often still an analytical procedure. To stand as substantive evidence it needs an expectation precise enough to detect a misstatement that could be material and a threshold for investigating differences set before the procedure is run. Most population scans sold into firms have neither.

where_it_does_not.claim: The tool assesses risk, sets materiality and plans the engagement.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Materiality and risk assessment are judgements the engagement partner is responsible for and has to document, and the standards on supervision and engagement responsibility put that on a named person, not on software. The arithmetic was never the constraint anyway: materiality is a benchmark choice and a percentage, and it takes a partner ten minutes. What actually takes time is knowing the client, and a model that has read last year's file does not know that the CFO left in March, that the bank covenant was renegotiated verbally, or that the new revenue contracts have side letters. Firms that buy planning automation end up with a well-formatted planning memo that a reviewer has to redo, which is worse than a blank one.

where_it_does_not.claim: Point a firm-wide assistant at all your client files and let anyone ask it anything.
where_it_does_not.why_not: The regulatory problem and the technical problem coincide, which is rare and should be taken seriously. Tax return information may not be disclosed or used outside narrowly defined permissions without written taxpayer consent obtained in the prescribed form, and consent cannot be bundled into general terms. Confidential client information generally cannot be given to a third-party service provider without either a confidentiality agreement with the provider or the client's consent. And an audit file is a legal record that can be produced in litigation, where a memo containing another client's facts because the retrieval crossed engagement boundaries is not a bug you can explain away. A firm-wide corpus is the default architecture vendors propose and the one that should be refused; the defensible shape is retrieval scoped to the engagement, with cross-client access an exception that is logged.

where_it_does_not.claim: We will generate the financial statements for your audit clients.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Preparing an attest client's financial statements is a nonattest service that creates self-review and management-participation threats. For issuers, bookkeeping and preparing the accounting records or financial statements for an audit client is essentially off the table under the SEC's auditor independence rules. For private clients it has to clear the AICPA's general requirements for nonattest services, including a client with suitable skill, knowledge and experience who accepts responsibility, and it has to be documented. A tool does not change who did the work or whose judgement is embedded in it. A firm that buys this is buying an independence finding at its next peer review.

where_it_does_not.claim: Anomaly detection will catch the fraud.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Material fraud is usually committed by someone with the authority to make the entry look ordinary, or it lives outside the ledger entirely: side agreements, verbal channel-stuffing arrangements, undisclosed related parties, revenue recognised on contracts whose real terms are in an email. Anomaly detection scores the ledger, and the ledger is the artefact being manipulated. Then the base rate finishes the argument: material fraud is rare, so even a well-calibrated model returns overwhelmingly false positives, and a team that clears two hundred false positives has learned, by construction, to clear the two hundred and first without looking. Anomaly scoring is a decent way to choose a sample. It is not a detection control and should never be described to an audit committee as one.

where_it_does_not.claim: This will solve busy season.
where_it_does_not.why_not: The binding constraint in most firms is reviewer and signer hours plus client responsiveness, not preparer hours. Accelerating preparation moves the queue to the reviewer, who is the same overcommitted partner as last year, and a longer reviewer queue in March is not an improvement. The two most common reasons a return sits untouched are a missing K-1 and an unanswered client question, and neither is a model problem. Unless the review step changes or the client-chase changes, throughput does not change. The honest first-year expectation is less overtime for staff rather than more returns out of the door, which is worth having and is not what was sold. Measure it on your own engagements before repeating anyone's figure, including this one.

where_it_does_not.claim: It lets us run the same practice with fewer preparers, or without the first-year intake.
where_it_does_not.why_not: The preparer tier is also the training pipeline. Reviewers and signers are produced by people who spent two or three seasons keying source documents, tying out statements and clearing exceptions, and that is where the error signature of a bad K-1 or a wrong cut-off is learned. Cut the tier that does the mechanical work and you have optimised the step that was not binding while starving the step that was, with the damage arriving four to six years later as an absence of managers. There is a second-order version of the same problem: a staff member whose first three seasons consist of accepting extracted output learns to accept output, and that is precisely the reviewer you do not want on the file when the tool is wrong.

preconditions: You can produce a complete general ledger extract for a client, tied to the signed trial balance, by a documented method a second person could repeat next year. If you cannot do this, every analytics tool you buy will produce output you cannot put in a workpaper, because you will not be able to evidence the completeness and accuracy of what it analysed, which PCAOB AS 1105 requires on issuer audits and AU-C 500 requires on everything else.

The consent and contracting layer is in place before any client data reaches a third-party model. That means written taxpayer consent in the prescribed form where tax return information is involved, a confidentiality arrangement with the provider or client consent to its use, engagement letter language that matches what you are actually doing, and a provider contract that excludes training on your data, caps retention, names sub-processors and states where processing happens. Retrofitting this after a pilot is expensive and sometimes impossible.

Output lands inside the system of record: the return in the tax software, the workpaper in the engagement file, the adjustment in the trial balance software. If the tool's result has to be copied by hand, the saving is gone, a transcription error has been introduced, and the review trail now runs through someone's clipboard. Integration is the precondition, not a later phase.

The firm's own methodology exists in a current, machine-readable form: the disclosure checklist, the workpaper templates, the clause library, the tickmark conventions. A tool checking work against last year's checklist is worse than no tool, because it returns a clean report.

One named person owns AI tooling as part of the firm's system of quality management. Who approves a tool for engagement use, what testing supported that approval, what happens when the vendor changes the model version underneath you mid-season, and how the change is documented. Both the AICPA and PCAOB quality management regimes expect a firm to identify and respond to risks arising from the resources it uses, and a tool nobody owns is a finding waiting to be written. Note the timing: SQMS No. 1 systems were to be designed and implemented by 15 December 2025, while PCAOB QC 1000 was postponed to 15 December 2026, so a firm doing both work streams is running them a year apart.

Reproducibility discipline is agreed before the first engagement, not after. An experienced auditor with no prior connection to the engagement has to understand from the workpaper alone what was run, on what data, with what parameters and tool version, what exceptions came out, and how each was resolved. 'The tool flagged nothing' is not documentation. Note also that the PCAOB's documentation completion window is now 14 days after report release, so there is less room than there was to tidy a file after an analytic produced more exceptions than expected.

You have run the independence and conflicts question first: whether what the tool does for an attest client is a nonattest service, whether your client uses the same tool in a way that creates a self-review issue, and whether anything in the arrangement gives the provider or the firm a financial interest in the outcome.

You are piloting on an engagement with clean data and a cooperative client, and you have accepted that the messiest client is the last one to move, not the first. The instinct to pilot where the pain is greatest is how these programmes die in month four.

You have decided what happens to the staffing model before the tool arrives, not after, because the preparer tier is also the manager pipeline and the decision is much harder to reverse than the licence is.

regulation.name: PCAOB AS 1105, Audit Evidence (technology-assisted analysis amendments)
regulation.citation: PCAOB AS 1105, Audit Evidence, as amended by PCAOB Release No. 2024-007, approved by the SEC in August 2024 (Exchange Act Release No. 34-100774); see in particular paragraph .10A. Effective for audits of financial statements for fiscal years beginning on or after 15 December 2025. See also PCAOB Release No. 2025-004 (18 September 2025), a Board policy statement on implementation of paragraph .10A(b), and the accompanying staff guidance from the Office of the Chief Auditor giving examples of its application.
regulation.what_it_requires: Sets out the auditor's responsibilities when designing and performing procedures that involve technology-assisted analysis of information in electronic form, including establishing that information produced by the company and used as audit evidence is complete and accurate. Paragraph .10A addresses external information in electronic form provided by the company: the auditor obtains an understanding of the source and of the company's process for receiving, maintaining and processing that information, and tests the information or the relevant controls. The requirements are principles-based and scalable to risk; the September 2025 policy statement describes circumstances, broadly where there is no more than a remote possibility that the information has been modified so as to be unreliable for the audit, in which the Board will not treat the absence of separate testing under .10A(b) as noncompliance. In practice this is the standard that makes the extract, not the analytic, the audited object. It applies to issuer and broker-dealer audits only.

regulation.name: PCAOB AS 2301, The Auditor's Responses to the Risks of Material Misstatement
regulation.citation: PCAOB AS 2301, amended in the same package as AS 1105 by PCAOB Release No. 2024-007; effective for audits of financial statements for fiscal years beginning on or after 15 December 2025.
regulation.what_it_requires: Addresses designing and performing audit procedures that use technology-assisted analysis, including distinguishing when such a procedure serves as a risk assessment procedure, a substantive procedure, or both, and what has to be true for it to provide substantive evidence. A scan that identifies items for further examination is not, without more, substantive testing of the items it did not identify.

regulation.name: PCAOB AS 1215, Audit Documentation
regulation.citation: PCAOB AS 1215, Audit Documentation. The documentation completion date was shortened from 45 days to 14 days after the report release date by the amendments adopted alongside AS 1000 on 13 May 2024, phased by firm size: for firms that issued audit reports for more than 100 issuers during calendar 2024, audits of fiscal years beginning on or after 15 December 2024; for all other registered firms, fiscal years beginning on or after 15 December 2025. Retention remains seven years from the report release date. A further version of AS 1215 carrying conforming amendments from the postponed QC 1000 package takes effect 15 December 2026, so check which version of the text applies to the engagement in front of you rather than relying on this summary.
regulation.what_it_requires: Documentation must be sufficient for an experienced auditor with no previous connection to the engagement to understand the nature, timing, extent and results of the procedures performed, the evidence obtained, and the conclusions reached, and to determine who performed and who reviewed the work. This is the requirement that machine-assisted procedures most often fail: the output is retained but the inputs, parameters, tool version and disposition of exceptions are not. The shortened assembly window also compresses the time available to complete a file after an analytic produced more exceptions than expected.

regulation.name: AU-C 230, Audit Documentation (AICPA, non-issuer audits)
regulation.citation: AU-C section 230, Audit Documentation (SAS No. 122, as amended). Assembly of the final audit file no later than 60 days following the report release date, and retention for a period no shorter than five years from the report release date. Confirm both against the current text of the section; they differ from the PCAOB's.
regulation.what_it_requires: The non-issuer analogue of AS 1215, built on the same experienced-auditor standard: the documentation must let an experienced auditor with no previous connection to the engagement understand what was done, by whom, on what evidence, and with what conclusion. Firms that audit only private companies are governed by this section and not by the PCAOB's 14-day window, a distinction vendors routinely blur when selling documentation urgency.

regulation.name: AU-C 500, Audit Evidence (SAS No. 142)
regulation.citation: AU-C section 500, Audit Evidence, as superseded by SAS No. 142 (issued July 2020), effective for audits of financial statements for periods ending on or after 15 December 2022.
regulation.what_it_requires: Modernised the evidence framework to contemplate automated tools and techniques explicitly. Directs the auditor to consider attributes of information including relevance, reliability, authenticity and susceptibility to management bias, and contemplates a procedure performed with automated tools serving both a risk assessment and a substantive objective where the objectives of both are actually achieved. That last point is routinely misquoted by vendors as permission to treat any population analytic as substantive evidence. It is not. This is the non-issuer counterpart to the PCAOB's AS 1105 amendments and is the standard most mid-market firms are actually working under.

regulation.name: AU-C 315, Understanding the Entity and Assessing Risks (SAS No. 145)
regulation.citation: AU-C section 315, Understanding the Entity and Its Environment and Assessing the Risks of Material Misstatement, as superseded by SAS No. 145 (issued October 2021), effective for audits of financial statements for periods ending on or after 15 December 2023.
regulation.what_it_requires: Requires the auditor to understand the entity's IT environment and to identify risks arising from IT, including from the entity's use of automated tools, and separates the assessment of inherent and control risk. Relevant here in both directions: it governs how the auditor treats a client that has itself deployed AI in its accounting processes, and it is the section under which a firm's own automated risk assessment procedures have to be evaluated.

regulation.name: Substantive analytical procedures: PCAOB AS 2305 and AU-C 520
regulation.citation: PCAOB AS 2305, Substantive Analytical Procedures; AICPA AU-C section 520, Analytical Procedures. Requirements described rather than quoted by paragraph.
regulation.what_it_requires: To use an analytical procedure as substantive evidence, the auditor must develop an expectation precise enough that a difference which could be material would be identified, and must establish, before performing the procedure, the amount of difference that will be investigated. This is the line between an analytical procedure and substantive testing, and it is the line most AI-driven population analytics fall on the wrong side of.

regulation.name: Journal entry testing for fraud: PCAOB AS 2401 and AU-C 240
regulation.citation: PCAOB AS 2401, Consideration of Fraud in a Financial Statement Audit; AICPA AU-C section 240, Consideration of Fraud in a Financial Statement Audit.
regulation.what_it_requires: Requires testing of journal entries and other adjustments for evidence of possible material misstatement due to fraud, including selection of entries made at the end of a reporting period. A risk-scoring tool can inform selection, but the auditor remains responsible for the completeness of the population from which the selection was made, and for the conclusion drawn.

regulation.name: Materiality, supervision and who is responsible for the engagement
regulation.citation: PCAOB AS 2105, Consideration of Materiality in Planning and Performing an Audit; PCAOB AS 1201, Supervision of the Audit Engagement; PCAOB AS 1000, General Responsibilities of the Auditor in Conducting an Audit. AICPA counterparts: AU-C section 320, Materiality in Planning and Performing an Audit, and AU-C section 220, Quality Management for an Engagement Conducted in Accordance With Generally Accepted Auditing Standards (SAS No. 146). Requirements described rather than quoted by paragraph; confirm the effective date of SAS No. 146 for your engagements.
regulation.what_it_requires: Materiality determination, risk assessment and the direction, supervision and review of the engagement are the responsibility of named individuals, with the engagement partner responsible for the engagement and its performance. Work performed by anyone or anything else has to be directed, supervised and reviewed, and the conclusions remain the engagement team's. There is no route by which a tool holds that responsibility, which is why 'the system set materiality' is not an answer available to a firm in an inspection or a peer review.

regulation.name: Independence: AICPA nonattest services rules and SEC auditor independence rules
regulation.citation: AICPA Code of Professional Conduct, ET section 1.295, Nonattest Services, including the general requirements interpretation at 1.295.040; SEC Regulation S-X, Rule 2-01, 17 CFR 210.2-01, in particular paragraph (c)(4) on non-audit services, including (c)(4)(i) bookkeeping and (c)(4)(ii) financial information systems design and implementation; PCAOB Rule 3520, Auditor Independence, and Rule 3525 on audit committee pre-approval of non-audit services related to internal control over financial reporting.
regulation.what_it_requires: Nonattest services to an attest client create self-review and management-participation threats and are permitted only where the client accepts responsibility, designates an individual with suitable skill, knowledge and experience to oversee the service, and the arrangement is documented. For SEC issuer audit clients, bookkeeping and preparing the accounting records or financial statements, and designing or implementing financial information systems, are restricted or prohibited outright. Deploying a tool that produces a client's accounting records or financial statements does not move the judgement off the firm, and neither does describing the tool as the client's.

regulation.name: Confidentiality and third-party service providers
regulation.citation: AICPA Code of Professional Conduct, ET section 1.700.001, Confidential Client Information Rule, and the interpretation at ET section 1.700.040, Disclosing Information to a Third-Party Service Provider.
regulation.what_it_requires: A member in public practice may not disclose confidential client information without the client's specific consent. Before disclosing such information to a third-party service provider, the member must either enter into a contractual confidentiality arrangement with the provider, with reasonable assurance the provider has procedures preventing unauthorised release, or inform the client that a provider may be used and obtain consent. A cloud AI vendor processing client files is a third-party service provider for this purpose, whatever the vendor's marketing calls it, and so is a sub-processor the vendor uses. Verify the interpretation number against the current Code before quoting it in a policy document.

regulation.name: Tax return information: IRC section 7216 and its regulations
regulation.citation: 26 U.S.C. section 7216 (criminal) and section 6713 (civil penalty); Treas. Reg. sections 301.7216-1 through 301.7216-3, in particular 301.7216-2 (permissible disclosures and uses without consent) and 301.7216-3 (disclosure or use permitted only with the taxpayer's consent). For Form 1040 series returns, the required form and content of consents is in Rev. Proc. 2013-14, which modified and superseded Rev. Proc. 2008-35 and whose effective date was extended by Rev. Proc. 2013-19.
regulation.what_it_requires: A tax return preparer may not disclose or use a taxpayer's tax return information except as specifically authorised, without a knowing and voluntary written consent that names the recipient, states the purpose, and is obtained in the prescribed form and before the disclosure. Auxiliary services within the United States that assist in preparing, processing or filing a return may fall within the permissible-disclosure rules, but assistance involving substantive determinations on the return does not. Disclosure outside the United States carries additional consent content requirements. Criminal and civil penalties apply. This is the single most likely place for an enthusiastic tax practice to break the law with an AI pilot.

regulation.name: Safeguarding client data: FTC Safeguards Rule
regulation.citation: FTC Standards for Safeguarding Customer Information, 16 CFR part 314, as amended in 2021 with compliance for the amended provisions from 9 June 2023, and further amended in 2023 to require notification to the Commission of a notification event involving unencrypted customer information of 500 or more consumers, effective 13 May 2024. See also IRS Publication 4557, Safeguarding Taxpayer Data.
regulation.what_it_requires: Tax preparers are treated as financial institutions subject to the Rule and must maintain a written information security programme with a qualified individual responsible for it, risk assessment, access controls, encryption, vendor oversight, incident response, and reporting of qualifying breaches to the FTC within 30 days of discovery. Adding an AI vendor is a change to your data flows and belongs in the risk assessment and the vendor oversight process, not in a footnote.

regulation.name: AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services
regulation.citation: AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services No. 1 through 4, adopted May 2023 and effective 1 January 2024; in particular SSTS No. 1 section 1.3, Data Protection, and section 1.4, Reliance on Tools.
regulation.what_it_requires: Requires reasonable efforts to safeguard taxpayer data, including data held or transmitted electronically, with regard to applicable law; and provides that a member may rely on tools such as preparation software and research platforms but must exercise due professional care in doing so, with reliance on a tool not relieving the member of responsibilities under the Code. The stated purpose of a tool is to improve the member's performance of the service, not to replace the member's judgement.

regulation.name: Circular 230
regulation.citation: Regulations Governing Practice before the Internal Revenue Service, 31 CFR part 10 (Treasury Department Circular No. 230), including section 10.22 (diligence as to accuracy), section 10.34 (standards for signing and advising on returns) and section 10.35 (competence).
regulation.what_it_requires: A practitioner must exercise due diligence in preparing and filing returns and other documents and in determining the correctness of representations made to the IRS and to clients, and must be competent in the matters undertaken. Reliance on the work product of another person is permitted only with reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training and evaluating that person. A model is not a person, so the diligence sits entirely with the practitioner who signs.

regulation.name: Quality management: AICPA SQMS No. 1 and PCAOB QC 1000
regulation.citation: AICPA Statement on Quality Management Standards No. 1, A Firm's System of Quality Management, with systems required to be designed and implemented by 15 December 2025 and the first evaluation of the system within one year after that date; PCAOB QC 1000, A Firm's System of Quality Control, whose effective date the Board postponed in August 2025 by one year to 15 December 2026, with PCAOB Rule 3400T and the interim quality control standards remaining in effect until then.
regulation.what_it_requires: Both regimes require a firm to identify and assess quality risks arising from its resources, including technological resources, and to design responses. In practice that means the firm must be able to say which AI tools are approved for engagement use, on what basis, who monitors them, and how a change by the vendor is detected and evaluated. An unmanaged tool in use across engagements is a quality management deficiency independent of whether it ever produced a wrong answer.

regulation.name: Using the work of a specialist
regulation.citation: PCAOB AS 1210, Using the Work of an Auditor-Engaged Specialist; AICPA AU-C section 620, Using the Work of an Auditor's Specialist. Requirements described rather than quoted by paragraph.
regulation.what_it_requires: Where a firm relies on an external party's model or methodology as specialist work rather than as a tool it controls, these standards govern evaluating the specialist's knowledge, objectivity and the appropriateness of the work as evidence. Relevant when a vendor supplies not just software but a valuation, estimation or scoring methodology the engagement team cannot itself explain, which is a question worth asking of any scoring tool whose weighting the vendor treats as proprietary.

regulation.name: Scope note: jurisdiction and other regimes not covered here
regulation.citation: Described, not cited.
regulation.what_it_requires: Everything above is United States federal law, PCAOB standards and AICPA standards, and it is what a US firm's general counsel needs. A firm with UK, EU, Canadian or Australian practices is additionally subject to that jurisdiction's audit regulator, ethics code and data protection law, and in the EU to the AI Act's obligations, which turn on the use case rather than on the sector. State boards of accountancy impose their own rules and adopt the AICPA Code with variations, and state breach-notification statutes apply alongside the Safeguards Rule. Take local advice before assuming this list is complete for a non-US engagement.

sectors.economics:
The licence is the small number and the only one most firms model. Per-seat AI add-ons in audit and tax suites typically sit in the low hundreds to low thousands of dollars per user per year at list, and some vendors price per return, per engagement or as an uplift folded into the suite renewal rather than as a visible line, which makes year-on-year comparison harder than it looks. A firm with a hundred chargeable staff is looking at a mid five-figure to low six-figure annual line. Treat that as roughly a quarter of the real first-year cost. These are estimates, they move with negotiated pricing and volume, and they should be checked against your own quotes rather than against this paragraph.

Integration into the system of record is the first unbudgeted item. Output that cannot land in the engagement file or the return has to be re-keyed, which eliminates the saving and adds a transcription risk. Where the vendor has no native bridge into your practice management, audit or tax platform, budget the integration as its own project, commonly one to three times the first-year licence as an order of magnitude, and assume it recurs at a smaller scale every time either vendor ships a major release.

The second unbudgeted item is per-client data extraction, and it is the one that catches audit practices. Every client's general ledger extract is bespoke. It has to be complete, tied to the trial balance, and repeatable by someone else next year, and it breaks when the client upgrades their ERP or changes their chart of accounts. This is a per-client onboarding cost that recurs partially every year, it is invisible in any vendor demonstration because the demonstration data is already clean, and for a firm with sixty audit clients it can plausibly exceed the licence cost outright.

The human review does not go away, and in year one it gets worse. Everything going into a workpaper or a return is reviewed at the same standard as before. Reviewers who have not yet learned a tool's error signature review its output more slowly than a competent preparer's, because they do not yet know which fields to distrust. Expect throughput on piloted engagements to fall for the first season and to recover in the second. Budget calibration time explicitly: several weeks of reduced output per team, not a two-hour training session.

Model governance and documentation is a standing cost with a name attached. Tool approval, testing evidence, version-change monitoring, the quality management response under SQMS No. 1 or QC 1000, the peer review file, and the answers you will give an inspector. This is a fraction of a partner or director's time every year, and it is the line most often costed at zero. Add to it the professional liability question: your carrier will ask about AI use at renewal, and the answer you give is a representation.

Then there is the cost of the failure mode. It is not a wrong number in a spreadsheet. It is a workpaper narrative describing a procedure that was not performed, a population analytic whose extract was incomplete, a memo citing authority that has been superseded, or client data disclosed without the consent the statute required. The consequences are a peer review finding, an inspection comment, an engagement re-performed at the firm's own cost, a restatement, a section 7216 exposure, or a claim. Any single one of those can cost more than the programme saved in its first three years, which is why the preconditions in this document are not optional preliminaries.

Finally, the economics that nobody says out loud. If you bill hourly and the work takes fewer hours, the saving arrives as a revenue reduction unless you convert it into fixed fees or into more engagements with the same headcount. The mechanism points to the first-year benefit landing as less overtime and better staff retention through busy season rather than as margin, and that is a real and defensible return. It is also a claim you should test on your own realisation and utilisation data before you put it in a business case, because it is not where the software was aimed and it is not what the vendor's model assumed.
sectors.first_step: Before buying anything, pick your three largest audit clients and attempt to produce a complete prior-year general ledger extract for each: every module and sub-ledger, every consolidation-layer and topside entry, agreeing to the signed trial balance, with the extraction method written down well enough that a different person could repeat it next year. Time how long each one takes and note who had to be involved on the client side. Most firms discover they cannot do this repeatably for at least one of the three, and that finding is worth more than any pilot, because the extract is the input every analytics tool needs and the thing you have to defend under AS 1105 on issuer work or AU-C 500 on everything else. If the practice is tax-led, run the equivalent test instead: take last season's fifty largest 1040 engagements and measure how many calendar days each return spent waiting on a missing document or an unanswered client question, versus how many hours were spent preparing it. Whichever number is larger tells you where the constraint actually is, and it is usually not where the software is aimed.

sectors.label: Manufacturing
sectors.lede: Manufacturing has more genuinely useful AI applications available to it than most plants are shown, and a worse hit rate than the pipeline of proposals suggests, for one reason: the applications that work need plant-floor data sitting behind an OT network deliberately built to keep software out, and the application that gets bought first — predictive maintenance — usually fails on a data problem that no amount of modelling fixes. If your maintenance history holds four examples of the failure you want to predict, you do not have a modelling problem, you have nothing to model. The honest reading of most plants puts vision inspection, supplier document handling and warranty text analysis well ahead of the thing on the vendor's first slide.

where_it_helps.name: Automated visual inspection on a defined defect set
where_it_helps.the_work: An inspector on each shift compares parts against a boundary-sample board and the visual characteristic on the control plan, tallies defects on a check sheet, and dispositions suspects to the quarantine cage. On a high-volume line this 100% visual screen exists because the process is not capable enough to drop it, and it is written into the control plan as a containment — often added after a customer complaint and never removed.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: A fixed camera station with supervised classification or segmentation, trained on your own labelled parts, flags defects to a reject gate and writes the result against the serial or lot. It works on defects that present as contrast under controlled light — surface porosity, missing features, weld spatter, solder bridging, label and print faults, seal integrity. It does not work on defects you cannot see in the image, and no model recovers information the optics never captured.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Repeatable part presentation, fixed optics and lighting chosen for the defect physics rather than for general use, a PLC trigger and handshake with a defined behaviour on no-read, and confirmation that the reject actually left the line. As a rule of thumb, several hundred to a few thousand labelled images per defect class, including examples either side of the accept line; one agreed defect taxonomy; MES write-back keyed to serial; a named person who owns disposition of the ambiguous ones. Agree the acceptance criteria before the build — the escape rate and false-reject rate you will hold it to — and plan for an attribute measurement systems analysis against the boundary samples, because in a customer-audited plant the station cannot be relied on for disposition until it passes one.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Estimate, volume-dependent: it displaces part of an inspection position per shift, but the money is in escape reduction. One avoided containment event at a customer plant — sorting labour, premium freight, line-down charges — can exceed the cost of the whole cell. Below a few thousand parts a shift the headcount arithmetic rarely works on its own, and should not be the basis of the case.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Drift, and then abandonment. A new supplier lot changes surface finish, a lamp ages, a fixture is nudged during changeover — the false-reject rate climbs, operators start overriding at the HMI, and within a month everything is being re-inspected by hand behind the machine. Usually nobody is trending the false-reject rate, so the drift is invisible until scrap or sort hours move. The second failure is taxonomy collapse: it turns out four inspectors meant four different things by "scratch", so the labels contradict each other and the model learns the disagreement.

where_it_helps.name: Incoming inspection and supplier document handling
where_it_helps.the_work: An SQE or receiving inspector opens a PPAP package, an EN 10204 3.1 mill certificate, a certificate of analysis or a certificate of conformity, keys values into the receiving record, compares them against the drawing and the approved specification, chases the supplier for the dimension that is missing, and decides whether to raise a deviation or reject the lot. Most of this is transcription, and the transcription is where errors enter the record.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Extracts values from certificates, first-article reports and ballooned drawings, checks them against the specification limits held in the item master, and raises a discrepancy for a human rather than a pass. Also flags the missing document and the required characteristic that is simply not on the certificate — the failure most often missed by a tired reviewer at the end of a shift.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: An item master holding machine-readable specification limits rather than a scanned drawing, a document store where certificates actually land, write-back into ERP or the QMS so the result lives in the receiving record, a list of which documents each supplier owes, and confidence thresholds with mandatory human review on anything near or outside limit. Mark your key, critical and safety characteristics so those never auto-pass regardless of confidence.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Estimate: minutes per document across thousands of documents a year, plus the harder-to-price gain of catching an out-of-spec certificate that would otherwise have been signed off. It scales with the number of certificate-bearing receipts, not with revenue — count those receipts before sizing anything.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Silent mis-extraction from a fax-quality scan. A wrong hardness or chemistry value posted into the record as verified is worse than no automation at all, because it now carries the authority of the system and will be cited back at you in a traceability exercise. This only stays safe if out-of-range and low-confidence readings are routed to a person, and that routing is where part of the time saving goes back.

where_it_helps.name: Warranty and field-failure narrative analysis
where_it_helps.the_work: A warranty analyst reads dealer and field-service narratives — the complaint, cause and correction text — assigns a failure code, builds the monthly Pareto, and tries to see a spike early enough to contain it before it becomes a campaign. Coding is inconsistent because labour operation codes are chosen for how they pay, not for what broke, so the Pareto describes the reimbursement scheme as much as the product.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Classifies free-text claim narratives into engineering failure modes, joins them to build genealogy — serial or VIN to lot, line, shift and build date — and surfaces emerging-issue signals against a baseline rather than waiting for the monthly cut. The value is in time-to-detection, not in the classification itself.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Genealogy that actually resolves: a serial that ties to component lots and build conditions. Claim-level text, not a summary table. A defined baseline so "emerging" means something. An escalation owner, because an early signal with nobody empowered to contain is just a report. And a route to legal or compliance built in from the start, because in regulated product categories an early signal is knowledge, and knowledge can start a statutory reporting clock — see the defect-reporting entry below.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Estimate: weeks off time-to-detection on an emerging field issue. Each week earlier is population not yet built, not yet shipped and not yet in service — on a running line that is a directly countable number of units, and it dominates any analyst-hours saved. Do the count on your own build rate before accepting anyone's figure.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The model learns the payment code rather than the physics, so it reproduces the existing distortion faster and with more authority. And where genealogy breaks — a component lot not recorded, a supersession that renamed the part — the signal points at the wrong plant or the wrong month, and the containment lands on the wrong population, which is expensive in both directions.

where_it_helps.name: Maintenance and work-instruction retrieval
where_it_helps.the_work: A technician at two in the morning with a line down, an OEM manual as a 400-page PDF, electrical schematics in a binder, and a machine modified three times since that manual was printed. Separately, a process engineer rewriting a work instruction after an engineering change, reconciling it against what the cell actually does.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Retrieval across OEM manuals, schematics, closed work orders, engineering change notices and internal write-ups, answering with a citation to the source page so the technician can check it before acting. For work instructions it produces a draft for a human to approve through document control — never a published revision.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: The documents to have been collected and to be current, red-lines reconciled against as-built, an explicit rule that output is a draft, and document control that stamps the revision. Where a plant has real as-built drift and no red-line discipline, this is not ready — fixing the documents is the project, and it is a larger project than the software.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Estimate: diagnostic minutes per breakdown, concentrated in the long tail of faults a given technician has not seen before. On a constrained line, downtime minutes convert directly at the line's contribution rate, so the arithmetic is easy to do and easy to check afterwards against the downtime log.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Confidently citing the superseded revision, or the sister machine's schematic. Retrieval is exactly as current as your document control, and in most plants document control is not current on the floor. A technician who is burned once by a wrong pin-out stops using it permanently, and tells the others — the tool dies by word of mouth in a week.

where_it_helps.name: Finite scheduling and sequencing
where_it_helps.the_work: A planner rebuilds the week in a spreadsheet every Monday and repairs it hourly against a changeover matrix, tool and fixture availability, one qualified operator on the grinder, a hot customer pull-in, and material that did not arrive. The published schedule and the schedule actually run diverge by Tuesday.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: This is mathematical optimisation — mixed-integer or constraint programming — not a language model, and buyers should be clear which they are being sold; finite scheduling has existed for decades and its failures are adoption failures, not algorithmic ones. Machine learning has a narrower and genuinely useful role feeding it: predicting realistic run rates, yields and changeover durations from historical performance instead of the standards last touched years ago.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Routings and cycle times that reflect reality, a maintained changeover matrix, tool and fixture availability as data rather than as a whiteboard, material availability from the real ERP position, and — hardest — the planner's unwritten rules written down. Every one of those rules that stays in their head becomes an infeasible schedule. It also needs a decision about who owns the published sequence, because two schedules in circulation is worse than one bad one.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Estimate: recovered changeover hours per week on a constrained cell, plus reduced expediting.
