Within two years you have automated your own historical habits and lost the ability to see it. Separately, any model that influences case reserves changes reported loss development, which changes actuarial indications, which changes rate filings — and almost nobody budgets the actuarial work needed to separate the model's effect from real trend. Geographic features in a severity model are a redlining exposure; if ZIP code or anything that stands in for it is driving the routing, you have a problem under the unfair trade practice statute regardless of your intent.

where_it_helps.name: Policy wording and form deviation comparison
where_it_helps.the_work: A coverage lawyer, a wholesale broker or a reinsurance underwriter compares a manuscript wording or a competitor's form against the company's standard form, or against the bureau base form plus the endorsement schedule, and produces the list of deviations that actually change the coverage grant, the exclusions, the definitions or the conditions.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Aligns the two documents clause by clause and produces a deviation list, quoting both texts side by side, flagging where a definition has been altered, where an exclusion has been narrowed or deleted by endorsement, and where a condition precedent has moved.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: A fixed, authoritative comparison base — your standard form at a specific edition date, with the endorsement library — held as text rather than scanned images. Output must be quote-and-cite with clause references, never paraphrase. A reviewer who knows the line of business, because the tool produces the candidate list and a human decides what matters. Note also that bureau forms are licensed: check what your advisory organisation's licence permits you to load into a third-party system before you load it.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: The mechanism is that the reviewer stops hunting for the differences and starts judging them. Order of magnitude, an estimate: on a long manuscript wording this is the difference between an afternoon and an hour, and the value is concentrated in the deviations a tired reviewer would have missed at clause ninety of a hundred and forty.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Paraphrase. The moment the output summarises a deviation rather than quoting it, it is unusable — and worse than unusable, because it reads as though the work has been done. The second failure is that what changes coverage is frequently not in the clause under comparison: a definition three pages away, a state amendatory endorsement, or a single deleted word in a condition. Comparison tools are good at finding textual differences and poor at knowing which ones matter, which is why the maturity rating here is early: the extraction works, the judgement does not, and the judgement is the job.

where_it_does_not.claim: Automated claim decisioning — a system that approves, denies, reduces or delays a claim payment without a person making the decision.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Adjusting a loss is a licensed act. Texas Insurance Code Chapter 4101 governs insurance adjusters, and Texas Commissioner's Bulletin B-0003-26 (12 June 2026) points to it in terms: the official acts of an adjuster include investigating or adjusting losses and supervising the handling of claims, and where a regulated entity uses AI to make a consequential decision the department expects a person to review and agree with all decisions before action is taken. On the health side the rule is now statutory rather than expectational: Texas Insurance Code § 4201.156, added by SB 815 (2025) and effective 1 September 2025, provides that a utilization review agent may not use an automated decision system to make, wholly or partly, an adverse determination; California's SB 1120 (2024) and Arizona's HB 2175 (2025, effective 1 July 2026) require a qualified human to make the medical necessity determination. Underneath all of that sits the unfair claims settlement practices statute in every state, which requires a reasonable investigation based on the available information. A denial you cannot attribute to a named adjuster who reviewed the file is a denial you cannot defend in a market conduct exam or in a bad-faith action, and the extra-contractual exposure on a single bad-faith verdict is larger than the entire programme's savings.

where_it_does_not.claim: A "bias-free", "fairness-certified" or "regulator-ready" third-party underwriting or pricing model.
where_it_does_not.why_not: The certificate transfers nothing. New York DFS Insurance Circular Letter No. 7 (2024) states that an insurer may not rely solely on a third party's claim of non-discrimination or on a proprietary third-party process to determine compliance, and that an insurer may not rely on the proprietary nature of a vendor's algorithmic processes to avoid giving an applicant the specific information a declination or rate differential was based on. The insurer must itself assess disproportionate adverse effect by protected class, evaluate whether there is a legitimate lawful explanation, and search for less discriminatory alternatives — and repeat that on a regular cadence. Worse, in most lines you do not hold race or ethnicity data, so the testing requires a proxy estimate from surname and geography, a method your own actuaries will argue about and which produces a number you then have to defend. The vendor cannot do any of this for you, and buying the model does not start the work, it starts the clock.

where_it_does_not.claim: Generative AI answering coverage questions — for policyholders, for producers, or producing a coverage position for an adjuster.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Coverage depends on the specific form edition on that policy, the endorsements attached to it, the state amendatory endorsement, the limits and sublimits, and the case law in that jurisdiction. A model that is right ninety-five per cent of the time about coverage is a machine for misrepresenting policy provisions at scale — and misrepresentation of the terms of a policy is an enumerated unfair trade practice under the state statutes modelled on the NAIC Unfair Trade Practices Act (Model #880). There is no tolerable error rate, because the errors are not distributed randomly: they cluster on the unusual policies, which are exactly the ones where someone asked the question. Retrieval over the actual policy documents narrows this, and does not close it.

where_it_does_not.claim: Continuously learning or self-updating models used in rating.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Rates, rating rules and rating plans are filed and, in most states and most lines, approved or reviewed before use; the NAIC Property and Casualty Model Rating Law (Model #1780, prior approval version) carries the standard the state enactments repeat — that rates not be excessive, inadequate or unfairly discriminatory — and the NAIC Model Bulletin makes clear that the obligation holds regardless of the methodology used to develop them. A model that retrains itself is, by construction, charging a rate that is not the one you filed. A rating factor you cannot explain to a rate analyst does not get approved, and one that changes between the filing and the quote is a filing violation rather than a product feature. Adaptive learning belongs in triage and in operations, not in the rating algorithm.

where_it_does_not.claim: AI-generated claim file summaries replacing or standing in front of the adjuster's notes.
where_it_does_not.why_not: The claim file is the evidence. In a bad-faith action, in a market conduct exam, and in a coverage dispute, what is read is the file — and a generated summary is discoverable, will be compared with the underlying notes, and every divergence becomes a question for the adjuster on the stand. Summaries also propagate: a summary written at day thirty becomes what everyone reads at day two hundred, and the detail that would have changed the handling is gone. Summarisation is fine as a reading aid that sits beside the file with the underlying notes one click away. It is not fine as the artefact of record, and the distinction is operational, not philosophical — it is about which document the next handler actually opens.

where_it_does_not.claim: Predicting attorney representation or claimant litigiousness in order to adjust the settlement offer.
where_it_does_not.why_not: This is sold as segmentation and it is the single most dangerous thing in the category. Varying what you offer by predicted claimant behaviour rather than by the value of the loss is, on its face, a settlement practice not based on the facts of the claim, and the features that predict representation — neighbourhood, prior claim history, language of the first notice — track protected characteristics closely. Predicting likely litigation in order to route a claim to a more experienced adjuster earlier is defensible. Using the same prediction to decide what to pay is not, and the discovery of that model in a bad-faith case would be the worst day the claims organisation has.

preconditions: A complete inventory of every model, score and decision aid already making or supporting decisions about consumers — including the ones embedded in your policy administration and claims platforms that you did not build and may not have known were models, and the ones your vendors run on your behalf. Section 4 of the NAIC Model Bulletin, on regulatory oversight and examination considerations, puts the model inventory among the first things a department may request, and the NAIC's AI Systems Evaluation Tool asks for it in structured exhibits. It is rarely sitting on a shelf ready to hand over. Build it before you add to it.

A written AI systems programme in place before deployment, not written up afterwards. The bulletin expects a programme — the AIS Program — covering governance, risk management controls and internal audit, with responsibility vested in senior management accountable to the board or a board committee, proportionate to the potential harm to consumers. Documentation should be built to be handed to an examiner, which is a different standard from documentation built for the team that wrote the model.

A decision record, not just an outcome. For every decision a model touched: the model version, the input values as they were at the time, the output, the human who reviewed it, and when. Retained for as long as your record retention schedule requires — which is longer than most model-serving infrastructure keeps logs, and shorter than the tail on a bad-faith claim. If you cannot reconstruct in 2029 why a 2026 claim was routed to fast-track, you cannot answer the examination.

Adverse action machinery that can state, in specific terms, what a declination, limitation or rate differential rested on — including where the information came from a vendor, and including the applicant's route to correct inaccurate data. This is a federal obligation under the Fair Credit Reporting Act where a consumer report is involved, and a state expectation under the New York circular letter and the Colorado regulation. It is usually a systems change, not a policy change.

Data lineage for anything touching underwriting or pricing: for each external data source, where it came from, what it is a measure of, and the documented assessment of whether it is acting as a proxy for a protected class. Colorado's Regulation 10-1-1 and the New York circular letter both require the insurer to be able to say this about each source, and 'the vendor says it is fine' is explicitly not an answer. If you write private passenger auto, note that Colorado's 2025 amendment names telematics as an external consumer data source, so your usage-based programme is inside this.

Vendor contracts containing audit rights, a duty to cooperate with regulatory inquiries, and disclosure of data sourcing. The New York circular letter names these terms directly. Most standard insurtech agreements do not contain them, and renegotiating an in-force contract takes months — so put them in before signature, not after the pilot succeeds.

A measured baseline of the current human process, agreed before the pilot starts, in the metrics your own operation already reports: submission-to-quote cycle time and hit ratio by producer, first-notice miscoding rate measured at claim closing, subrogation identification rate from a blind re-review of closed files, SIU referral-to-established-fraud conversion. Most carriers cannot state any of these on demand. Without the baseline you will be unable to tell whether the system worked, and you will end up quoting the vendor's benchmark back to your own board.

An off-switch per use case, and the operational ability to run the old process alongside the new one for at least a full quarter — which means keeping enough trained handlers to take the volume back manually without waiting on a core system release, and knowing that your change freeze over catastrophe season and year-end may be exactly when you need to revert. Failure in this sector does not announce itself at deployment; it appears months later in the loss triangles, in reopened claims, or in a complaint pattern.

Named ownership that crosses the functions: actuarial, claims, underwriting, compliance and legal in one body with a decision record, because the question an examiner asks is who signed off, and the answer cannot be 'the data science team'.

regulation.name: NAIC Model Bulletin: Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems by Insurers
regulation.citation: NAIC Model Bulletin, "Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems by Insurers", adopted by the NAIC Executive (EX) Committee and Plenary on 4 December 2023. Adopted or issued in substantially similar form by a majority of US jurisdictions; as of the NAIC's Spring 2026 National Meeting the working group's implementation map showed twenty-four states plus the District of Columbia, with several further states — California, Colorado, New York and, since June 2026, Texas — regulating through their own insurance-specific guidance instead. Check the NAIC implementation map for the current count rather than relying on this one.
regulation.what_it_requires: It is guidance, not a statute, and it binds only where a state department has issued it. Where issued, it tells insurers to develop, implement and maintain a written programme — the AIS Program — for the responsible use of AI systems that make or support decisions related to regulated insurance practices. The programme must address governance, risk management controls and internal audit, vest responsibility with senior management accountable to the board, cover the whole insurance life cycle including underwriting, rating, claim administration and fraud detection, cover third-party systems as well as those built in-house, and be proportionate to the degree of potential harm to consumers. Section 4, on regulatory oversight and examination considerations, is the part to read first: it lists what a department may request in an investigation or market conduct action, including the written programme itself, the model inventory, documentation of data lineage and bias analysis, validation and drift testing records, third-party due diligence, and the vendor contracts.

regulation.name: State unfair trade practice and unfair claims settlement practice statutes
regulation.citation: State enactments modelled on the NAIC Unfair Trade Practices Act (Model #880) and the NAIC Unfair Claims Settlement Practices Act (Model #900). Citations differ in every state; cite your own state's code section rather than the model number.
regulation.what_it_requires: These are the enforceable backstop, and the NAIC bulletin expressly relies on them. The unfair trade practices act defines and prohibits unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts, including misrepresentation of policy terms and unfair discrimination. The claims settlement act sets standards for the investigation and disposition of claims — prompt acknowledgement and communication, reasonable investigation based on all available information, no unreasonable delay, no denial without a reasonable basis. The operative point for AI is the proposition the bulletin repeats: an insurer's conduct must comply with these statutes regardless of the methods it used to determine or support it. There is no technology defence.

regulation.name: New York DFS Insurance Circular Letter No. 7 (2024)
regulation.citation: New York State Department of Financial Services, Insurance Circular Letter No. 7 (2024), "Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems and External Consumer Data and Information Sources in Insurance Underwriting and Pricing", issued 11 July 2024, following a proposed version circulated 17 January 2024.
regulation.what_it_requires: The most demanding guidance in the United States, and worth reading in full even if you do not write in New York, because it is where other states are heading. It applies to insurers authorised to write insurance in New York — along with Article 43 corporations, HMOs, licensed fraternal benefit societies and the State Insurance Fund — using AI systems or external consumer data and information sources in underwriting or pricing. It requires demonstrated actuarial validity of each external data source, an assessment of whether a source acts as a proxy for a protected class, and a three-step analysis: test for disproportionate adverse effect by protected class, evaluate whether a legitimate lawful explanation exists, and search for less discriminatory alternatives — with the testing conducted before use, after material updates, and on a regular cadence thereafter, at least annually. It sets governance expectations at board and senior management level, requires written policies and documentation including drift testing, and requires internal audit involvement. On disclosure it is unusually blunt: adverse action notices must include details of all information the declination, limitation or rate differential was based on, and an insurer may not rely on the proprietary nature of a vendor's algorithm to avoid that specificity, nor rely solely on a vendor's claim of non-discrimination. Vendor contracts should include audit rights and an obligation to cooperate with regulatory inquiries.

regulation.name: Colorado SB 21-169 and Colorado Insurance Regulation 10-1-1
regulation.citation: Colorado Senate Bill 21-169 (2021), "Protecting Consumers from Unfair Discrimination in Insurance Practices"; implemented by Colorado Division of Insurance Regulation 10-1-1, 3 CCR 702-10, effective November 2023 for life insurers, amended by adoption on 20 August 2025 and effective 15 October 2025 to extend to private passenger automobile insurers and health benefit plan insurers.
regulation.what_it_requires: SB 21-169 prohibits unfair discrimination on the basis of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion, sex, sexual orientation, disability, gender identity or gender expression through the use of external consumer data and information sources (ECDIS) or algorithms and predictive models that use them. Regulation 10-1-1 puts the governance obligation on the insurer: a risk-based governance and risk management framework with board and senior management accountability, an inventory of ECDIS and of the models using them, documented design and testing processes, monitoring for model drift, and meaningful information to consumers about adverse decisions. The 2025 amendment names telematics as ECDIS, which brings usage-based auto programmes squarely inside. For the newly covered lines the amendment carried an interim narrative progress report due 1 December 2025 and an annual compliance report due 1 July 2026 and annually thereafter. Confirm current deadlines with the Division rather than relying on any secondary source, this one included.

regulation.name: Colorado quantitative testing — bulletin in force, testing regulation still unadopted
regulation.citation: Colorado Division of Insurance Bulletin B-10.004, "Concerning the Quantitative Testing Reporting Requirement for Life Insurers that Use External Consumer Data and Information Sources", originally issued 18 October 2024; a revised version was adopted and made effective 22 October 2025.
regulation.what_it_requires: This one is widely misdescribed and a general counsel should know the actual position. Regulation 10-1-1 requires the annual report to describe the quantitative testing conducted to detect unfair discrimination, but the Division has not, to date, adopted the separate regulation that would establish how that testing must be performed — a draft was circulated in September 2023 covering estimation of race and ethnicity by a Bayesian surname-and-geocoding method, application approval testing and premium rate testing, and it drew sustained actuarial objection on its error rate. Because the testing regulation was not adopted, B-10.004 waived the quantitative testing description for the life insurer annual reports due 1 December 2024 and 1 December 2025, and was revised in October 2025 to carry that guidance forward; the waiver has been granted report by report, not indefinitely, and every other provision of the regulation has remained enforceable throughout. Confirm the position for the current reporting year directly with the Division. The planning implication is specific: a testing obligation you cannot yet scope is coming, the proxy methodology it will most likely require is contested, and the data work to support it — clean geocoded policy and application records joined to outcomes — takes longer than the notice period will.

regulation.name: Texas Commissioner's Bulletin B-0003-26 and Texas Insurance Code Chapters 4101 and 4201
regulation.citation: Texas Department of Insurance, Commissioner's Bulletin # B-0003-26, "Use of artificial intelligence", issued 12 June 2026. Texas Insurance Code Chapter 4101 (insurance adjusters); Texas Insurance Code § 4201.156, added by SB 815, 89th Legislature (2025), effective 1 September 2025.
regulation.what_it_requires: The clearest statement to date that AI does not displace licensing. The bulletin reminds regulated entities that decisions or actions impacting consumers made or supported by AI must comply with all applicable insurance laws, including unfair trade practice and unfair discrimination laws, and extends TDI's governance expectations to third parties working with a regulated entity; it recognises the NAIC's 2020 Principles on Artificial Intelligence as an appropriate guide. It notes that the official acts of an adjuster under Chapter 4101 include investigating or adjusting losses and supervising the handling of claims, and points to Chapter 4201 on utilization review. The statutory prohibition there is sharper than the bulletin's summary: § 4201.156 provides that a utilization review agent may not use an automated decision system to make, wholly or partly, an adverse determination, while expressly permitting such systems for administrative support and fraud detection, and gives the Commissioner audit and inspection rights over their use. The bulletin's operative sentence for anyone building a claims pipeline: if a regulated entity uses AI to make a consequential decision, TDI expects a person to review and agree with all decisions before action is taken.

regulation.name: California SB 1120 (2024), the Physicians Make Decisions Act
regulation.citation: California Senate Bill 1120 (2023–2024 Regular Session), "Health care coverage: utilization review", signed September 2024, operative 1 January 2025; amends Health and Safety Code § 1367.01 (Knox-Keene) and Insurance Code § 10123.135.
regulation.what_it_requires: Where a health care service plan or disability insurer uses AI, an algorithm or other software tool in utilisation review or utilisation management, the tool may not deny, delay or modify health care services based in whole or in part on medical necessity. A determination of medical necessity must be made by a licensed physician or a licensed health care professional competent to evaluate the specific clinical issues. The statute imposes fairness and non-discrimination requirements on the tools themselves and requires that they be based on the individual enrollee's medical history and clinical circumstances rather than a group dataset alone. It does not prohibit using such tools for administrative support or to organise clinical information; the line it draws is about who makes the determination.

regulation.name: Arizona HB 2175 (2025)
regulation.citation: Arizona House Bill 2175, 57th Legislature, 1st Regular Session (2025), "claims; prior authorization; conduct", signed 12 May 2025, effective 1 July 2026.
regulation.what_it_requires: Prohibits a health care insurer from denying a claim or a prior authorisation on grounds of medical necessity, experimental or investigational status, or anything else requiring the use of medical judgement, unless a health care provider has individually reviewed the matter. The medical director must exercise independent medical judgement and is prohibited from relying solely on recommendations derived from any other source — which is the sentence that matters, because it forecloses the pattern where a human nominally signs off on a model's output at volume. Now in force.

regulation.name: Fair Credit Reporting Act — adverse action in insurance transactions
regulation.citation: 15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a); the definition of adverse action for insurance purposes sits at 15 U.S.C. § 1681a(k)(1)(B)(i).
regulation.what_it_requires: Where an adverse action in an insurance transaction is based in whole or in part on information in a consumer report, the user must give the consumer notice, identify the consumer reporting agency that supplied the report with its name, address and telephone number, and tell the consumer of the right to obtain a free copy and to dispute its accuracy. In insurance this reaches further than people expect: a denial or cancellation of, or an increase in any charge for, insurance existing or applied for is an adverse action, and the long-standing regulatory position is that failing to give an applicant the best available rate or a discount they would otherwise have had, because of a consumer report, is captured too. If a model uses any consumer-report-derived input, the notice obligation attaches to the model's output, and the notice must be specific enough to be useful — which the New York circular letter reinforces on the state side.

regulation.name: NAIC Property and Casualty Model Rating Law and state rate filing requirements
regulation.citation: NAIC Property and Casualty Model Rating Law (Prior Approval Version), Model #1780; a file-and-use variant exists separately. As with the unfair practices acts, the binding text is your own state's rating statute and the department's filing requirements, not the model.
regulation.what_it_requires: Rates, rating rules and rating plans must be filed, and in prior-approval states approved, before use, and must not be excessive, inadequate or unfairly discriminatory. The practical consequence for AI is threefold: a rating factor has to be explicable to a rate analyst at the department; the algorithm in production has to be the algorithm in the filing; and a model that retrains, reweights or drifts after approval is charging an unfiled rate. Several departments now ask supplementary questions about model methodology and data sources as part of the filing itself, and the NAIC bulletin's point that the standard applies regardless of methodology is aimed squarely here.

regulation.name: NAIC AI Systems Evaluation Tool (pilot)
regulation.citation: Developed by the NAIC Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (H) Working Group; multistate pilot running from 2 March 2026 through September 2026 across twelve states — California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Iowa, Louisiana, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia and Wisconsin — with the tool to be updated on pilot feedback, re-exposed for comment, and adoption anticipated at the 2026 Fall National Meeting.
regulation.what_it_requires: Not yet binding, and the reason it belongs on this list is that it is the instrument that turns the model bulletin's expectations into examination questions. It is designed to let regulators gather, in market conduct, financial analysis or financial examination contexts, information on the extent of an insurer's AI use across the enterprise, its governance framework and AIS Program structure, which of its models are high-risk, and what data feeds them — applying proportionality, so high-risk consumer-facing systems get the attention and back-office systems do not. If you are asked to participate in the pilot, that request is a live regulatory interaction and should be handled as one. The practical instruction for everyone else is to assume the questions and build the inventory and documentation to answer them, rather than waiting for the tool to be finalised.

regulation.name: Federal preemption pressure on state AI regulation
regulation.citation: Executive Order, "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence", issued 11 December 2025, under which the Department of Justice established an AI Litigation Task Force in January 2026; set against the McCarran-Ferguson Act, 15 U.S.C. §§ 1011–1015.
regulation.what_it_requires: Nothing, yet — and that is the point to make to a board that has heard otherwise. The executive order directs federal litigation and funding pressure against state AI laws considered unduly burdensome, and there has been commentary suggesting insurers can therefore slow down. Insurance is the weakest place for that argument: McCarran-Ferguson provides that no federal act shall be construed to invalidate, impair or supersede a state law enacted for the purpose of regulating the business of insurance unless the federal act specifically relates to insurance, so a general federal AI framework does not straightforwardly displace a state insurance regulation. State insurance AI requirements remain in force until a court or a legislature says otherwise, examinations continue on the existing standards, and the compliance work described above has a long lead time. Treat this as background risk to monitor, not as a reason to defer. Confirm the current litigation and legislative position before relying on any of it.

sectors.economics:
The model is the cheap part and everybody knows it, yet the budget is still usually drawn up around it. Four costs get left out, and in this sector they are larger than the line item they sit beside.

Integration with the system of record. Nothing here produces value until it writes into the policy administration or claims platform, and those platforms have their own release trains — typically a handful of releases a year, with change freezes over catastrophe season and year-end. A working prototype is weeks; the same thing writing into the claims system, through a supported interface rather than screen automation, with the regression testing the platform team will insist on, is quarters. If the carrier is on a heavily customised or older core system, add more. Screen-scraping around this is the single most common shortcut and it breaks at every platform upgrade, at which point you own a maintenance obligation nobody costed.

The human review that does not go away. Where the regulation requires a person to review and agree before action — which is most places a consumer is affected, and which Texas has now stated in those words — your savings are bounded by review time, not by handling time. Reviewing a machine's output properly is not five per cent of doing the work yourself; as a planning rule of thumb rather than a measured figure, treat it as roughly a third to a half, and be honest that if it falls below that your reviewers are rubber-stamping and you have acquired a compliance exposure rather than an efficiency. The Arizona provision barring a medical director from relying solely on an outside recommendation is that failure written into statute. This is why the strongest cases on this page are the internal-facing ones: submission structuring, subrogation screening, entity resolution. The review burden there is real but it is not a legal precondition, so it can genuinely fall over time.

Model governance and documentation, permanently. The written programme, the model inventory, annual bias testing with a documented search for less discriminatory alternatives, drift monitoring, vendor due diligence and contract remediation, and the standing capacity to answer an examination — which, once the NAIC evaluation tool is adopted, means answering a structured set of exhibits rather than an open-ended letter. This is a function, not a project. For a mid-size carrier, an order-of-magnitude estimate — and it is an estimate that scales with the number of material models rather than with premium — is a fraction of an actuarial or compliance FTE per material model on an ongoing basis, plus an owner. For carriers writing in Colorado and New York the testing component alone is credentialed statistical work repeated annually, and in Colorado the methodology it will be measured against is not yet fixed. It is entirely normal for year-one governance and integration together to exceed the licence or build cost of the model by a multiple; plan on two to four times as a budgeting assumption, and be pleased if it is less.

The cost of the failure mode. On the underwriting side: a market conduct examination that starts routine and becomes targeted, remediation of a book of decisions, re-rating and refunds, a consent order and a fine, and the cost of re-underwriting affected policies. On the claims side the number is different in kind — an extra-contractual or bad-faith exposure on a single claim can exceed everything the programme has saved, and the discovery of a model that influenced a settlement offer is the fact pattern plaintiff firms are actively looking for. There is also a quiet one: a severity or triage model that shifts case reserving distorts reported loss development, which distorts actuarial indications, which distorts rate filings, and the work to separate the model's effect from genuine trend is real actuarial time that nobody puts in the business case.

Set against that, the mechanism by which this pays is straightforward and worth stating plainly: elapsed time in submission handling, recovery dollars that would have been left on the table, organised fraud found as a network rather than one claim at a time, and complex claims reaching experienced adjusters while intervention still matters. Those are measurable. Measure your current position on each before you buy anything, because the vendor's benchmark is not your baseline and your board will eventually ask which one you used.
sectors.first_step: Commission a written inventory, due in three weeks, of every model, score, rule engine and vendor decision aid currently making or supporting a decision that affects a policyholder or applicant — across underwriting, rating, claims, recoveries and SIU. For each one record: what decision it makes or supports; who owns it by name; whether it was built in-house or supplied by a vendor, and if supplied, whether your contract gives you audit rights and a duty to cooperate with regulators; what data feeds it, including any external consumer data; whether a person reviews the output before anything reaches the consumer; where its documentation lives; and when it was last tested. Include the models you did not commission — the ones already running inside your policy administration and claims platforms, and the ones vendors run on your behalf. Structure the columns to the exhibits in the NAIC AI Systems Evaluation Tool, so the inventory is already in the shape a department will ask for rather than a shape you will have to convert later. Two things reliably come back from this exercise. The list is longer than the executive team expected, usually because scores embedded in purchased platforms have never been thought of as models. And several entries have no named owner and no documentation at all, which tells you precisely where to start, because those are the ones an examiner will find first.

sectors.label: Financial services
sectors.lede: Most of the work AI can reach in a bank, a broker-dealer or a lender is review work: somebody reads an alert, a file, a memo or a complaint, decides whether it is a problem, and writes down why. The technology is genuinely good at the reading and the drafting. What it cannot do is carry the evidentiary burden — and in this sector the evidence, not the reading, is where the cost and the liability sit.

where_it_helps.name: Alert triage assist for transaction monitoring
where_it_helps.the_work: A level-one analyst works a queue from the monitoring system: pull the KYC profile, look at prior alerts and prior SARs on the party, trace the wires or the cash structuring pattern, check adverse media, then write a disposition narrative. Commonly twenty to forty alerts a day per analyst, though the figure varies widely by scenario mix. The overwhelming majority close as no further action.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Assembles the case file automatically — entity profile, relationship history, prior alert and SAR history, the actual transaction strings, negative news hits — and drafts the disposition narrative with pointers back to the underlying records. The analyst reads, corrects and signs. The escalation decision stays with the analyst.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Read access to core banking or the payments hub, the monitoring system's case manager, the CDD repository, sanctions and adverse-media sources. Write-back into the case record, or the analyst re-keys and you have saved nothing. Per-analyst attribution on every disposition. A written position, taken before deployment, that the assembled pack, the prompt and the output are SAR supporting documentation — assume they are — and retention to match: five years from the filing date under 31 CFR 1020.320(d).
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: The mechanism is evidence-gathering time, which on a routine alert is typically the larger half of handle time. Scoping targets commonly land in the 20-40% range for average handle time. That is a target firms set at business-case stage, not an observed result — most published figures are vendor-sourced — and it depends heavily on alert volume and on whether the file already lives in one system rather than six.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The draft becomes the analyst's thinking. Narrative quality drifts to the model's template, QA samples start reading identically, and the examiner who reads thirty dispositions and finds the same six sentences asks who actually reviewed the alert. The sharper failure is quieter: the assembler cannot reach one source, omits a transaction string, and the narrative still reads complete. Nothing in the output says what is missing. Note also that because generative tools sit expressly outside the scope of the April 2026 interagency model risk guidance, there is no supervisory standard telling you what monitoring for that drift should look like — you write that specification yourself.

where_it_helps.name: Entity and beneficial-ownership extraction at onboarding and refresh
where_it_helps.the_work: An analyst reads formation documents, trust deeds, ownership charts, board resolutions and certificates of incumbency, then keys entity names, jurisdictions, ownership percentages and control persons into the KYC system — resolving the 25 per cent equity prong and the control prong under the CDD rule. Repeated on every periodic or perpetual refresh cycle.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Structured extraction from the documents, assembly of the ownership chain, and a flag where the chain does not reach a natural person at the applicable threshold or where a document is stale or missing.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: The document store, the KYC system's schema, and a confidence threshold below which a human keys the field by hand. Screening and risk rating stay downstream and unchanged. Complex structures should be routed to a person by rule — entity type, jurisdiction, layer count — not by model confidence, because the model is least calibrated exactly where the structure is hardest.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Keying and re-reading. On standard corporate structures it removes most of the extraction time; the estimate falls apart on layered structures. Depends on your customer mix — a commercial bank with private-investment-vehicle clients will see far less than a small-business lender.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: It is reliable on the simple structures and confidently wrong on exactly the ones you care about: multi-jurisdiction trusts, nominee arrangements, non-English documents, scanned faxes of scanned faxes. The aggregate error rate looks excellent while the errors concentrate entirely in the high-risk tail. Measure accuracy by risk band or you will measure nothing useful.

where_it_helps.name: Scenario threshold tuning and customer segmentation
where_it_helps.the_work: Periodic tuning of the monitoring scenarios: above-the-line and below-the-line sampling, segmentation review, productivity statistics per scenario, and a tuning memo explaining why a threshold moved. Usually a small quantitative team plus outside help, annually or semi-annually.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: This is not generative work. It is statistics and machine learning on your own alert outcome history — clustering customers into behavioural segments rather than static risk-rating buckets, and modelling which alerts will close unproductively so threshold changes rest on evidence rather than judgement.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Several years of alert outcome history where the label means something, joined end to end from alert through escalation to filing. This is one of the few AI applications here that sits squarely inside the April 2026 interagency model risk guidance rather than outside it — it is statistical, not generative — so the expectations are at least legible: documented conceptual soundness, independent validation, ongoing monitoring, and below-the-line testing showing no productive alert class was suppressed.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Fewer alerts generated per productive alert. Double-digit percentage reductions in alert volume at constant filing yield are a common target. An estimate, and it depends almost entirely on how badly tuned the current scenarios are — a firm that has never tuned will see a lot, a firm that tunes annually will see little.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Suppression you cannot defend. Alert volume falls, filings fall with it, and you must demonstrate the fall is noise rather than missed activity — using labels that are contaminated, because 'closed, no further action' has historically also meant 'the queue was four thousand deep'. The second failure is procedural: a segmentation you cannot explain in an examination gets reversed at the next examination, and you have paid twice.

where_it_helps.name: Credit memo and annual review drafting
where_it_helps.the_work: A credit analyst or relationship manager writes the memo: financial spreads, covenant compliance, industry and guarantor commentary, primary and secondary repayment sources, risk-rating rationale. Days of work per credit, and at many banks the annual review queue is chronically late.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Drafts the narrative sections from the spreads, the prior memo, the covenant certificate and the borrower's statements, and flags year-on-year movements that the prior narrative did not anticipate. The analyst rewrites. The risk rating itself comes from the rating model and the analyst, not from the drafting tool.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Access to the spreading system, loan accounting, the credit file and prior memos. A written rule that the rating is not generated, enforced in the tool rather than in a policy nobody reads — because the moment the tool's output feeds the rating, it is in the credit risk model perimeter and inherits validation obligations. Retention of the draft and its source set alongside the memo in the credit file.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Drafting and retrieval. It is a meaningful fraction of the hours in a routine annual review and much less on a new or complex facility. An estimate that depends on portfolio complexity and on the quality of your spreads — bad spreads in, confident nonsense out.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Last year's language carries forward, including last year's wrong conclusion. A memo that said 'performing in line with projections' keeps saying it while debt service coverage degrades, because the prior memo is the strongest signal in the context. And a fluent draft is reviewed less carefully than a blank page — the reviewer's attention is the control you just weakened.

where_it_helps.name: Complaint classification and root-cause clustering
where_it_helps.the_work: Complaints arrive from the regulator's portal, the call centre, branch email, executive correspondence and social channels. Someone reads the free text, codes product and issue, decides what is a reportable complaint, spots the ones that are really an allegation of discrimination or an unfair-practice claim, and routes them. Done by hand, at volume, inconsistently between coders.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Two different things of different maturity. Classification into the firm's taxonomy and flagging of allegation language is ordinary supervised text classification and works well. Clustering themes across channels to surface root cause is the weaker half — it is exploratory, its output is a hypothesis, and it needs a person to decide whether a cluster is a cause or an artefact of how the channels are worded.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: The complaint corpus with its existing labels, a taxonomy that has actually been stable, mandatory human review of anything flagged as a regulatory allegation, retention consistent with FINRA Rule 4513 where you are a broker-dealer, and an audit trail showing what was escalated and what was not.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Triage time and, more usefully, the elapsed time to a root-cause finding — plausibly weeks to days on the reporting cycle. An estimate that scales with complaint volume; below a few thousand a year the clustering has nothing to work with and you are buying a classifier.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The classifier learns your historical coding. If the firm has under-coded discrimination allegations, the model will faithfully continue under-coding them, at speed and with an audit trail proving you did it consistently. That exposure did not shrink when the CFPB removed the effects test from Regulation B in April 2026: disparate treatment and proxy discrimination remain actionable, the Fair Housing Act is untouched, and state regulators and private plaintiffs are not bound by the Bureau's reading. Also worth saying plainly: complaint counts by category are a metric people manage to, and automating the categorisation moves the incentive onto the model.

where_it_helps.name: Supervisory review of recommendations and communications
where_it_helps.the_work: Principal review of recommendations — concentration, switches, annuity exchanges, complex products against conservative profiles, rollover recommendations — driven by exception reports, plus review of registered representatives' correspondence. The principal reads a sample, because a sample is what a person can read.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Reads the free text that exception reports cannot: the rationale field, the representative's CRM notes, the client email thread, the rollover disclosure — and flags mismatches between the stated objective and what was recommended. It widens the population reviewed rather than replacing the reviewer.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: The books-and-records archive, CRM notes, the client profile of record, written supervisory procedures under FINRA Rule 3110 that name the tool and describe how its output is reviewed, and a principal who still evidences the review. Capacity to clear every flag raised, budgeted before launch.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Coverage, not headcount. The same supervisory cost looking at a far larger share of the population. An estimate; the value is concentrated in firms whose current sample is small relative to representative count.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: A tool that reviews everything badly displaces a principal who reviewed a little well. And the flag queue becomes its own exposure: an unreviewed flag is affirmatively worse evidence than no flag, because it shows the firm was told. Enforcement in this area turns repeatedly on what the supervisor knew and did not act on.

where_it_helps.name: Payment and reconciliation exception handling
where_it_helps.the_work: Investigations, returns, recalls, chargebacks, nostro and suspense breaks. An operations analyst reads the payment message, the prior correspondence, the ledger entries and the counterparty's claim, decides what happened, and either posts an adjustment or sends a message.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: What is sold is autonomous resolution — the agent reads the break and clears it. What actually works is narrower: assembling the investigation pack, matching the break to its likely cause, drafting the counterparty message, and proposing the entry. The posting stays with a person.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Access to the payment messages, the ledger and the correspondence history; entitlements that make the tool read-only against anything that moves money; and a maker-checker control that the tool cannot satisfy on both sides.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Investigation assembly time on breaks that have a repeating cause. An estimate, and a modest one — the long tail of genuinely novel breaks is where the hours actually go, and that tail does not automate.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: This is rated oversold because the saving and the safety are the same control. Remove the human approval before posting and a wrong action is a realised loss or an error-resolution failure with a statutory clock attached — Regulation E gives ten business days to investigate a consumer error notice, extendable to forty-five, or ninety in defined cases, and Regulation Z gives two complete billing cycles to resolve a billing error. Those clocks do not pause while you debug a model. Keep the approval and most of the promised saving goes with it. The common pattern is that firms which buy the autonomous version are running it in recommend-only mode within a few quarters, having paid for the other thing.

where_it_does_not.claim: Explainable-AI tooling gives you your adverse action reasons, so you can underwrite with a machine learning model.
where_it_does_not.why_not: The statute requires a statement of the specific principal reasons for the action actually taken. Post-hoc attribution methods give you a locally approximated ranking of feature contributions, which is a different object. 'Revolving utilisation across trades opened in the last twenty-four months, interacted with inquiry velocity' is not a reason an applicant can act on, and different attribution methods disagree about the same denial. Someone still has to hand-map model features to defensible reason codes and defend that mapping — which is the work you were told the tooling removed. The regulatory weather changed and the obligation did not: the CFPB withdrew Circulars 2022-03 and 2023-03 effective 12 May 2025, and said that withdrawal was itself provisional pending further review, while 15 U.S.C. 1691(d) and 12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2) are untouched. The FCRA key-factor disclosure at 15 U.S.C. 1681m(a)(2) is a second regulator's version of the same problem.

where_it_does_not.claim: The system can decide and file the suspicious activity report, clearing your backlog without more analysts.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Filing is a legal determination that the institution knows, suspects, or has reason to suspect. It carries a named decision-maker, a thirty-calendar-day clock from initial detection, five-year retention of supporting documentation, and a safe harbour that protects the institution's judgement — not a vendor's. Nothing about the volume problem is solved by removing the analyst, because the analyst was never the constraint; assembling the evidence was. Firms that pilot autonomous filing converge on a human reviewing every machine decision: the same headcount, plus a model to govern.

where_it_does_not.claim: Sentiment and behavioural analytics over representative and trader communications will surface conduct risk before it becomes an enforcement matter.
where_it_does_not.why_not: The base rate of genuine misconduct in communications is minute, so even an excellent classifier produces an alert population that is almost entirely false. Surveillance becomes the new triage backlog, staffed by people who are not the ones you took out of triage. Worse, the tool manufactures evidence of notice faster than it manufactures capacity to act, and 'the system flagged it and nobody looked' is the fact pattern in the matters you are trying to avoid. This gets sold hardest to firms that have just been through an off-channel communications settlement, which is exactly when their capacity to clear alerts is lowest.

where_it_does_not.claim: A chat assistant over your policies and procedures will take the load off the compliance advisory desk.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Staff treat the answer as the firm's position. When the model paraphrases a procedure and a representative acts on it, the firm has issued guidance with no author, no version, no approval and no supervisor. Either that exchange is a record you are not retaining, or it is a control you cannot evidence. The honest fix — logging every question and answer and having compliance review them — costs more than a good search index over the policy manual, which is what most firms needed in the first place.

where_it_does_not.claim: AI-assisted validation will finally get your model risk backlog under control.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Validation's product is not a document. It is independent challenge by a person who is accountable for the challenge and can be examined on it. A generated validation report is the artefact without the challenge, and it fails the moment an examiner asks the validator a question the report does not answer. There is a further trap specific to this moment: the April 2026 interagency guidance expressly places generative and agentic AI models outside its scope, so for those tools there is no supervisory standard to point at. Your own committee owns the defence, and a generated defence is not one.

where_it_does_not.claim: A continuously learning fraud or AML model retrains itself on new typologies, so detection keeps improving without a project each time.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Continuous retraining and model governance are in direct tension, and governance wins on examination. A model whose parameters move weekly is a model whose validation is of a version you are no longer running, whose champion-challenger evidence is stale, and whose change control cannot answer the only question that matters after an incident: what was the model doing on the date of the transactions under review. Firms that deploy this end up either freezing the retraining cadence to something a validation function can keep up with — at which point it is periodic retraining with a marketing name — or reconstructing model lineage under deadline during a look-back. Retraining on your own confirmed outcomes also compounds whatever your investigators already miss, and nothing in the pipeline will tell you that the recall figure is measured against labels the model helped produce.

preconditions: A model inventory that already exists and has an owner — not a spreadsheet of production models, but an inventory whose boundary you can defend. The April 2026 interagency guidance is risk-based and tailored, and puts generative and agentic AI outside its scope entirely. If your inventory was built on the old SR 11-7 boundary, you must decide in writing which governance track each AI tool sits under before it deploys, because neither the regulator nor the vendor will decide it for you.

Outcome labels that mean what they say. Alert dispositions, complaint codes, QA results, risk ratings. If 'closed, no further action' has historically also meant 'the analyst was three weeks behind', a model trained on that history learns your backlog rather than your risk, and every accuracy figure you produce afterwards is measuring the wrong thing.

Write access into the system of record, or an explicit decision that there will be none. A tool producing output an analyst must re-key into the case manager, the origination system or the credit file saves nothing. Most of the integration cost lives here, and most pilots avoid it by running on exports — which is why pilot savings so often fail to survive production.

Retention designed before deployment rather than retrofitted. Whatever the tool reads, drafts and outputs is likely part of the record: SAR supporting documentation runs five years from filing, broker-dealer and adviser records have their own prescribed periods and format requirements, credit files have theirs. Prompts, retrieved context and model version must be capturable at the item level from day one. Adding this to a deployed tool is a rebuild, not a change request.

A named human decision-maker for every decision the tool touches, and evidence that the human actually decided. Attribution in the case record, handle times that are not implausible, and QA that samples the human's edits rather than only the final outcome. 'Human in the loop' is not a control until you can show what the human changed.

A second-line function that can say no and be supported when it does. If model risk or compliance cannot stop a deployment, your governance is documentation, and documentation is what gets criticised.

A tested rollback, and a process that can still run without the tool. Turning it off must be a decision someone can make on a Tuesday without a project. Expect to be asked, in examination and in vendor due diligence, how you would run the process for a quarter if the tool were withdrawn — and to be asked for evidence you have tried it, not an assertion that you could.

regulation.name: Revised interagency guidance on model risk management (replacing SR 11-7)
regulation.citation: SR 26-2 (Federal Reserve); OCC Bulletin 2026-13, 'Model Risk Management: Revised Guidance'; FDIC FIL-15-2026 — all 17 April 2026. Supersedes SR 11-7 (4 April 2011) and SR 21-8 (9 April 2021); the OCC rescinds Bulletins 2011-12, 2021-19 and 1997-24 and the 'Model Risk Management' booklet of the Comptroller's Handbook; the FDIC rescinds FIL-22-2017 and FIL-27-2021
regulation.what_it_requires: Validation covering conceptual soundness, outcomes analysis and ongoing monitoring; effective challenge by people with the expertise and standing to exercise it; a model inventory; independent validation of vendor models including any customisation. Three things have changed and most material still describes the old regime. First, the approach is risk-based and tailored — governance intensity follows model materiality, and the guidance states it is expected to be most relevant to banking organisations with over $30 billion in total assets, while still reaching smaller institutions with significant model risk. Second, the guidance states it does not set forth enforceable standards or prescriptive requirements and that non-compliance will not itself result in supervisory criticism; supervisory action still follows from violations of law or unsafe and unsound practice. Third, and most important for this subject, the text is explicit that generative AI and agentic AI models 'are novel and rapidly evolving' and are not within its scope. The principles apply to traditional statistical models and to non-generative, non-agentic AI. Generative tools must still be governed — your own risk management determines the controls — but you are building that track without a standard to point at.

regulation.name: ECOA and Regulation B — statement of specific reasons for adverse action
regulation.what_it_requires: Notice of the action taken and either a statement of specific reasons for it or disclosure of the right to obtain one. The reasons must be specific and indicate the principal reasons for the adverse action; a statement that the applicant failed to achieve a qualifying score, or that the decision rested on internal standards, is expressly insufficient. This obligation is indifferent to the technology: a creditor's inability to understand its own model is not a defence. The CFPB's circulars on the point — 2022-03 (complex algorithms) and 2023-03 (sample forms) — were withdrawn effective 12 May 2025 as part of a withdrawal of 67 guidance documents, which removed the Bureau's articulation of the requirement but not the requirement. The Bureau also stated that withdrawal was provisional pending further review, so the articulation may return.

regulation.name: Regulation B amendments removing the effects test
regulation.citation: CFPB final rule, 'Equal Credit Opportunity Act (Regulation B)', 91 FR (FR Doc. 2026-07804), published 22 April 2026, effective 21 July 2026
regulation.what_it_requires: The rule adds to 12 CFR 1002.6(a) the statement that the Act does not provide that the effects test applies, removes the effects-test references from the regulation and commentary, narrows the discouragement prohibition to statements of intent to discriminate, and restricts special purpose credit programmes offered by for-profit entities. Read it carefully before concluding that fair lending testing of a model is now optional. Disparate treatment, including facially neutral criteria applied as proxies, remains actionable under the amended commentary itself. The Fair Housing Act is a separate statute with its own body of law. States run their own fair lending regimes and examinations. And the rule is being challenged — National Fair Housing Alliance v. CFPB, No. 1:26-cv-01820 (D.D.C.) — on APA and statutory-authority grounds; the plaintiffs did not seek preliminary relief, so the amendments took effect on schedule, but a lender that dismantled its testing would be relying on a rule under active review. The practical point: the testing you did for disparate impact is still the testing that tells you whether a variable is acting as a proxy.

regulation.name: FCRA obligations where a consumer report is used
regulation.citation: 15 U.S.C. 1681m(a), in particular § 1681m(a)(2) (credit score and key factors, as added by Dodd-Frank § 1100F); key factors defined at 15 U.S.C. 1681g(f)(1)(C)
regulation.what_it_requires: Separate adverse action disclosure duties for users of consumer reports, distinct from the ECOA notice and not satisfied by it — including, where a credit score was used in taking the action, disclosure of the score, its range, and the key factors adversely affecting it. A model that consumes bureau attributes brings these obligations with it, and the key-factor disclosure has the same explainability problem as the ECOA reason statement, for a different regulator and with a different private right of action behind it.

regulation.name: FINRA supervision of generative AI tools
regulation.citation: FINRA Regulatory Notice 24-09 (27 June 2024); FINRA Rule 3110; FINRA Rule 2210 where output reaches customers; FINRA 2026 Regulatory Oversight Report (published December 2025)
regulation.what_it_requires: FINRA's rules are technology-neutral and apply to the use of generative AI and large language models as they apply to any other technology. Notice 24-09 creates no new requirements; it confirms that a firm's supervisory system must reasonably cover the technology it uses, including model risk management, data integrity, reliability and accuracy, privacy and confidentiality, and that the obligation is the same whether the tool was built in-house or supplied by a vendor. The 2026 oversight report adds a section on generative AI that addresses hallucinations, bias and privacy specifically, and asks firms contemplating AI agents to assess whether the agents' autonomy creates new supervisory obligations and to adopt agent-specific controls, including action logging and restrictions on system access.

regulation.name: Books and records — what becomes a record when a model writes it
regulation.citation: 17 CFR 240.17a-4, including the electronic recordkeeping requirements at § 240.17a-4(f) (broker-dealers); 17 CFR 275.204-2 (investment advisers); FINRA Rules 4511 and 4513
regulation.what_it_requires: Records of the business and records evidencing supervisory review must be preserved for prescribed periods in a compliant electronic format — since the 2022 amendments, either the audit-trail alternative or write-once-read-many. No rule says 'retain your prompts'. The prevailing industry reading is that where a tool generates a communication, a disposition, or the record of a supervisory review, the output is a record, and the inputs evidencing how the review was conducted generally are too. This is where recordkeeping bites an AI deployment: the tool must be able to produce, per item, what it was given, what it returned, and which model version returned it. Decide your position in writing before deployment, because it cannot be reconstructed afterwards.

regulation.name: Suspicious activity reporting and supporting documentation
regulation.citation: 31 CFR 1020.320 (banks), with parallel provisions across 31 CFR Chapter X for other institution types; filing deadline at § 1020.320(b)(3); retention at § 1020.320(d)
regulation.what_it_requires: Filing within thirty calendar days of initial detection of facts constituting a basis for filing, extendable to sixty where no subject has been identified. A copy of each report and the original or business-record equivalent of its supporting documentation must be kept for five years from the filing date, and supporting documentation is deemed to have been filed with the report. If a model assembled the evidence or drafted the narrative, that assembly is part of the supporting documentation — and five years is longer than most vendor contracts and most model versions.

regulation.name: Supervisory encouragement of innovation in BSA/AML
regulation.citation: Interagency Statement on Innovative Efforts to Combat Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing, 3 December 2018 (FinCEN with the Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC and NCUA; OCC Bulletin 2018-44; FDIC FIL-79-2018)
regulation.what_it_requires: The agencies encourage banks to consider, evaluate and where appropriate responsibly implement innovative approaches, and state that pilot programmes which expose gaps in a BSA/AML compliance programme will not, on their own, result in supervisory criticism — while equally confirming that banks choosing not to innovate will not be criticised for that either. This is the document to cite internally when the objection is 'the regulator will punish us for trying'. It relieves no programme obligation. FinCEN's AML/CFT programme notice of proposed rulemaking of April 2026 goes further, discussing machine learning and generative AI explicitly and proposing that responsible adoption of innovative technology should not by itself increase supervisory or enforcement risk — but that is a proposal, and should not be relied on as law or assumed into a business case.

regulation.name: Regulation Best Interest and suitability
regulation.citation: 17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Regulation Best Interest); FINRA Rule 2111
regulation.what_it_requires: A care obligation and a reasonable basis for each recommendation, supported by policies and procedures reasonably designed to achieve compliance. A tool that screens, scores or generates recommendations sits inside that obligation and does not discharge any part of it. Where the tool influences what is recommended rather than merely reviewing it, expect the conflicts analysis to become the harder question — including whether the tool's ranking reflects anything other than the customer's interest.

regulation.name: Third-party risk management for vendor-supplied models
regulation.citation: Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management, 6 June 2023 — SR 23-4, OCC Bulletin 2023-17, FDIC FIL-29-2023
regulation.what_it_requires: Risk management across the full life cycle of a third-party relationship — planning, due diligence, contracting, ongoing monitoring, termination — proportionate to risk. For AI vendors the pressure points are concrete: the right to information sufficient to validate a model you cannot see inside, notice before the underlying model version changes, subcontractor disclosure where the vendor is itself reselling a foundation model, and an exit that returns your data and leaves the prior process runnable.

regulation.name: New York cybersecurity requirements and AI
regulation.citation: 23 NYCRR Part 500; NYDFS industry letter, 'Cybersecurity Risks Arising from Artificial Intelligence and Strategies to Combat Related Risks', 16 October 2024; NYDFS industry letter on heightened cybersecurity risks associated with frontier AI models, May 2026
regulation.what_it_requires: For covered entities, the existing Part 500 framework must be applied to AI-related risk: AI-enabled social engineering and deepfake-assisted fraud, the concentration of non-public information created by feeding data to a model, and third-party and supply-chain exposure. The letters impose no new requirements and set no new deadlines, but are explicit that the existing ones reach these risks — access controls, vendor management, and the risk assessment that drives the rest. Insurers should read these alongside NYDFS Insurance Circular Letter No. 7 (2024) on AI and external consumer data in underwriting and pricing, which is a separate and more substantive instrument.

regulation.name: EU AI Act, for institutions with EU operations
regulation.citation: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Annex III point 5(b) (creditworthiness assessment and credit scoring of natural persons, excepting fraud detection); amended by the digital omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, published in the Official Journal 24 July 2026
regulation.what_it_requires: Where it applies, a high-risk classification brings a risk management system, data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight and conformity assessment. The dates moved: Annex III obligations were to apply from 2 August 2026 and are deferred to 2 December 2027, with product-safety-linked systems under Annex I moving to 2 August 2028. The Article 50 transparency obligations were not deferred. Treat the deferral as time to build, not a reprieve — the documentation burden is unchanged and the lead time on conformity assessment, and on the harmonised standards it depends on, is long.

regulation.name: State automated-decision law for consumer lending
regulation.citation: Colorado SB 26-189 (Automated Decision-Making Technology), repealing and replacing the Colorado AI Act, SB 24-205; effective 1 January 2027 — described, not cited, as to the detail of its lending provisions
regulation.what_it_requires: Lending is a 'consequential decision' in every US state framework of this kind, and the state layer is now moving faster and less predictably than the federal one. Colorado's original 2024 statute imposed a duty of care, risk management and impact assessments; its 2026 replacement narrows that substantially toward disclosure, transparency and targeted protections for automated decision-making technology, and pushes the effective date to 1 January 2027. Treat the specific obligations as a matter for counsel and confirm against the enacted text: this area has been amended twice in under two years, and other states are legislating on different models. The planning point is that a national lender should expect to answer state-specific disclosure and notice questions about a model that is federally governed under an entirely different framework.

sectors.economics: The licence and inference cost is the smallest number in the business case, and it is usually the only one in the pilot's business case. Four costs decide whether the deployment pays. First, integration into the system of record. The pilot ran on exports; production must read and write the case manager, the origination system or the archive, with entitlements, attribution and retention. This is routinely the largest single line and is underestimated precisely because the pilot avoided it. Second, model governance and documentation. For a firm with an established model risk function, a material validation is a multi-month exercise with a queue in front of it — and the queue, not the fee, is the constraint. Note the specific trap in 2026: because the revised interagency guidance puts generative and agentic AI outside its scope, you are standing up a second governance track for tools your validation function has no standard for. That is net new cost, not reuse of what you already built, and it is the line most often assumed away. Firms below the guidance's $30 billion centre of gravity have a different problem, not a smaller one — less machinery to reuse, and the same examiner question about how you know the tool works. Third, the human review that does not go away. Budget at steady state for the same reviewers doing a different job; the return arrives as throughput or coverage, not as headcount, and a business case that promised headcount will either fail to deliver or will deliver by cutting the control. Fourth, ongoing monitoring — someone examining performance on a defined cycle and evidencing it. Half a full-time equivalent per material model is a reasonable planning figure to argue from, not an observed average; it scales with the number of models, not their size. Two costs nobody budgets at all. The evaluation set: several hundred to a few thousand cases graded by senior people, refreshed as the population drifts. Without it you cannot demonstrate the tool works, cannot detect degradation when a vendor changes the model underneath you, and cannot answer the first question an examiner asks. It is usually the most valuable thing built and the hardest thing to fund, because it looks like overhead. And vendor version drift: your validation was of a model version you may no longer be running. Either contract for version pinning and advance notice of change, or budget revalidation on the vendor's release schedule rather than your own. Then the failure cost, which is the number to hold against the saving. If a monitoring, screening or underwriting change is later found to have suppressed activity that should have been reviewed, the remediation is a look-back over the affected period — reworking alerts at a per-item cost, with outside help, on a regulator's timetable, often alongside an agreed programme of corrective work. A mid-sized look-back is a seven- or eight-figure programme; the largest publicly known ones at global institutions have run to hundreds of thousands of items and programme costs an order of magnitude beyond that. Those are estimates, and they scale with volume and with the length of the period before anyone noticed — which is the argument for monitoring that would have noticed. As an order of magnitude for a first material deployment: expect governance, integration and evidence together to run several times the technology cost across the first two years. An estimate, and it depends on institution size and on how mature your model risk function already is.
sectors.first_step: Before you scope a tool or take a vendor meeting, take two hundred closed items from your highest-volume review queue — AML alerts at most banks, complaints or annual reviews elsewhere. Draw them so the sample is not all easy: include the escalated and the filed, not only the no-further-action population, or you will measure agreement on the cases that were never in doubt. Strip the disposition and the narrative. Have two experienced reviewers independently re-decide each one, blind, without seeing each other's answer or the original. Then compare three ways: reviewer against reviewer, and each against what the file actually says was decided. You get two things, both of which you need and neither of which anyone can sell you. You will have measured your own consistency, which is the ceiling on what any tool can be held to — if your own people agree seventy per cent of the time, a vendor claiming ninety-four per cent accuracy is measuring something other than correctness. And you will have built the graded evaluation set that every later decision depends on: whether to deploy, whether performance has drifted, and what to hand the examiner who asks how you know it works. Two people, roughly a week. Do it first, because it is the only number in the conversation that belongs to you.

sectors.label: Staffing and recruitment
sectors.lede: Staffing is the sector where AI regulation arrived first, because staffing is where the decisions are. An agency that screens on a client's behalf is an employment agency under New York City's rules and an agent under a theory a federal court has already allowed to proceed against a screening vendor — the exposure does not stay with the client, and it does not stay with the software company. The genuinely useful AI work in this sector is mostly not in the screen at all; it is in the bench, the timesheet run and the credential file, where nobody is selling you anything.

where_it_helps.name: Recall over your own database (the silver-medallist problem)
where_it_helps.the_work: A recruiter takes a req and searches the ATS with a boolean string written from memory. They find the twelve people they already know. The 340 people who applied to a near-identical req eighteen months ago and were never called again sit in the database unfound, because nobody ever parsed 'RN, telemetry, ACLS current' the same way twice — and the last recruiter who worked that desk left, taking the search strings with them.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Embedding-based retrieval across resumes, recruiter notes and placement history, so a req returns candidates whose records never used the words the recruiter typed. Not a score — a longer and better-ordered list to work through.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Resumes that actually parsed. Deduplicated candidate records. Assignment and placement history in the same system. Read access to recruiter notes, which means first deciding what recruiters are permitted to write in them, because those notes become discoverable and the model reads whatever is there. A retention position that survives the four-year record-retention rule California now applies to applications, selection criteria and automated-decision system data.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: submittals per recruiter-hour, from less time re-sourcing people you already own and already paid to acquire. Order of magnitude: hours per week per desk, not headcount. An estimate; it scales with database size and depends entirely on record quality.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: It surfaces the same over-represented population your database already over-represents, and now does so faster and with the appearance of neutrality.
