Second-order: recruiters stop reading past result four, and the retrieval layer quietly becomes a ranking layer nobody audited — which is also the point at which it starts looking like a tool that substantially assists a discretionary decision.

where_it_helps.name: Redeployment watchlist for contractors rolling off
where_it_helps.the_work: Somebody keeps a spreadsheet of contractors whose assignments end in the next six weeks. It is updated on Fridays. A third of the end dates are wrong, because the extension came through the client's VMS and nobody told the recruiter.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Watches assignment end dates in the system of record, matches the finishing contractor's actual placement history — not their resume — against open reqs and live pipelines, and puts a named person in front of a named recruiter with a stated reason and a workable rate.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Assignment records with trustworthy end dates, including extensions arriving through a VMS you do not control. A rule about who owns the contractor conversation. Bill rate and pay rate visible, so the suggestion is not commercially absurd. Where the contractor is on a visa or a per-diem arrangement, the eligibility and tax-home constraints have to be in the record too, or the suggestion is unplaceable.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: redeployment rate. A redeployed contractor carries no sourcing cost and usually no ramp, so the margin effect is direct. Order of magnitude: a few points of redeployment rate on a bench of several hundred is material to gross margin. An estimate; depends on assignment length and mix.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Wrong end dates. The tool flags a redeployment for someone who extended three weeks ago, the recruiter calls, and the contractor learns the agency does not know where they are working. You have spent trust to save time.

where_it_helps.name: Job adverts and client submittal summaries from intake notes
where_it_helps.the_work: A recruiter takes a 25-minute intake call and writes four bullets. The advert goes out as the client's internal job description with the internal grade code still in it. The submittal summary gets written at 18:40 in the applicant tab, in whatever shape that recruiter favours.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Drafts the external advert and the client-facing submittal summary from intake notes and the candidate record, in your house format, with the pay range placed where the jurisdiction requires it — Colorado, New York State, California, Washington, Illinois and a growing list of cities each phrase that requirement differently.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Intake notes that exist in the system rather than in a notebook. A house format worth copying. A pay range the client has agreed to publish, which is usually the blocker, and a rule for what you post when the client refuses. A jurisdiction lookup keyed to where the work is performed, including remote roles that can be performed from a disclosure state.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: writing time per req and per submittal, and fewer adverts pulled for a missing range. Order of magnitude: tens of minutes per req. An estimate; small per unit, and only adds up at volume.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: It invents a requirement the client never stated — five years where the manager said three — and candidates are then screened against a bar that came from a language model. Second: every agency's adverts start reading identically, and the advert stops differentiating you.

where_it_helps.name: Timesheet and VMS exception triage
where_it_helps.the_work: Monday morning. Four thousand timesheets, a hundred and eighty exceptions: missing punches, a shift crossing midnight, overtime at the wrong multiplier, a weighted-average calculation for a contractor who worked two rates, a California meal-break premium nobody applied, a per-diem stipend paid to someone who no longer has a tax home, a rate that does not match the purchase order, hours billed against a closed assignment. Back office works the list by hand, invoices go out late, and the client disputes the ones that went out wrong.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Classifies each exception by cause, proposes the correction together with the rule it applied, and routes what it cannot resolve to a person with the evidence already attached. Writes nothing to the payroll or invoice record without a human commit.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: The rate card, overtime, daily-overtime and break rules by state and by client, the assignment record, the MSP's billing rules where submittals and time flow through a client VMS you do not control, and a hard boundary: the tool drafts, a person commits. Client-specific rules have to be written down somewhere other than in one payroll clerk's memory.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: exceptions cleared per back-office hour, plus fewer late and disputed invoices — a working-capital effect, not only a payroll one. Order of magnitude: a substantial share of routine exceptions handled on first pass. An estimate; depends on volume and how many bespoke client rules you carry.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: It normalises an exception that was a real signal — unapproved overtime, a misclassified per-diem, or hours billed at the wrong client rate — and the error is now inside an approved invoice with an audit trail saying a machine tidied it. The client finds it, not you, and the correction arrives as a credit note plus a wage claim.

where_it_helps.name: Credential and compliance file completeness checks
where_it_helps.the_work: Healthcare and regulated industrial: before a submittal you need a licence current on the start date, immunisation records, competency tests, client-specific orientation, an exclusion-list screen, and a background check of the right vintage. A coordinator opens twelve PDFs and reads dates off them.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Extracts dates, licence numbers and issuing bodies from uploaded documents, checks the file against that client's checklist, and flags what is missing or expiring before the start date rather than on the morning of it.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Client checklists held as data, not as a Word document. Document storage the tool can read. A human verifier for anything that fails — and a standing rule that the tool never marks a credential verified, because primary-source verification against the issuing board, and the exclusion-list match review, stay with a named person under healthcare staffing certification standards and most client credentialing policies. Background-check content is consumer-report territory and stays inside that process rather than this one.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: avoided start-date slips and avoided pull-backs, plus coordinator minutes per file. Order of magnitude: the coordinator time is minutes; the value sits in the slipped starts you stop losing. An estimate; depends on credential density in your mix.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: It reads an expiry date off a renewal receipt rather than the licence itself, marks the file complete, and a contractor works a shift unlicensed. That is a client incident and a regulator conversation, not a paperwork error. Adjacent failure: a fuzzy name match against an exclusion list that a person should have adjudicated.

where_it_helps.name: Interview scheduling and coordination
where_it_helps.the_work: Three candidates, two panel members, a hiring manager two time zones away, and a client VMS that will only accept slots the client posted. The coordinator sends fourteen emails and one of them has the wrong dial-in.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Negotiates times across calendars and stated candidate availability, handles reschedules, sends confirmations and reminders, and keeps the ATS record in step with what was actually agreed.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Calendar access on at least the client side — which is exactly what most client IT departments will not grant a supplier. A contact route the candidate answers, and SMS consent that stands up independently of who drafted the message. A clear escalation rule for when a candidate stops responding, so the tool hands over rather than persisting.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: coordinator handling time per interview, and fewer no-shows from missed reminders. Order of magnitude: this is one of the few places where the automation is boring and the saving is straightforward. An estimate; depends on interview volume.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: It books over a candidate's shift at their current job, because it knows their calendar and not their life. Or it keeps politely rescheduling a candidate who has gone cold, where a person would have recognised it on the second miss and moved on. The honest rating caveat: calendar-and-reminder automation is long proven, but agentic negotiation across a client calendar you cannot see and a VMS that owns the slots is not — most of the saving evaporates against the client's access policy rather than against the model.

where_it_helps.name: Match scores on inbound applicants
where_it_helps.the_work: A req attracts 600 applications, a growing share of them generated. Somebody has to decide who gets a phone screen this week.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Sold as a 0-100 fit score per applicant so the recruiter can work top-down. What it mostly does is rank on lexical and structural similarity to a job description that was written badly on a Tuesday from a 25-minute call.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: To be defensible it needs what almost nobody has: a validation study connecting the score to job performance, demographic data sufficient to test adverse impact, an annual independent bias audit where one is required, candidate notice, an accessible alternative process, and a version-controlled record of which model version scored whom on which date.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: reading time across a large applicant pile, which it genuinely does compress. Order of magnitude: real at high application volume — but the saving is only bankable if you keep the human review that keeps it lawful, and that review is most of the cost. An estimate.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The score becomes the decision. Nobody decides this; it happens because the recruiter is carrying nine reqs. And once the output is relied on solely, weighted more heavily than any other criterion, or used to overrule conclusions a human reached, you are inside New York City's definition of an automated employment decision tool whether you intended to be or not — with an audit, a published summary and a ten-business-day notice you never built. The scale is the exposure: in the leading federal case the vendor's system was alleged to have rejected applications in the hundreds of millions, and the collective was certified on that basis.

where_it_does_not.claim: One-way video interviews scored by AI on facial expression, tone or word choice
where_it_does_not.why_not: The construct never held: a model trained to predict interviewer ratings predicts interviewer ratings, not job performance — and a prominent vendor in the category withdrew facial analysis from its own product in 2021, which tells you what its own review found. The legal surface is worse than the product. Illinois requires pre-interview notice, an explanation of how the AI works and what general types of characteristics it evaluates, and consent — and bars evaluating anyone who has not consented, plus destruction within 30 days on request, including copies held by anyone who received the video. Maryland requires a signed plain-language waiver before a facial template is created during an interview; a tick-box does not satisfy it. Illinois's biometric statute attaches to the template itself, independently, with a private right of action. You are standing up a biometric compliance programme in order to obtain a score you cannot defend in front of an expert.

where_it_does_not.claim: "Bias-free" hiring by blinding names and demographic signals
where_it_does_not.why_not: Stripping a name does not strip the signal — graduation year, postcode, employment gaps, the name of a single-sex college, a visa status field, the difference between writing HGV and writing CDL. Since 1 January 2026 Illinois treats using ZIP code as a proxy for a protected class as a civil rights violation in its own right. The deeper problem is that blinding is usually sold alongside not collecting demographic data at all, and if you do not hold that data you cannot compute a selection rate or an impact ratio. You then cannot run the bias audit New York City requires, cannot rebut a plaintiff's statistician, and cannot tell whether the tool is doing harm. You have bought the appearance of fairness and dismantled the only instrument that measures it.

where_it_does_not.claim: Autonomous end-to-end "AI recruiter" agents that source, screen, schedule and reject
where_it_does_not.why_not: The work an agency is actually paid for is not the search. It is persuading a passive candidate to take the call, reading a hiring manager who says "culture fit" and means "too expensive", and holding a counter-offer together at ten at night. An autonomous agent removes the part of the job that was never the fee and adds an unattributable decision: when a candidate asks why they were rejected — or a court does — somebody has to be able to say who decided. A federal court has allowed a screening vendor to be sued directly on the theory that it acted as its customers' agent when it scored, ranked, sorted and screened candidates, and California's FEHA regulations now reach agents acting on an employer's behalf expressly. Distance from the decision is not distance from the liability, in either direction.

where_it_does_not.claim: Mass AI-written candidate and client outreach
where_it_does_not.why_not: Both sides now run the same models. Candidates generate applications at volume, recruiters generate approaches at volume, and the equilibrium is that nobody reads either. The costs land on you first and are measurable: sending-domain reputation, bulk-sender authentication requirements at the large mailbox providers, spam filtering that takes your genuine messages with the generated ones, and — for SMS and calls — federal and state consent rules that are wholly indifferent to whether a machine drafted the text, several of which carry statutory damages per message. The asset being spent is the only durable one a database confers, which is that your name in an inbox is still worth opening.

where_it_does_not.claim: A vendor's own bias audit as your compliance position
where_it_does_not.why_not: New York City's rules require an independent auditor and define independence to exclude anyone involved in using, developing or distributing the tool, anyone employed by the employer or agency seeking to use it, and anyone with a direct financial interest in the vendor. A summary produced by the vendor is not the artefact the law asks for. The obligation sits on the employer or employment agency that uses the tool, not on the company that sold it — so an agency accepting a vendor PDF as "covered" has bought coverage for the vendor. The notice obligation, the published summary and the accessible alternative process are all yours, and none of them arrive in the box. A December 2025 State Comptroller audit found the city's enforcement of this law had been ineffective and the agency has committed to tightening it, so the period in which nobody checked is the period that is ending.

where_it_does_not.claim: AI that sets or "optimises" pay and bill rates from market data
where_it_does_not.why_not: Two separate problems, both landing on you rather than the vendor. First, a model trained on what people were previously paid reproduces the pay gaps in that history, and it does so in a form a plaintiff can subpoena; where the output feeds an offer it is a compensation decision, which is a covered consequential decision under Colorado's new regime and squarely inside pay-equity law in California and Illinois. Second, a rate engine fed by pooled market data across competing suppliers raises an antitrust question that has nothing to do with AI and everything to do with who else is in the pool. Rate cards are a commercial negotiation with the MSP; automating them does not make them a data-science problem.

where_it_does_not.claim: AI as a way to avoid fixing the ATS
where_it_does_not.why_not: Retrieval quality is bounded by record quality, and no model repairs a record it cannot read. Where a third of candidate records are duplicates, resumes never parsed into structured fields, assignment end dates are stale, and half the recruiter context lives in Outlook, a semantic layer over the top returns fluent nonsense with a confidence score attached. Every firm that has attempted this discovers the same thing: the project was a data project, the data project is unglamorous and slow, and the budget was approved for the other one.

preconditions: One system of record for candidates, reqs and assignments, that recruiters genuinely work in. Where the real pipeline lives in a recruiter's head and a WhatsApp thread, nothing built downstream of the ATS is true.

The ability to reconstruct, for any named candidate on any date, which tool touched their record, what it output, which model version produced it, and which person acted on it. If your ATS audit log cannot produce that, you cannot answer a bias audit, a candidate's question, or a discovery request — and "we cannot reconstruct it" is the most expensive sentence in this sector. Hold it for at least four years, which is what California's amended retention rule now requires for applications, selection criteria and automated-decision system data.

Demographic data collected lawfully and held apart from the hiring record — voluntary self-identification, never inferred from names or photographs. Without it, no impact ratio can be calculated; inferring it creates a larger problem than the one it solves.

A written, honest statement of which decisions the tool makes and which a human makes, drafted to be read back to you in a deposition rather than to reassure a client in a QBR. If a recruiter cannot override the tool in practice because of their req load, the honest answer is that the tool decides.

Vendor contracts that give you the audit artefacts you are legally required to publish, advance notice of model changes rather than silent updates, and the right to test the tool against your own data. Standard terms in this category give you none of the three.

Client and MSP contract terms that work in the other direction too: whether the client's VMS applies its own scoring to your submittals before a human sees them, who holds the notice and audit obligation when it does, and what the indemnity says when the tool in the decision path belongs to neither of you.
A named owner for each tool who has the authority to switch it off without convening anyone. Not a committee, and not the person whose bonus depends on the tool's adoption.

A jurisdiction map of your reqs and your placements. A national agency filling roles in New York City, Illinois, Maryland, California and Colorado is under several regimes simultaneously, and the one that binds is generally where the work sits, not where your head office sits.

regulation.name: NYC Local Law 144 of 2021 — bias audit, published summary, candidate notice
regulation.citation: N.Y.C. Admin. Code §§ 20-870 to 20-874; implementing rules at 6 RCNY §§ 5-300 to 5-304 (DCWP final rules adopted April 2023); enforcement from 5 July 2023
regulation.what_it_requires: Applies to employers and to employment agencies using an automated employment decision tool to substantially assist or replace discretionary decision-making for hiring or promotion for a role in New York City — location of the job, not of your office. Three obligations. First, a bias audit within the previous year by an independent auditor, calculating selection rates and impact ratios by sex, by race and ethnicity, and by the intersectional categories. Second, publication on your website of a summary of the most recent audit results and the tool's distribution date. Third, notice to candidates at least ten business days before use, identifying the job qualifications and characteristics the tool assesses, with an alternative selection process or accommodation available on request. The rules define the triggering use narrowly — relying solely on the output, weighting it more than any other criterion, or using it to overrule conclusions reached by other means — and define an independent auditor to exclude anyone who used, developed or distributed the tool, is employed by the user, or holds a direct financial interest in the vendor. Penalties run to $500 for a first violation and $500 to $1,500 for each subsequent one, with each day of non-compliant use a separate violation. A State Comptroller audit released in December 2025 found the city's enforcement to date ineffective and DCWP has accepted recommendations to strengthen complaint handling and investigation, so historic under-enforcement is a poor basis for planning.

regulation.name: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act
regulation.citation: 820 ILCS 42/1 et seq., in force since 1 January 2020; demographic reporting added at 820 ILCS 42/20 by Public Act 101-0260 series amendment effective 1 January 2022
regulation.what_it_requires: Before a video interview that AI will analyse, the employer must notify the applicant that AI may be used to consider their fitness for the position, provide information explaining how the AI works and what general types of characteristics it uses to evaluate applicants, and obtain consent. An employer may not evaluate an applicant who has not consented. Videos may be shared only with people whose expertise is necessary to evaluate the applicant, and on an applicant's request must be destroyed within 30 days, including all copies held by anyone who received them. An employer that relies solely on AI analysis of a video interview to decide who advances to an in-person interview must collect race and ethnicity data for applicants who are and are not advanced and for those hired, and report it annually by 31 December to the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity, which reports to the Governor and General Assembly on whether the data discloses racial bias. The public act number for the reporting amendment is stated from secondary sources — verify it before quoting the number, though the obligation itself is not in doubt.

regulation.name: Illinois Human Rights Act, as amended for AI in employment
regulation.citation: 775 ILCS 5/2-102, as amended by Public Act 103-0804 (HB 3773), effective 1 January 2026 — subsection lettering described rather than cited
regulation.what_it_requires: In force now. Makes it a civil rights violation for an employer to use artificial intelligence that has the effect of subjecting employees or applicants to discrimination on a protected basis in recruitment, hiring, promotion, renewal, selection for training or apprenticeship, discharge, discipline, tenure or the terms of employment — and, separately, to use ZIP code as a proxy for a protected class. Employers must give notice when AI is used for such decisions; the circumstances, timing and means of that notice were left to Illinois Department of Human Rights rulemaking, which was proposed in May 2026 and has not been finalised, so the notice mechanics remain unsettled while the underlying prohibition does not. Note the standard: effect, not intent, and it reaches the tool you licensed as readily as the one you built.

regulation.name: Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act, where an interview tool touches a face or a voice
regulation.citation: 740 ILCS 14/1 et seq.; notice, written release and retention schedule at 740 ILCS 14/15; private right of action at 740 ILCS 14/20, amended by Public Act 103-0769 (2024)
regulation.what_it_requires: Independent of any AI statute. A private entity that collects a face geometry scan or voiceprint must first give written notice of the purpose and retention period and obtain a written release, must publish a retention and destruction schedule, and must not sell or profit from the data. It carries a private right of action with statutory damages of $1,000 for negligent and $5,000 for reckless or intentional violations; the 2024 amendment limits recovery to a single accrual per person per method of collection rather than per scan, which reduced the arithmetic without removing the exposure. Texas and Washington impose comparable duties enforced by their attorneys general. If a video or voice screening product creates a template, this attaches whether or not the product is described as AI.

regulation.name: Maryland — facial recognition during interviews requires a signed waiver
regulation.citation: Md. Code Ann., Lab. & Empl. § 3-717 (HB 1202, ch. 446 of 2020, effective 1 October 2020)
regulation.what_it_requires: An employer may not use a facial recognition service to create a facial template during an applicant's interview unless the applicant consents by signing a waiver. The statute prescribes what the waiver must state in plain language, including the applicant's name, the date of the interview, that the applicant read the consent waiver, and that they consent to the use of facial recognition during the interview. An "I agree" checkbox in an application flow does not meet it.

regulation.name: Federal anti-discrimination law and the selection-procedure guidelines
regulation.citation: Title VII disparate impact: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(k); ADA qualification standards and screening out: 42 U.S.C. § 12112(b)(6)-(7); ADEA: 29 U.S.C. § 623; Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures: 29 C.F.R. Part 1607, four-fifths rule at § 1607.4(D)
regulation.what_it_requires: A tool that screens people is a selection procedure and has always been treated as one. Under Title VII, where a procedure produces a substantially different selection rate for a protected group, the employer must show it is job related and consistent with business necessity, and remains liable where a less discriminatory alternative existed and was refused. The Uniform Guidelines set out what a validation study must look like and treat a selection rate below four-fifths of the highest group's rate as evidence of adverse impact — the source of the 80% figure every vendor quotes, usually without the rest of the guidance around it. Under the ADA, a tool that screens out a person with a disability must be job related and consistent with business necessity, and candidates must be able to request a reasonable accommodation for the assessment itself, including an alternative format. What changed is posture, not law: the EEOC removed its 2023 Title VII and 2022 ADA technical assistance documents on AI in January 2025, Executive Order 14281 of 23 April 2025 directed agencies to deprioritise disparate-impact liability, and the EEOC moved to close pending disparate-impact-only charges during 2025 — issuing right-to-sue letters, which routes those claims to private plaintiffs rather than extinguishing them. The statutes, the regulations, the plaintiffs' bar and state fair-employment agencies are unchanged.

regulation.name: Mobley v. Workday — the screening vendor as the employer's agent
regulation.citation: Mobley v. Workday, Inc., No. 3:23-cv-00770-RFL (N.D. Cal.); agent-theory ruling 2024, preliminary ADEA collective certification May 2025 — docket and order dates stated from secondary sources
regulation.what_it_requires: Not a statute, but the reason the statutes above now reach further than a staffing firm expects. The court allowed disparate-impact claims to proceed against the vendor itself on the theory that, in scoring, sorting, ranking and screening applicants, it performed a traditional hiring function as agent of its employer-customers and so falls within the definition of employer under Title VII, the ADEA and the ADA, and it granted preliminary certification of a nationwide ADEA collective. The reasoning does not stop at software companies: an agency, RPO or MSP that screens on a client's behalf is performing the same function under the same theory. Read it alongside California's FEHA regulations, which reach agents expressly. Verify the current procedural posture before relying on it — this is live litigation and the merits are undecided.

regulation.name: Colorado — Automated Decision-Making Technology Act, replacing the 2024 AI Act
regulation.citation: SB 26-189, signed 14 May 2026, effective 1 January 2027, repealing and re-enacting the Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205, whose commencement had been delayed to 30 June 2026 by SB 25B-004); Attorney General rulemaking proposed August 2026
regulation.what_it_requires: Correct the common assumption first: the 2024 framework with its duty of reasonable care to protect against algorithmic discrimination and its impact assessments was repealed before it ever took effect. What replaces it is a disclosure and individual-rights regime. Employment is a covered consequential decision and job applicants and employees are covered individuals. Covered technology is technology that processes personal data to generate a prediction, recommendation, classification, ranking or score used to make, guide or assist a decision, where it materially influences the outcome. Deployers — which includes an agency operating a covered tool on a client's behalf — owe pre-use notice that the technology is being used, a plain-language post-decision notice within 30 days of an adverse consequential decision explaining the role the technology played and the individual's rights, and a route to request human review and reconsideration so far as commercially reasonable, plus correction of inaccurate personal data. Tools used solely to summarise, organise, translate, draft, route or present information for human review are excluded, as are low-stakes processes that do not materially influence the outcome. That exclusion is the line your product decisions should be drawn against. Rulemaking is unfinished; treat the mechanics as unsettled and the direction as settled.

regulation.name: California — FEHA regulations on automated-decision systems
regulation.citation: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 2, §§ 11008, 11008.1, 11013 and related sections (Civil Rights Council automated-decision system employment regulations, approved 30 June 2025, effective 1 October 2025)
regulation.what_it_requires: Applies FEHA directly to automated-decision systems in employment, and reaches agents acting on an employer's behalf — which is precisely how a staffing firm, RPO or screening vendor sits. It is unlawful to use an automated-decision system or selection criteria, including a qualification standard, employment test or proxy, that discriminates on a FEHA-protected basis; the presence or absence of anti-bias testing, and the quality and scope of it, is treated as relevant evidence in a discrimination claim. Record retention under § 11013 runs four years and expressly covers applications, employment referral records, selection criteria and automated-decision system data. The precise section list and the scope of the defined "ADS data" were narrowed during rulemaking — verify against the adopted text before relying on a specific subsection.

regulation.name: EU AI Act — recruitment as a high-risk use, with the high-risk deadline deferred
regulation.citation: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Annex III point 4 (employment, worker management and access to self-employment); deployer obligations at Article 26. Deferral effected by the AI digital omnibus amending regulation in force from 27 July 2026 — amending regulation number described, not cited
regulation.what_it_requires: AI systems intended for recruitment or selection — including targeted job advertising, analysing and filtering applications, and evaluating candidates — are high-risk, as are systems used for promotion, termination, task allocation and performance monitoring. Deployers must operate the system in line with the instructions for use, assign human oversight to people with the competence, training and authority to actually exercise it, retain automatically generated logs, and inform workers' representatives and affected workers before putting a high-risk system into service. Timing moved in 2026: the obligations for stand-alone Annex III high-risk systems, originally due 2 August 2026, are deferred to 2 December 2027, and those for AI embedded in products under EU product-safety law to 2 August 2028. The Article 50 transparency duties were not deferred. Confirm the operative dates against the consolidated text before relying on them — this instrument has been amended once already and the deferral is recent.

regulation.name: Fair Credit Reporting Act, where a third party supplies the assessment
regulation.what_it_requires: Where a third party assembles information about a candidate and furnishes it to you for an employment decision, that may be a consumer report and the supplier a consumer reporting agency — regardless of how the product is marketed or what the contract calls it. That triggers a stand-alone written disclosure and the candidate's written authorisation before the report is procured, and a two-step adverse action process: a pre-adverse-action notice with a copy of the report and the summary of rights, a reasonable interval, then a final notice. AI screening and social-media or scraped-data products have been argued into this definition. Ask each vendor in writing whether they take the position that they are a consumer reporting agency, and keep the answer.

sectors.economics: The licence is the smallest number on the page. Budget it as a fraction of the total and you will be roughly right. Integration into the system of record is the first unbudgeted cost: staffing ATS platforms are old, heavily customised, and commonly reached through an API that reads well and writes badly — and for contract business there is a second integration into a VMS you do not own and cannot change, because it belongs to the client's MSP. Expect first-year integration to cost a multiple of the annual licence, and expect to pay it again each time a major client changes VMS. That is an estimate and it scales with the number of client systems you touch, not with your revenue. The second unbudgeted cost is the human review that does not go away. The posture that keeps you lawful — a person reads the file before anyone is rejected — is the same posture that consumes the saving. The honest framing is that these tools raise throughput per recruiter rather than removing recruiters; if you budget for headcount reduction, what actually gets removed is the review, which is precisely the failure the regulation is aimed at. Third is governance and documentation: an annual independent bias audit for each covered tool, published summaries maintained on your site, notice text in postings and on careers pages, an inventory of every tool that scores or ranks a person, model version records, four-year retention of applications, selection criteria and automated-decision system data where California reaches you, and a re-audit whenever a vendor ships a change — which they do silently, and which resets the clock on your published summary without telling you. Independent audits for a single tool commonly run into the low five figures a year, and rise where one tool is used across several job families, because the intersectional breakdowns multiply; that is an estimate, scaling with tools and job families rather than with headcount. Fourth is the data work — deduplication, resume re-parsing, note consolidation, correcting assignment end dates. It is the real project, it is unglamorous, and it is not optional. Then the failure cost, which has three shapes, and the fine is the smallest. A civil penalty for a missing notice or audit is an irritation, even at a per-day accrual. A discrimination claim over a screening tool is not an individual matter: it is a class or collective covering everyone the tool touched across years, discovery lands squarely on your ATS logs, and the expensive answer is "we cannot reconstruct what the tool did" — and note that where a federal agency closes a disparate-impact charge it issues a right-to-sue letter, so a quieter regulator means more private plaintiffs, not fewer. The third shape is the most likely and the least insured: an MSP or a large client removing you from the approved supplier list following a compliance finding. That takes out a revenue line immediately, and no policy covers it.
sectors.first_step: Build the tool inventory from the ATS audit log rather than by asking recruiters. Pull every component in your stack that scores, ranks, filters, sorts or recommends a person — including the ATS features nobody switched on deliberately, the sourcing extensions recruiters installed themselves, the job-board matching that orders your inbound applications, and anything a client's VMS applies to your submittals before a human sees them. For each one, write a single line: what it outputs, which named person acts on that output, whether any candidate could have been rejected in the last twelve months without a human opening the file, and which jurisdictions the reqs it touched were located in. Then ask each vendor two written questions and keep the answers: do you take the position that you are a consumer reporting agency, and will you give us the independent audit artefacts and advance notice of model changes. Most agencies find between three and eight tools they did not know were in the decision path, and at least one that is already inside a notice or audit obligation. The inventory is the artefact everything else — the audits, the notices, the vendor conversations, the defence — is built from, and it takes days rather than months.

sectors.label: Warehousing and logistics
sectors.lede: Logistics has been buying algorithms since long before anyone called them AI — route optimisers, slotting engines, forecast packages. What is genuinely new is the ability to read unstructured material at volume: the carrier's PDF invoice and its weight certificate, the exception note scrawled on a POD, the photograph of a crushed corner, the EDI 214 that arrived with a status code this carrier uses differently from everyone else. That is where most of the recoverable money sits, and it is not where the marketing points.

where_it_helps.name: Freight invoice audit and overcharge recovery
where_it_helps.the_work: An analyst opens the week's carrier invoice file, re-rates a sample against the contract, checks the accessorials against the BOL and the POD, chases the handful that look wrong, and releases the rest because payment terms run out on Friday. Post-payment recovery is then handed to a contingency vendor who finds some of what was already paid.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Re-rates every line, not a sample, against the rate table in force on the ship date, and classifies each variance by cause: wrong NMFC class or density subprovision, re-weigh or re-dim, duplicate invoice, accessorial billed with no supporting event on the BOL or POD, fuel surcharge from the wrong index or the wrong week, a mileage engine other than the one named in the contract, a load tendered outside the routing guide. Two distinct maturities sit inside this. The re-rating and variance engine is decades old and thoroughly proven. What language models add is the part that used to block automation entirely: turning a carrier's PDF invoice, scanned weight certificate or ocean demurrage statement into the same structured shape as an EDI 210, and drafting the dispute with the evidence attached. That extraction layer is newer and needs its own accuracy measurement against re-keyed documents, not an assumption that it inherits the engine's reliability.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Every rate agreement as a structured table with effective dates, the accessorial schedule, the named fuel index and its lag, the named mileage engine and version. Dim and weight captured at source. EDI 210 and 214, POD images, and a write path into AP that can place a hold code rather than just print a report. Critically, a history of disputes already adjudicated — won and lost — because an audit engine cannot be evaluated against activity, only against outcomes. And the limitation date on every case at creation, because an overcharge surfaced after the statutory window has closed is not collectable.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Two mechanisms. It moves audit from sample to census, and from post-payment recovery to pre-payment prevention, so the money never leaves. And it collapses the analyst hours spent re-rating by hand, which in most operations is the larger of the two lines. Be sceptical of published error rates: nearly all of them originate with audit vendors paid a share of what they find, they are not comparable across mode mix, and none of them is a measurement of your freight. The only number worth planning against is the one your own full manual re-rate of a single period produces. Whatever that turns out to be, it moves with mode mix, contract complexity and how much accessorial-heavy LTL, drayage and parcel you run. Everything in this paragraph is an estimate and the arithmetic is yours to do.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Over-disputing. Tune for recall and the system generates disputes on legitimate charges; the carrier's billing team stops answering, your escalations queue behind everyone else's, and in a tight market that costs more than the recovery. The second failure is rate-table drift: procurement signs an amendment that never reaches the audit system, and it flags every load on that lane for six weeks until someone works out why. The table needs a permanent owner. The third is quieter — the extraction layer mis-reads a scanned weight certificate, the variance looks real, and the dispute goes out with wrong evidence attached, which is how a carrier learns to ignore your disputes generally.

where_it_helps.name: Load building and route planning with learned travel and service times
where_it_helps.the_work: A planner builds tomorrow's outbound at three in the afternoon — drops orders onto trailers, respects pick sequence, dock doors, driver hours and each receiver's window — then rebuilds it when the late orders land at half four.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: The optimisation itself is classical operations research and has been for forty years; nothing about it is new. What machine learning adds is the inputs the optimiser has always had to guess: travel time by lane and time of day learned from telematics rather than from a static matrix, service time learned per stop and per receiver, trailer cube and weight yield learned from order profile, and the probability that a given stop runs long. Better inputs, same solver.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Telematics history joined to stop-level arrive and depart events. Accurate dimensions and stackability, not order-line weights. Honest receiving windows rather than the ones in the customer master. The driver's full on-duty window and required breaks modelled, not drive time alone. And the constraints written down — in most operations a meaningful share of them live only in the head of the planner who has done the job for eleven years.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: fewer trailers dispatched for the same volume, and a smaller gap between plan and actual so dispatch stops absorbing the difference. Publicly quoted figures cluster in the single-digit percent on miles or trailer count where planning is currently manual, but those figures come from the people selling the software. Test it yourself before buying: re-solve last quarter's outbound with the learned inputs and compare against what was actually dispatched. Where a competent optimiser already runs, the learned-input layer buys much less. Estimate, and heavily dependent on stop density.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: A plan that is optimal and undrivable. Drivers reject it, planners override it, and within a month the system is in advisory mode and everyone has quietly gone back to the spreadsheet. A plan that cannot be run inside the hours-of-service limits is worse than undrivable — it is an illegal plan, and the ELD record will say so. The subtler failure is that learned service times encode a badly run receiver's behaviour as normal and permanent, so the system plans around the problem instead of surfacing it.

where_it_helps.name: Exception management for shipments
where_it_helps.the_work: Someone works a list of four hundred open loads, rings the carriers who have sent no status, updates the customers who have asked, and decides what to actually do about the forty that are genuinely late.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Normalises status events across carriers into one vocabulary, scores each open shipment against the promised date rather than the carrier's own ETA, ranks by consequence instead of by lateness, drafts the customer notification and the recovery option, and closes out the ones that need no action at all.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: EDI 214 or API feeds with a documented, tested status-code mapping per carrier — carriers use the same codes to mean different things, and this is the single most common reason these projects stall. The promise date from the order, not the carrier's estimate. Timestamps with a stated zone. A consequence model that knows which customer has an OTIF penalty and which production line stops. And a named owner per exception type with authority to spend to fix it.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: the exception queue is mostly noise, and removing the noise lets the same team work the loads that matter rather than triaging. Teams that have measured it usually find a large share of flagged exceptions required no action at all; measure your own by sampling one week's queue and recording which entries produced an action and which did not. That sample is also the only sensible baseline for judging a vendor's claimed suppression rate. Estimate, entirely dependent on feed quality.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Silent feed death. A carrier's 214 stream stops, no exceptions are raised for that carrier, and the dashboard turns greener — absence of an event is read as on-time. Monitor message volume per carrier per day as a first-class alert, not exception counts. The second failure is notification fatigue: a system that tells the customer about every fifteen-minute slip trains them to ignore the one that matters.

where_it_helps.name: Damage and OS&D claim processing
where_it_helps.the_work: Assemble the packet — BOL, POD with the exception noted, photographs, the commercial invoice, repair or replacement cost, salvage disposition — file it inside the contractual window, then chase the carrier through the acknowledgement and disposition clocks while the file sits in someone's inbox.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Separate the two halves honestly. The half that works is ordinary workflow automation with no model in it: assembling the packet, tracking the nine-month filing window, the thirty-day acknowledgement and the hundred-and-twenty-day disposition clock, and prompting before each expires. The half that is still early is the model work — extracting damage descriptions from photographs and signed PODs, valuing the packet, drafting the reply to a declination, and finding the recurring pattern behind the claims: this lane, this pack configuration, this receiver, this one cross-dock. The pattern-finding is where the durable value is and also where it is hardest to show the result is real rather than an artefact of which claims happened to get filed.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Images captured at the right handover point and tied to a specific handling unit. POD exception text captured, not just a signature. Item cost data, salvage policy, and a claims system that records the date of written disallowance, because that is when the two-year suit clock starts. A defined evidence standard, agreed with whoever argues your claims, that an automated packet must meet before a human signs it.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: fewer claims abandoned because nobody had time to assemble the packet, and fewer lost to the calendar. In most operations the quiet leak is not denied claims, it is claims never filed. Order of magnitude scales with how many small claims you currently write off; count those for a quarter before assuming there is a business case. An estimate, and it depends on volume and claim size distribution.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The model asserts concealed damage as carrier liability without the evidence an adjuster will accept, the claim is denied on the merits, and you have burned the filing window doing it. That is worse than not filing. The mirror failure is a model that triages a claim as not worth filing — that is a legal decision dressed as a queue decision, and it needs a named human owner. Any automated claim needs a human signature against a defined evidence standard before it goes out.

where_it_helps.name: Dock scheduling, detention and demurrage defence
where_it_helps.the_work: An appointment book run by email. Carriers ask for slots, receiving has three live doors and a lumper crew of six, trucks arrive early or late, and the detention invoices turn up six weeks later with times nobody in the building can contradict.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Predicts unload duration from trailer content, carrier and receiver history rather than a flat sixty-minute default, builds the appointment grid against actual labour availability, re-slots when arrivals move, and reconciles your own gate and yard timestamps against every detention and demurrage charge before it is paid. On the ocean side it also checks each demurrage and detention invoice against the required content and the issuance window, which is the one place in freight where an invoice can be challenged on its face rather than on the facts.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Gate in and out timestamps you control — a yard system or a gate app, not the carrier's word. Labour roster by shift. ASN content with case and pallet counts. Carrier detention terms and free-time rules, and for ocean the free time, the invoice date and the charge accrual dates. And a person with the authority to refuse a slot request, because a scheduler with no authority just reproduces the email queue.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: detention and demurrage you stop paying because you can evidence the times, plus overtime avoided by levelling the arrival curve instead of absorbing a two-hundred-truck morning peak. Largest where dock labour, not door count, is the binding constraint. Estimate; pull your last twelve months of detention, demurrage and per-diem accessorials and size it before starting, because in some networks the whole line is too small to justify the integration.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: It optimises the door and ignores the labour, producing a grid that is feasible on paper and unstaffable in practice. And it is right on average and wrong in the tail — one four-hour unload wrecks the day, and the system cascades a reschedule across every downstream appointment in a way the receiving manager will simply override, after which nobody trusts it again.

where_it_helps.name: Demand forecasting for the stable baseline of DC replenishment
where_it_helps.the_work: A demand planner produces a statistical baseline for what each DC needs to hold and pull, then overrides most of it with what merchandising said about the promotion in a Tuesday meeting, and the override is not recorded anywhere the model can see. Meanwhile the inbound plan is built on a lead time that assumes the container clears in the usual number of days.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Hierarchical baseline forecasting across SKU, DC and network with proper reconciliation; intermittent-demand handling on the long tail, where the honest answer is usually a service-level stocking policy rather than a point forecast; and the underrated function — flagging which items the model should not be trusted on, so planner attention goes where it changes something. In a distribution setting the output that matters is usually cases and pallets through a specific door in a specific week, not units in the abstract, because that is what sizes labour, storage and inbound appointments.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Demand history de-censored for stockouts, because shipments are not demand and a model trained on shipments learns to forecast your own shortages. The promotion calendar as structured data with start, end, mechanic and depth — not a PDF from merchandising. Price history. New-item mapping to predecessors. Lead time distributions by origin and mode, not a single planning number. And a stated forecast target, because units at the DC, cases through the door and consumer offtake are three different series and teams routinely argue while measuring different ones.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: less safety stock held for the same service level on the stable portion of the catalogue, and fewer expedites and emergency inter-DC transfers. Note the leverage is sublinear — a given percentage improvement in baseline accuracy yields a smaller percentage change in inventory, not one for one, and in most networks lead time variability contributes more to safety stock than forecast error does. Estimate, and worth checking which of the two dominates yours before funding the forecast rather than the lead time.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Discontinuity, and the metric that hides it. Promotions, price changes, new items, a competitor's stockout, a channel shift, a customer restructuring their own DC network — none of these is in the history in a form the model can learn from, and models trained to minimise average error systematically under-forecast the peak and then over-forecast the decay after it. A MAPE computed across the whole catalogue is dominated by high-volume stable items and will look fine in the week you lose a promotion. Measure accuracy separately on promoted, new and stable items or you are measuring nothing.

where_it_helps.name: Carrier selection and routing-guide repair
where_it_helps.the_work: A quarterly bid, then eleven months defending the routing guide while primary carriers reject tenders and loads fall down the guide to the spot market at a substantial premium that nobody attributes back to the bid.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Predicts tender acceptance by carrier, lane and day of week; prices the true cost of a routing guide including the expected cost of fallback rather than the headline rate; scores carriers on delivered outcomes rather than bid price; and flags the lanes where the guide has already failed, usually weeks before the quarterly review does.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Tender accept and reject history with timestamps — most shippers have years of this in the TMS and have never analysed it. A spot market reference. Carrier performance joined to your own OTIF and claims outcomes, not to a third-party scorecard. Live operating authority and insurance status checked at the moment of tender, not at onboarding. And, for brokered freight, a decision about how far down the chain you can actually see.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: fewer loads falling out of the guide to spot, and a bid priced on expected rather than headline cost. The size depends entirely on your current fallout rate and the current spread between contract and spot; if fallout is low or the market is soft, there is very little here. Estimate, and check your fallout rate and your spot spread first — this is the item most often funded on a market condition that has already passed.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: Optimising against your own carriers. Rank on accepted cost alone and you select for carriers who accept everything and service badly, and you degrade relationships with the ones you need when capacity tightens. Carrier selection is a repeated game and a model optimising one period at a time does not know that. The related failure is a scoring model that quietly rewards a broker who accepts everything and re-brokers it, which is a fraud exposure rather than a service one.

where_it_does_not.claim: AI forecasting that finally gets promotions, new products and seasonal peaks right
where_it_does_not.why_not: These are discontinuities, and the causal driver is not in the data. A promotion's effect depends on depth, mechanic, competing activity, display position and the retailer's own execution — most of which never reaches your planning system in structured form, and some of which is decided after the forecast is due. Deep models do not fix this; they make it worse, because they are better at extrapolating the smooth part and equally blind to the break. There is also no sample: you have a handful of comparable promotions on a given item, not thousands. The honest answer is a structured promotional lift process with human judgement and recorded assumptions, a baseline model that explicitly excludes promoted periods, and separate accuracy measurement for promoted and non-promoted demand. Anyone selling a single model that handles both is selling you an average that is wrong in both directions.

where_it_does_not.claim: Agentic dispatch — the system finds capacity, tenders the load and books the carrier end to end without a human
where_it_does_not.why_not: A tender is a contract and a load on a trailer cannot be recalled. The vetting that matters — operating authority, insurance in force today, safety record, whether this is the carrier you booked or someone they double-brokered it to — changes daily and is the exact surface fraud operates on. Cargo theft through fraudulent carrier onboarding is a working criminal industry, and it targets automated, low-friction booking specifically. The liability does not move to the software vendor when it goes wrong; it stays with you, and so does the customer's freight. Automate the search, the rate comparison and the paperwork. Keep a human on the decision to hand goods to a specific carrier, and re-verify authority and insurance at the moment of tender rather than at onboarding.

where_it_does_not.claim: A control tower with predictive ETAs that eliminates track-and-trace calls
where_it_does_not.why_not: You do not own the position data, and on large parts of your network it does not exist. Truckload with a cooperative carrier and an API is fine. LTL, drayage, cross-border and most brokered freight give you a status message at a terminal scan, hours apart, if at all. No model can predict what it cannot observe, and the residual uncertainty is not driving time — it is dwell at facilities you do not control. The result is an ETA with a band several hours wide against a delivery window of two, which changes nobody's decision. Meanwhile the calls do not stop, because the customer is not ringing for an estimate, they are ringing for a commitment. Fix feed coverage per carrier first and only then talk about prediction; a control tower built on 60 percent coverage displays confident nonsense about the other 40.

where_it_does_not.claim: Computer vision at the dock that detects damage and replaces the receiving inspection
where_it_does_not.why_not: What the claims process needs is timestamped, chain-of-custody evidence tied to a specific handling unit at a specific handover, in a form a carrier's adjuster will accept. A classifier output of "probably damaged" is not that, and the adjuster on the other side has no obligation to accept your model's opinion. Physically, the job is hard in the wrong way: stretch wrap, slip sheets, mixed pallets, shrink film glare, variable dock lighting, and the damage that matters most is often concealed. Vision is genuinely useful as a prompt — flag this pallet for a human look, capture the image set automatically so the packet is complete — and useless as a substitute for the inspection and the signed exception on the POD.

where_it_does_not.claim: Labour management AI that predicts under-performance and coaches associates in real time
where_it_does_not.why_not: Two reasons, and the compliance one is the smaller. An algorithmic pace or task-allocation system is a quota, and warehouse quota statutes now in force in California, New York, Minnesota, Washington, Oregon, Connecticut and Rhode Island require it to be disclosable in writing to the person it governs and prohibit it where it interferes with breaks, bathroom access or health and safety compliance; New York additionally requires an ergonomist's written worksite evaluation under its injury reduction programme, which is where the algorithm gets examined. In the EU, the same system is high-risk under the AI Act. That is a serious governance burden, and it applies to a system you cannot explain in writing — which rules out most of them. The larger reason is that it optimises the wrong variable: in most buildings the binding constraint on throughput is slotting, replenishment timing, trailer arrival variance and dock congestion, not the individual picker's rate. You take on a fundamental-rights compliance programme to squeeze the one input that was not limiting you.

where_it_does_not.claim: A model that reads all your EDI and carrier feeds and self-heals the data
where_it_does_not.why_not: The data problem in this sector is not malformed messages — parsers have handled those for thirty years. It is messages that are perfectly valid and semantically wrong: a 214 carrying a status code this carrier uses to mean "arrived at terminal" and that one uses to mean "out for delivery"; a weight field holding the estimated weight rather than the scaled weight; a SCAC belonging to a subsidiary that bills under a different contract; an appointment time in the facility's local zone with no zone stated. No amount of reading the message detects valid-but-wrong. Only reconciliation against an independent source does — the scale ticket against the invoice weight, the gate log against the carrier's arrival event, the contract against the SCAC. Budget for the mapping work per carrier. It is unglamorous, it does not compress, and it is the actual project.

preconditions: Every rate agreement currently in force exists as a structured table with effective dates, the accessorial schedule, the named fuel index and its lag, and the named mileage engine and version — not as a signed PDF in a shared drive that only procurement can find.

One identity per facility, per carrier (including subsidiaries billing under a different SCAC), and per handling unit, with dimensions and weight captured at source rather than inferred from the order line, and every timestamp carrying an explicit time zone.

A documented and tested status-code mapping per carrier for the EDI transactions you rely on, plus a monitor that alerts when a carrier's daily message volume drops. An absent feed must never read as good news.
A history of adjudicated outcomes — disputes won and lost, claims paid and denied, tenders accepted and rejected, with dates. Nothing here can be trained or honestly evaluated on activity data alone.
A named owner, with authority to spend or to refuse, for every exception type and every variance cause code. A queue nobody owns does not get worked faster by being sorted better.

A write path into the system of record — an AP hold code, a TMS tender, a WMS appointment — with an audit trail showing what the machine proposed and who approved it. Output that lands in a report changes nothing and costs the same to build.

Statutory and contractual clocks under system control rather than in someone's memory: the nine-month minimum cargo claim window, the carrier's thirty-day acknowledgement and hundred-and-twenty-day disposition duties, the two-year suit clock running from written disallowance, the eighteen-month overcharge limitation, and the ocean demurrage and detention invoice and mitigation windows. Automation that misses a deadline is more expensive than the manual process it replaced.

Written legal review before deploying anything that monitors, rates, paces or allocates work to identifiable associates, in every jurisdiction where you run a building — the quota states now number seven and their thresholds differ — and in the EU, before procurement, not after.

regulation.name: Carmack Amendment — carrier liability for cargo loss and damage
regulation.what_it_requires: Sets the liability regime for interstate carriage and the minimum time limits a carrier may impose: no less than nine months to file a written claim, and no less than two years from the date the carrier gives written notice disallowing any part of the claim to bring a civil action (§ 14706(e)). Contracts routinely set exactly those minimums. Any system that assembles, files or triages claims must treat those windows as hard, and a model that decides a claim is not worth filing is making a legal decision that needs a named human owner.

regulation.name: Loss and damage claim processing rules for motor carriers
regulation.what_it_requires: § 370.3 sets what a communication must contain to count as a filed claim: enough facts to identify the shipment, an assertion of carrier liability, and a demand for a specified or determinable amount of money. § 370.5 requires the carrier to acknowledge a proper claim in writing within 30 days of receipt unless it has already paid or declined it. § 370.9 requires the carrier to pay, decline or make a firm compromise settlement offer in writing within 120 days of receipt, and where it cannot, to advise the claimant in writing of status and reason at that point and at each succeeding 60-day interval. These are the clocks an automated claims queue has to respect on either side of the transaction. (The draft of this briefing originally attributed the 30-day acknowledgement to § 370.9; it is § 370.5.)

regulation.name: Limitation on actions by and against carriers
regulation.what_it_requires: Eighteen months to begin a civil action to recover overcharges, with the claim accruing on delivery or tender of delivery; the same eighteen-month limit applies to a carrier suing to collect its charges. The period is extended by six months from the time the carrier gives the claimant written notice of disallowance. An audit that surfaces an overcharge after the window has closed has surfaced nothing collectable. Put the limitation date on the case record at creation and let the queue sort by it.

regulation.name: Ocean demurrage and detention billing requirements
regulation.citation: 46 C.F.R. Part 541 (Federal Maritime Commission final rule published 26 February 2024, effective 28 May 2024; § 541.4 vacated)
regulation.what_it_requires: Mandates specified minimum information on each demurrage or detention invoice, requires vessel-operating common carriers and marine terminal operators to issue invoices within 30 calendar days of the date charges last accrued, and sets windows for the billed party to request mitigation and for the billing party to resolve. Important correction to the common summary: the provision limiting who may properly be invoiced (§ 541.4) was set aside by the D.C. Circuit in World Shipping Council v. FMC on 23 September 2025 as arbitrary and capricious, and the FMC published notice of that removal in December 2025. The rest of Part 541 remains in force. For invoice audit this is still the strongest single lever in ocean freight — an invoice missing required elements, or issued outside the window, is challengeable on its face — but a system built on the vacated section is auditing a rule that no longer exists. Confirm the operative text with counsel.

regulation.name: Hours of service and electronic logging devices
regulation.citation: 49 C.F.R. Part 395 (driving limits at § 395.3; ELD requirement at § 395.8)
regulation.what_it_requires: Federal driving and on-duty limits for property-carrying drivers, recorded electronically. A routing, load-planning or appointment system that produces a plan a driver cannot legally run has produced an illegal plan, and the ELD record is the evidence of what actually happened. Check that any optimiser models the on-duty window and required breaks, not just drive time — this is the most common way a planning tool quietly pushes a fleet out of compliance.

regulation.name: California warehouse distribution centre quota law (AB 701)
regulation.citation: Cal. Lab. Code §§ 2100–2112
regulation.what_it_requires: Employers with at least 100 employees at a single California warehouse distribution centre, or 1,000 across multiple sites in the state, must give each employee a written description of any quota they are subject to, including the quantified tasks, the time period, and any adverse action that may follow from failing to meet it. Quotas that prevent meal and rest breaks, bathroom access, or compliance with occupational health and safety law are prohibited. An algorithmic pace or task-allocation system is a quota for these purposes and must be describable in writing to the person it governs — which rules out anything you cannot explain.

regulation.name: New York warehouse worker quota disclosure and injury reduction duties
regulation.citation: N.Y. Labor Law art. 21-A (Warehouse Worker Protection Act, effective 19 June 2023) and N.Y. Labor Law § 27-e (Warehouse Worker Injury Reduction Act, signed December 2024, effective 1 June 2025)
regulation.what_it_requires: Article 21-A requires covered employers — 100 or more employees at a single warehouse distribution centre, or 1,000 or more in the state — to give each employee a written description of every quota, with recordkeeping and anti-retaliation duties. Section 27-e separately requires a formal injury reduction programme: a written worksite evaluation of ergonomic risk factors by a qualified ergonomist for each manual materials handling job, employee and supervisor training, consultation with employees or the safety committee, and evaluations kept accessible to workers on request. If you deploy a system that sets pace or allocates tasks, both files apply, and the ergonomic evaluation is where the algorithm gets examined. Section numbering verified against secondary legal sources rather than the consolidated statute — confirm before quoting.

regulation.name: Warehouse production-quota statutes in other states
regulation.citation: described, not cited — Washington, Minnesota, Oregon, Connecticut and Rhode Island each have their own warehouse quota statute, with differing coverage thresholds and effective dates
regulation.what_it_requires: The common pattern is written disclosure of any quota to the worker it governs, a prohibition on quotas that interfere with meal, rest and bathroom breaks or with health and safety compliance, recordkeeping on individual work-speed data, and anti-retaliation protection. Thresholds and definitions differ state by state, and the list has grown in each of the last four legislative cycles, so treat any published roster of states as out of date by default. Counsel should confirm the current list and the specific text for every state where you run a building before an algorithmic pace or task-allocation system is deployed.

regulation.name: EU AI Act — employment and worker management as high-risk
regulation.citation: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Annex III, point 4
regulation.what_it_requires: AI used to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits, to monitor and evaluate performance, or to make decisions affecting terms and conditions of work, is classified high-risk. That pulls in risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight, technical documentation, registration and conformity assessment, with obligations on deployers as well as providers. Warehouse labour-management and pick-rate systems sit squarely inside this. The application date for stand-alone Annex III systems was deferred from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027 by the 2026 digital omnibus amendment; the classification itself did not change, and transparency obligations elsewhere in the Act were not deferred. Confirm the operative dates and the amending instrument with counsel rather than relying on any published summary, including this one.

regulation.name: Property broker records
regulation.what_it_requires: Brokers must keep a record of each transaction, and each party to a brokered transaction has the right to review the record relating to it. FMCSA's Transparency in Property Broker Transactions rulemaking (docket FMCSA-2023-0257, NPRM published 20 November 2024, comment period reopened to 20 March 2025) would require electronic records and change the disclosure mechanics; it is not final, and the existing section governs. Relevant if you are building audit coverage across brokered freight — some of the data you need may be obtainable by right rather than by negotiation.

regulation.name: Customs reasonable care and recordkeeping
regulation.citation: 19 U.S.C. § 1484 (entry and reasonable care), 19 U.S.C. § 1508 (maintenance of records) and 19 U.S.C. § 1509 (examination and production); retention period at 19 C.F.R. § 163.4
regulation.what_it_requires: The importer of record must use reasonable care in making entry, including classification, valuation and origin, must maintain the records supporting it for five years from the date of entry, and must produce them on demand, with substantial penalties for failure to produce. A model that proposes HTS classifications does not transfer that duty to anyone; it makes the reviewer's sign-off the control. Keep the model's stated rationale in the entry file so the exercise of reasonable care is demonstrable.

regulation.name: Powered industrial trucks
regulation.citation: 29 C.F.R. § 1910.178 (training and evaluation at § 1910.178(l))
regulation.what_it_requires: Operator training, evaluation and certification for forklifts and similar equipment, plus operating requirements on the floor. Relevant whenever vision or telematics systems are sold as safety controls: they can inform the training and evaluation programme, they do not satisfy it, and using their output to discipline individual operators reopens every quota and worker-monitoring question above.

sectors.economics:
The pilot is not the cost. In this sector the integration into the system of record is reliably the largest line and the one that gets left out of business cases: EDI mapping and testing per carrier, AP hold-code handling, TMS and WMS write-back, and the reconciliation that proves the machine's view and the ledger agree. Budget that in carrier-weeks, not sprints, and expect the long tail of small carriers to cost as much as the top five combined.

Then there is the permanent cost nobody owns at the start: rate-table maintenance. Contract amendments, annual general rate increases, weekly fuel index changes, accessorial schedule revisions, and periodic classification restructuring — the NMFTA's Docket 2025-1, effective 19 July 2025, moved roughly two thousand item numbers onto a density-based scale and widened the density subprovisions from eleven tiers to thirteen in a single docket. If nobody owns that table, the audit engine's false-positive rate climbs quietly until the team stops trusting it, which is the normal way these systems die. One named person, with time in their week, indefinitely.

Human review does not go away; it changes shape. Disputes still need someone to argue them with a carrier who has their own view. Claims still need a person on the other side to accept the packet. A forecast override still needs a planner who knows about the promotion. Plan for roughly the same headcount doing higher-value work through the first year, and say so internally — if the saving is promised as headcount, people will hide the tool's errors to protect the number, and you lose the error data you need to improve it.

Governance and documentation are real line items now, not paperwork. Model and decision logs, retention aligned to obligations you already carry (customs records for five years from entry, claims files through the limitation period), and in the EU a worker-facing system pulls you into conformity assessment with documentation requirements that outlast the vendor relationship — the deferral of the high-risk application date to December 2027 buys scheduling room, not an exemption. If a vendor cannot tell you what their model saw and why it flagged a line, you cannot evidence reasonable care or defend a dispute, and you are buying a liability with a dashboard on it.

On contingency-fee freight audit: the structure is a share of what is recovered, commonly quoted somewhere between a fifth and a half depending on mode and whether the work is pre- or post-payment, and it looks free. It is not. The vendor is paid on recoveries, so their incentive is to find errors, not to prevent them — the two are in direct tension, and prevention is worth more. Your rate agreements and shipment history also leave your control. If you go that way, bound it with a data-return clause, get the cause-code detail back in structured form, and measure prevented errors separately from recovered ones.

Finally, cost the failure mode, because it is asymmetric. The upside of freight audit is basis points of freight spend. The downside of an over-tuned auto-dispute is a carrier who deprioritises you when capacity tightens, and the downside of a missed claim window is money that is simply gone. A wrongly withheld payment can cost more in one peak week than the programme recovers in a quarter. Size the programme against the arithmetic you can check in advance: audited spend, observed error rate from your own manual sample, and current labour hours. If that does not clear the integration cost in year one, do not start. All of these are estimates and all of them move with volume.
sectors.first_step: Take 90 days of invoices from your three largest carriers on one mode, and re-rate every single line by hand against the contract that was in force on the ship date — not a sample, all of them. Record four things: how many you could not re-rate at all and exactly why (no structured rate table, no dim capture, missing accessorial schedule, no POD, ambiguous SCAC, no time zone on the timestamp), the error rate and its direction, the value of the errors, and the hours it took. Check each one against the eighteen-month limitation date while you are there, so you learn how much of what you find is already uncollectable. That produces four things you cannot buy: a ground-truth labelled set, a defensible error rate of your own, an exact list of the data that is missing, and the only honest yardstick against which to judge any vendor's claimed hit rate. It also tells you whether to proceed. Do not start with the forecast.

sectors.label: Professional services
sectors.lede: A professional services firm sells hours it cannot store, through people it cannot quickly replace, at a realisation rate it usually discovers after the fact. AI lands on that business differently from any other: the places it works best — time capture, pre-bill narrative, precedent retrieval, scoping — attack the top line of an hourly book before they touch the cost base, so the business case is a pricing decision wearing a technology costume.
