And the governance problem here is not privacy in the abstract. It is that a knowledge system able to see every client's work at once is one bad retrieval away from ending an engagement.

where_it_helps.name: Timesheet reconstruction from activity trails
where_it_helps.the_work: Fee-earners writing Friday afternoon timesheets from memory. The resourcing or revenue team chasing the eleven people who are four days behind, then a partner reconstructing a fortnight the day before the billing cut-off.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Assembles a draft day from the trails the firm already holds — calendar entries, document check-in/check-out history in the DMS, sent mail, call logs, case management events — and proposes matter code, phase code and a narrative for each block. The fee-earner edits and confirms; nothing posts unconfirmed.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Read access to the document management system, mail and calendar, mapped to matter and phase codes; a matter taxonomy that is actually used rather than a free-text field; write access into the practice management system's time API; and per-matter access filtering so the draft for one timekeeper never surfaces another matter's activity. A confirmation step that records who approved and when, and a hard stop that prevents confirmation of a day more than a day or two old on any matter subject to contemporaneous-record rules.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: recovers the hours that fall out of memory-based reconstruction and shortens the write-up itself. Order of magnitude in firms with poor discipline: low single-digit percentage points of recorded hours recovered, plus roughly 20-40 minutes per fee-earner per week returned. This is an estimate and it scales with how bad your current lock-up and late-entry position is — a firm that already enters time daily will get close to nothing. Vendors quote recovery in the 5-10% range; treat anything above low single digits as unproven in your book until you have measured your own late-entry gap.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: It mis-codes time to the adjacent matter for the same client group, or worse to a different client, and the error survives into an invoice — which turns a coding slip into a document that tells one client what you were doing for another. Separately, machine-reconstructed time is not contemporaneous time: on government-funded or audited work that distinction is the entire point, and a reviewer will treat a batch of identical AI-phrased narratives as evidence of a systemic timekeeping weakness rather than as a tidy set of records.

where_it_helps.name: Pre-bill narrative review against client billing guidelines
where_it_helps.the_work: The billing partner and the revenue controller scrubbing a pre-bill: block billing, 'attention to file', 'review documents', task codes that do not match the phase, two timekeepers of the same grade on one call, a paralegal task charged at associate rate. Then the e-billing rejection three weeks later and the write-down nobody appeals.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Checks each line against that client's outside counsel guidelines and historical reduction patterns before the bill leaves — flags what will be cut and why, and proposes a narrative that describes the same work in terms the guideline accepts. Flags only; the timekeeper approves any wording change.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: The text of each client's billing guidelines in machine-readable form, historical line-item appeal and reduction data from the e-billing channel, UTBMS or equivalent task-code mapping, and an absolute rule that only the person who did the work can approve a changed description. Log the before and after, and keep both in the matter file.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: converts write-downs discovered at collection into corrections made before billing, where they cost an edit rather than a fee. Order of magnitude: one to three points of realisation on guideline-governed matters. An estimate; it depends entirely on what share of your book runs through client e-billing with enforced guidelines, and a firm billing mostly on trust will see little. Note that rules-based versions of this check predate language models by a decade, so measure the increment over the e-billing validation you may already own rather than against doing nothing.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The model improves the narrative past what was actually done. A description edited to survive an audit rather than to describe the work is not a cleaner bill, it is a false record — and because the edit is systematic, discovery of one instance implicates the whole billing cycle. The second failure is quieter: everyone's narratives converge on the same four accepted phrasings, and the bill stops carrying information the client's reviewer can use, which is the thing that eventually loses you the panel seat.

where_it_helps.name: Precedent and prior-engagement retrieval inside the existing access model
where_it_helps.the_work: The associate or manager who loses most of a day asking three people whether the firm has done this before — a carve-out with a transition services agreement shaped like this one, a three-tier earn-out mechanism, a s.75 apportionment, a fixed-asset impairment memo for a client with this fact pattern. Usually it ends with someone remembering a matter from four years ago.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Retrieval over the engagement archive and know-how store, restricted at query time to what the asker is already entitled to see, returning the specific clause, schedule or working paper with its source document, matter and date — not a synthesis that hides its provenance.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: An access model that works before AI touches it: information barriers and ethical walls enforced in the DMS rather than by convention, matter-team membership that is current, lateral-hire screens, and destruction and retention schedules actually applied so closed-and-purged matters cannot resurface. Every result carries a link to its source; every query is logged against the asker; and the index inherits permission changes within minutes rather than at the next rebuild.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: replaces the ask-around-and-hope search with a direct one, and raises the rate at which existing work product gets reused instead of rebuilt. Order of magnitude: several hours per fee-earner per month, concentrated in the mid grades. An estimate, and it depends on how much of your know-how is already curated — retrieval over an uncurated archive mostly finds old drafts.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The index is built from a file share or an archive whose permissions live outside the DMS, and the retrieval layer becomes the path of least resistance around the wall. The characteristic incident is not a leaked document — it is a summary that reveals the existence of a matter, which is a conflicts and confidentiality problem at the same time and is not cured by the document itself never being opened. The second failure is retrieval of a superseded precedent with no signal that the law, the accounting standard or the client's own position has moved.

where_it_helps.name: Proposal and scope-of-work drafting
where_it_helps.the_work: A pursuit team assembling a sixty-page response over a weekend: methodology, CVs, references, the assumptions and exclusions schedule, the phasing table. All of it non-chargeable, most of it assembled from documents somebody remembers.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Produces the first draft from the firm's own bid library and the notes of the scoping conversation, and — the part that carries the margin — drafts the assumptions, exclusions and change-control section from the same inputs, so the margin-protecting clauses are present before the partner reads it rather than added if someone notices.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: A curated bid library with an owner, prior client identities and confidential detail stripped from anything reusable, pricing held outside the drafting tool entirely, and a check that reusing the structure of a prior deliverable does not breach the terms of the engagement that produced it. The engagement partner signs the scope, always.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: compresses first-draft assembly on RFP-shaped pursuits from days to hours, against time that is pure cost because it is never billed. Order of magnitude: 30-50% of drafting time on structured responses. An estimate; it depends on pursuit volume, and a firm doing six bids a year should not build anything for this. Note also that drafting is rarely the binding constraint on win rate, so do not book this as revenue.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The boilerplate scope drifts from what the partner intends to deliver, and the gap only appears when the client holds you to the document. The specific and common version: an exclusion that protected margin on the last engagement quietly does not make it into this one, and nobody notices because the draft reads fluently. Fluency is exactly what stops the scope being read properly.

where_it_helps.name: Realisation and utilisation decomposition
where_it_helps.the_work: The finance team building the monthly practice pack, and the partner asking why their realisation is down three points — a question that currently takes an analyst two days and often ends in a plausible story rather than an answer.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Decomposes the movement into its actual causes — agreed rate discount, write-down at billing, write-off at collection, grade mix and leverage drift, unbilled scope, and time recorded late — matter by matter, and writes the explanation in plain language with the three matters driving most of it named. The arithmetic should be a deterministic bridge in the reporting layer; the model's job is to narrate it, not to compute it.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: A chart of accounts and a billing system that keep those causes apart. Most firms collapse discount and write-down into one figure, and no model can separate them afterwards; fixing that is a finance project, not an AI one. Standard hours, standard rates and budgets must exist in the system, and the decomposition must reconcile to the reported realisation figure before anyone reads the words.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: removes analyst days per month and, more usefully, replaces an argument about the numbers with an argument about the matters. Order of magnitude: a few analyst days per practice per month. An estimate, and the real return is decision quality, which does not appear in a savings line and should not be claimed in a business case.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: It writes a confident decomposition the underlying data cannot support — the numbers reconcile, the attribution is invented. Because the output reads like analysis rather than a model estimate, nobody interrogates it, and the practice spends a quarter fixing the wrong thing. Rated early rather than workable for a blunt reason: at most firms the precondition fails, so what actually ships is a fluent narrator sitting on a collapsed general ledger, and that is worse than the analyst it replaced.

where_it_helps.name: Early warning on engagement overrun
where_it_helps.the_work: The engagement manager and the project review partner reading WIP ageing, budget-to-actual, hours by grade against plan, unsigned change requests and a weekly status that says amber for six weeks running.
where_it_helps.what_it_does: Ranks live engagements by likelihood of write-off using leading indicators the firm already records — grade mix drifting senior against plan, hours accruing to a phase marked complete, WIP ageing past the billing cycle, change requests raised but unsigned, a sudden fall in time entered on an active matter — and routes the top few to a named person weekly.
where_it_helps.what_it_needs: Matter and phase coding that people use, budgets held in the system rather than in a partner's spreadsheet, change control that produces a record, and — the hard precondition — someone with the standing to make a partner have the scope conversation. Without that last one the flag has nowhere to go.
where_it_helps.what_it_saves: Mechanism: moves the discovery of an overrun from the final bill, where the remedy is a write-off, to around 60% completion, where the remedy is a conversation. Order of magnitude: recovers a fraction of current write-offs, in the tens of percent of the flagged population at best. An estimate, heavily dependent on engagement size and how disciplined change control already is, and one you can only validate by tracking flagged matters against unflagged ones for two or three quarters.
where_it_helps.failure_mode: The model learns which partners always write off and flags their matters permanently, so the list stops being read. Or it fires on the first honest amber and teaches managers to report green, which destroys the very indicator the system depends on. Prediction on a small book of large heterogeneous engagements is statistically thin — a practice closing forty matters a year cannot support a calibrated probability, so treat the output as a prompt for a review, never as a number to put in a forecast.

where_it_does_not.claim: Fine-tune a model on all the firm's accumulated work product to build a single firm brain.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Confidentiality in this sector binds information to the matter, not to the firm. Engagement letters, outside counsel guidelines and the professional rules all assume you can put information back in a box — for an ethical wall, for a lateral hire's conflict, for a client exercising a contractual destruction right, for a matter that has hit its retention date. Trained weights cannot be un-learned document by document, and you cannot tell a client's auditor which of their documents influenced an output. Retrieval with a permission check at query time is revocable and auditable; a fine-tune is neither. The engineering argument for training is usually about answer quality, and the quality gap over well-built retrieval does not come close to paying for an unbounded and unprovable confidentiality position. The narrow exception worth arguing about is a tune on house style and document structure using material stripped of client facts — which is a formatting project, not a firm brain, and should not be sold as one.

where_it_does_not.claim: AI means you can reduce graduate, trainee or analyst intake.
where_it_does_not.why_not: The work AI takes first is the work juniors learn on — first drafts, tie-outs, document review, research. Cut intake and the saving arrives immediately while the consequence arrives in five years as a hole in the grade you cannot hire into, because everyone else made the same cut. The leverage pyramid is also how the firm prices: fewer juniors means a richer grade mix on every matter, which raises cost per engagement in a market where clients benchmark blended rates. And the review burden does not shrink — someone who never did the drafting reviews a machine draft slowly and badly, so you have traded a training investment for a permanent supervision deficit, in a sector where supervision is a regulated obligation with a named person attached to it.

where_it_does_not.claim: Price AI-assisted work at a premium, or add an AI or technology surcharge to the bill.
where_it_does_not.why_not: For US lawyers this is close to settled: under the ABA's 2024 guidance a lawyer billing hourly must bill the time actually spent rather than the time the task would once have taken, may not bill a client for learning the tool for general practice (as opposed to a tool that client specifically asked for), and may pass a per-use AI charge through only as a disclosed out-of-pocket expense at actual cost, not as a marked-up line or a share of a subscription that is plainly overhead. Accountants, consultants and engineers are not bound by that fee rule, but they meet the same wall commercially: client billing guidelines increasingly require the efficiency to be passed on and require disclosure of AI use on substantive work, and legal-ops and procurement functions now benchmark this openly, so the surcharge is a conversation you will lose. The real answer is uncomfortable and structural: efficiency only becomes margin under fixed fee, capped fee or retainer. Fix the pricing model or accept that the efficiency belongs to the client.

where_it_does_not.claim: Automated conflicts clearance — the system checks conflicts and clears the matter.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Conflicts is a legal determination with a bright-line consequence: disqualification, fee disgorgement, and a claim. Entity resolution across corporate family trees, funds, SPVs, trading names and post-merger renames produces false negatives on exactly the structures that matter, and false positives that stall a live deal while someone unpicks them. A model can surface candidate matches, rank them and pull the relevant prior engagement history — that is genuinely useful and saves the conflicts team real time. It cannot clear, because clearing requires a judgement about the relationship and the information held, and the sanction for getting it wrong falls on a named person who must be able to say why they decided as they did. The same reasoning applies to independence checks on the audit side, where the consequence is the opinion itself.

where_it_does_not.claim: An AI resourcing engine that allocates people to engagements automatically.
where_it_does_not.why_not: Staffing is the firm's principal development and political instrument, not an optimisation problem. Partners will override the allocation, the overrides will not be recorded with a reason, and within two quarters the system is a record of decisions it did not make. The input data is the deeper problem: skills and experience profiles are maintained by nobody, and pipeline probabilities are entered by the person whose forecast they are. Optimise on utilisation and you will systematically staff the strongest people onto the largest matters, which maximises this quarter and destroys client continuity and the development path at once. There is also a regulatory edge: in the EU, AI used to allocate tasks or to inform promotion decisions is classified as high-risk, which is a conformity and documentation burden most firms have not priced. A scheduler that surfaces clashes and bench risk to a human resourcing manager is worth having; an engine that decides is not.

where_it_does_not.claim: Deliverable-grade drafting — it writes the memo, the report or the valuation and the partner just sends it.
where_it_does_not.why_not: The expensive input is the reviewing partner's time, and that time does not shrink; reviewing an unfamiliar draft for a fabricated authority or a wrong figure is slower per page than reviewing a junior you have trained. The public record settles the argument about whether verification actually happens: the publicly maintained AI Hallucination Cases database had logged over 1,600 court decisions worldwide involving fabricated AI-generated citations by mid-2026, against roughly 200 a year earlier, and a practising lawyer rather than a litigant in person was the responsible party in something like 650 of them. Every one of those went through a professional who intended to check. Under deadline, at volume, verification is the step that gets dropped, and the failure is non-obvious by construction because a fabricated citation looks exactly like a real one.

preconditions: Every hour, document and email is attributable to a matter and a phase, and the budget for that phase lives in the practice management system rather than in a partner's spreadsheet. Time capture, risk detection and realisation analysis are all the same dependency wearing different names: if your coding taxonomy is aspirational, none of them work and no amount of model quality compensates.

The access model already works without AI. You can answer, today, from the system rather than from memory: who can see this document, on what basis, and when does it have to be destroyed. Information barriers enforced in the DMS, current matter-team membership, lateral screens, applied retention schedules. Retrieval does not create this problem, it industrialises whatever you already have — and the predictable first serious incident in this sector is a retrieval layer indexing a file share whose permissions nobody had audited in six years.

A stated position in your engagement terms and a live register of client restrictions. Which clients' outside counsel guidelines prohibit AI, which require prior written permission and disclosure of the specific tool, which demand the efficiency be passed through. Boilerplate consent buried in an engagement letter is not informed consent to a tool that ingests confidential information — the client has to understand what the tool does with the data and what limits its use. On tax return information the bar is higher again: consent must be specific, in a prescribed form, and in a separate document.

A named individual owns each output and has the standing to act on it — in practice the engagement partner for a drafted scope, the timekeeper for a rewritten narrative, the practice group head or risk partner for a flagged matter. Not a committee, not the tool, and not the innovation function that bought it. Where the flag has no owner with authority to make a partner have an awkward conversation, the system becomes a weekly report nobody opens, which is the most common way these programmes die quietly.

The pricing decision is made before deployment, in writing. What happens to an hour that is no longer needed on an hourly matter? If the honest answer is 'revenue falls', say so and pick the part of the book you are moving to fixed or capped fee first. Deploying efficiency into a pure hourly book without that decision produces rational non-adoption by the people whose compensation depends on hours, and everyone will blame the technology rather than the compensation model.

Prompts, retrieved context and generated drafts are treated as firm records from day one — inside the retention schedule, inside legal hold, inside the matter file where they belong. They are discoverable, they may be privileged or may destroy privilege depending on how they were handled and who saw them, and deciding this after an incident is not a decision, it is a discovery exercise.

A reconstructable trail exists for anything that touches a client deliverable or an invoice: which tool and model version, which documents were retrieved, which human approved, on what date. Every professional standard in this sector puts responsibility on a named person, and under all of them 'the tool produced it' is not a defence. If you cannot reconstruct the decision months later for a client audit, a regulator, a government cost auditor or your insurer, you do not have a controlled system — you have an undocumented one that has not failed yet.

regulation.name: ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct and Formal Opinion 512 (US legal practice)
regulation.citation: ABA Standing Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility, Formal Opinion 512, "Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools" (29 July 2024); ABA Model Rules 1.1 cmt. [8], 1.4, 1.5, 1.6, 3.3, 5.1 and 5.3
regulation.what_it_requires: Competence extends to understanding a generative AI tool's benefits and risks before use. Client-informed consent is required before inputting confidential client information into a tool that may use or retain it — self-learning tools in particular; general engagement-letter boilerplate does not carry it. Candour to the tribunal means output is verified before it is filed. Lawyers remain responsible for supervising the output under the same rules that govern supervising people. On fees: a lawyer billing hourly must bill for actual time spent and not the time the task would otherwise have taken; may not bill a client for time spent learning the tool for general practice, though the opinion allows charging for learning a particular tool the client specifically requested for that matter; and may pass through per-use AI charges only as a disclosed out-of-pocket expense at actual cost, while flat subscription access is overhead. Note the Model Rules are adopted state by state and most US jurisdictions have now issued their own AI guidance — check the one you practise in rather than relying on the ABA opinion alone.

regulation.name: AICPA Code of Professional Conduct — confidentiality and third-party service providers
regulation.citation: AICPA Code of Professional Conduct, ET §1.700.001 (Confidential Client Information Rule) and interpretation ET §1.700.040 (Disclosing Information to a Third-Party Service Provider)
regulation.what_it_requires: A hosted AI service that processes client information is a third-party service provider. Before disclosing confidential client information to it, the member must either obtain specific client consent, or enter into a contractual agreement with the provider to maintain confidentiality together with reasonable assurance that the provider has appropriate procedures to prevent unauthorised release. In practice this means reading the AI vendor's data-processing and training-use terms and being able to show you did — and it means a consumer subscription with no such contract does not satisfy the rule. Note the Code offers these as alternatives; the common risk-management position is to do both.

regulation.name: US tax return information — disclosure and use restrictions
regulation.citation: 26 U.S.C. §7216 and §6713; Treas. Reg. §§301.7216-2 and 301.7216-3; Rev. Proc. 2013-14 (form of consent for Form 1040-series filers)
regulation.what_it_requires: A tax return preparer may not disclose or use a taxpayer's tax return information without prior written consent unless a specific exception applies. Consent must be knowing and voluntary, must identify the specific recipient of a disclosure or describe the particular use authorised, and — for 1040-series filers under Rev. Proc. 2013-14 — consents to use and consents to disclose cannot be carried in the same document. If the taxpayer declines, the preparer may not solicit again for a substantially similar purpose. Breach carries criminal penalty under §7216 and civil penalty under §6713 — this is a harder rule than general confidentiality, and pushing return data through a third-party AI service without qualifying consent or a qualifying exception is squarely within it.

regulation.name: EU Artificial Intelligence Act — transparency, AI literacy, and high-risk HR use
regulation.citation: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 50 (applying from 2 August 2026), Article 4 (AI literacy, applying from 2 February 2025) and Annex III point 4 (employment and worker management)
regulation.what_it_requires: Article 50 obligations apply regardless of whether a system is high-risk. People must be informed when they are interacting with an AI system; providers must mark synthetic output in machine-readable form; and AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must be disclosed as such. Article 4 requires providers and deployers to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff operating these systems on their behalf — which for a firm means documented, role-specific training, not an all-staff email. Most professional-services delivery use will not be high-risk, but AI used in recruitment, and in decisions on promotion or the allocation of tasks, falls under Annex III point 4 and is high-risk — which reaches firms' own HR and resourcing systems. Confidence is marked likely rather than certain on one point only: amending legislation under discussion through 2026 has proposed transitional relief on the machine-readable marking requirement for systems already on the market, so confirm the applicable date for marking before relying on it.

regulation.name: SRA warning notice on misuse of AI (England and Wales)
regulation.citation: Solicitors Regulation Authority, warning notice "Misuse of AI" (17 August 2026), citing SRA Principles 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7 and provisions of both the Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs and the Code of Conduct for Firms — including competence (para 3.2), supervision and accountability for work carried out through others (paras 3.5-3.6; Firms Code paras 4.3-4.4), duties to the court (paras 2.4-2.7) and client confidentiality (para 6.3)
regulation.what_it_requires: Firms and individuals must have appropriate oversight and controls over AI use; the individual remains responsible for the work produced and the advice given whether or not AI was used. Authorities must be checked to be genuine, relevant and verifiably cited before anything is put before a court. Client data must stay within a secure environment, with safeguards against unauthorised access and against use for model training — entering client information into public AI tools risks a confidentiality breach and loss of privilege. Supervisors remain accountable for supervised work, and the notice warns that failing to have proper regard to it risks disciplinary action. Treat this as an enforcement priority: the SRA was reported at publication to have received in the order of 40 reports of potential AI misuse over the preceding year, with open investigations covering inaccurate citations, supervision and confidentiality. That report figure comes from SRA statements and press coverage around the notice rather than from the notice text itself.

regulation.name: Data protection — processor obligations for client personal data
regulation.citation: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Article 28; UK GDPR Article 28 as retained
regulation.what_it_requires: Where client matter data contains personal data, any AI vendor processing it on your behalf is a processor and requires a written contract meeting Article 28 — documented instructions, confidentiality undertakings, security measures, no sub-processing without authorisation, deletion or return at the end of the engagement, and audit rights. If the vendor uses your inputs to improve its own models, it is arguably acting as a controller for that purpose and the arrangement does not sit within Article 28 at all. Transfers outside the UK/EEA need a lawful transfer mechanism, and a consumer-tier account almost never provides any of this.

regulation.name: US government contract timekeeping (firms billing federal work)
regulation.citation: FAR 31.201-2(d) (adequate records to support claimed costs); DFARS 252.242-7006 Accounting System Administration, criteria (c)(9) (timekeeping system identifying employees' labour by intermediate or final cost objective) and (c)(10) (labour distribution)
regulation.what_it_requires: Records must be adequate to demonstrate that claimed costs were incurred, are allocable to the contract and comply with the cost principles; without adequate support the contracting officer may disallow the cost. The DFARS clause requires a timekeeping system that identifies labour by cost objective and a labour distribution system that charges it correctly. DCAA's long-standing audit position — guidance rather than regulation, but the position you will be audited against — is that labour is recorded daily and contemporaneously by the employee who performed the work, with certification, supervisory approval, controls preventing backdating, and an audit trail on every correction. This is the rule that most directly constrains AI-assisted time capture: a draft proposed by a system and confirmed by the employee the same day may be defensible; a fortnight reconstructed by a model and approved in bulk is not, and a floor check or a pattern of uniform machine-phrased narratives will draw exactly that finding.

regulation.name: Responsible charge and sealing of engineering documents (US state licensure)
regulation.citation: NSPE Board of Ethical Review Case 24-2, "Use of Artificial Intelligence in Engineering Practice" (2024). The underlying obligation sits in state professional engineering statutes and board rules, which vary — described, not cited.
regulation.what_it_requires: State professional engineering statutes and board rules require that plans, drawings, specifications and reports be sealed by the licensed engineer in responsible charge — meaning actively engaged in the engineering process from conception to completion, with engineering decisions made personally or by others under the engineer's supervisory direction and control. Reviewing a document after preparation, without involvement in the design and development process, does not meet that definition. The NSPE Board of Ethical Review considered AI use in engineering practice and found that AI-generated technical work requires at least the same scrutiny as human-created work, and that an engineer who did not maintain responsible charge over it fell short of the Code. The operative point for any firm adopting design or calculation automation: 'the software generated it' has never been a defence, and the seal is a personal attestation that does not become a shared one because a model contributed. Check your own state board's rules and any AI-specific guidance it has issued; these vary and several boards have moved recently.

sectors.economics:
The licence is the small number and the only one that appears in the business case. Per-seat general assistants run roughly $30-100 per user per month at list; sector-specific legal research, audit or engagement tools run several hundred per user per month. For a 300-fee-earner firm that is a low six-figure annual line before the discount you will negotiate and before the seats you buy for people who log in twice. Treat those as list-price estimates that move with volume and term. They are not the cost.

Integration into the system of record is the cost nobody budgets. Every application above ends by writing back into practice management, billing or the DMS — the Elite and Aderant class of system, the iManage and NetDocuments class of repository, an ERP for the consulting and engineering side (named as categories to locate the problem, not as recommendations). Reading out of these is usually straightforward. Writing into billing is where projects stall for two quarters, because the billing system is the firm's cash, its change control is owned by someone who was not in the AI meeting, and the upgrade window is annual. The longest single task is almost never the model: it is remediating the matter and phase taxonomy so the data means what the system claims. Budget integration and data remediation at several multiples of the first-year licence, and in months rather than weeks. That is an estimate and it scales with how many systems of record you have — a firm that merged twice and never consolidated should assume the high end.

The human review does not disappear, it relocates — and it relocates onto non-chargeable time, which is the same utilisation number the programme was meant to improve. Every application above has a named reviewer: someone confirms the reconstructed timesheet, someone approves the rewritten narrative, a partner signs the drafted scope. For the first six months review is slower than doing the work, because reviewing an unfamiliar draft for a plausible error is harder than writing a familiar one. Budget it explicitly as a line, at a real percentage of the time notionally saved. Firms that leave it unbudgeted do not avoid the cost; they push it onto the same three seniors and get a supervision failure with a professional-rules name on it.

Governance and documentation is a permanent part-time job, not a project. An AI register, a data-flow record per tool, processor contracts and transfer assessments, a live map of which clients' billing guidelines restrict or condition AI use, model and version logging, a retention and legal-hold position on prompts and outputs, and the annual evidence pack for clients who now audit this. Call it 0.2-0.5 FTE of risk or compliance capacity for a mid-size firm on an ongoing basis, plus external privacy or regulatory advice at setup — an estimate that rises sharply with the number of jurisdictions and professional regimes you operate under, since a firm holding legal, audit and engineering work is answering to three different sets of rules with three different named-person obligations.

Then the failure cost, which is the number that should govern the decision. It comes in two shapes. A confidentiality breach across a client boundary is not priced as a fine; it is priced as the engagement and often the client relationship, so the honest reserve is the annual fee income of the largest matter the system can see, plus the notification and the regulatory report. A fabricated authority or a wrong figure reaching a tribunal, a filing or a signed report costs the write-off, the remedial work at your expense, the referral to the regulator, and the paragraph carrying your firm's name. That is an observed frequency rather than a hypothetical: the publicly maintained AI Hallucination Cases database, which only logs decisions where a court or tribunal found or clearly implied reliance on hallucinated material, held over 1,600 such decisions worldwide by mid-2026, up from roughly 200 a year earlier and growing at something like five to eight a day, with the United States accounting for the large majority. Read that as a floor on incidence, since it counts only the instances a court caught and wrote down. The third cost sits in the renewal file: professional indemnity and E&O markets are now asking AI questions at renewal, standardised generative-AI exclusion endorsements have appeared on the general-liability side, and professional-lines restrictions are so far mostly manuscript wording aimed at advice generated by or primarily based on AI output without human professional review. Read the endorsement before you deploy, not after, and be able to describe your human review step to the underwriter in a sentence.

Finally, the arithmetic that decides whether any of this is worth doing. In an hourly book, efficiency is negative revenue. A matter that billed 100 hours and now takes 70 bills 30% less, and under the US fee rules a lawyer cannot bill the 100. The saving only becomes margin under fixed fee, capped fee or retainer, where the hours you do not spend are hours you keep. So the business case for AI in professional services is not a cost-reduction case — it is a pricing-model case, and the firms where it pays are the ones that moved a defined slice of work to fixed price first and then made it cheaper to deliver. Anyone selling you the cost-reduction version of this has not read your income statement.
sectors.first_step: Take the last complete billing cycle for one practice group. Pull every line item that was discounted, written down or written off, and classify each by hand into one of five causes: vague or blocked narrative, wrong task or phase code, work outside the agreed scope, agreed rate discount, or time recorded more than 48 hours after the work was done. Count each cause in money and in hours. One cycle, one group, no tooling — a spreadsheet and two days of someone's attention. That distribution tells you which of the applications above is worth anything to you and which is someone else's marketing, and it is also the baseline you will be measured against afterwards. Most firms that do this find the money is sitting in coding and late time capture rather than in drafting speed, which is the opposite of what they were about to buy.
